articles.title: Iran's 'new Hezbollah:' How powerful are the Houthis now?
articles.summary: After Houthi victories in Yemen, the group's importance in the US-Iran war has grown. Previously Lebanon's Hezbollah was considered most significant in Iran's "axis of resistance." Now the Houthis…

image.caption: A 2025 UN report said the Houthi group had likely recruited as many as 350,000 fighters, up from around 30,000 a decade agoImage: Hamza Ali/IMAGO

blocks.text: After recent events in Yemen, a small crowd marched down an Iraqi street holding signs that were almost identical to those seen not too long ago further south.

The signs said, "death to America" and insulted Saudi Arabia and Israel, with slogans very similar to those used by the Houthi rebel group in Yemen. The men in the Iraqi video are members of one of Iraq's Shiite Muslim paramilitary groups.

Both the Iraqi paramilitaries and the Houthi group in Yemen are part of what is known as the "axis of resistance" in the Middle East, groups supported by Iran that often act at Iran's behest. Other members are Hezbollah in Lebanon and Hamas in Gaza.

After the US and Israel began attacking Iran in late February 2026, "axis of resistance" members responded by targeting sites associated with the US or Israel. But up until recently, the Houthi group had remained more or less on the sidelines.

However their latest military campaign, which has seen Houthi fighters take further control of the Yemeni coast and several islands in the Red Sea, "sets up conditions to establish… an axis of resistance-controlled body of water as part of [an] effort to assert control over regional oil exports," US-based research organization the Institute for the Study of War explained last week.
Iran and the US are already fighting for control over the Strait of Hormuz, another important waterway for oil exports and trade.
In Iran, hardline regime-supporting newspapers published laudatory articles about the Houthis' territorial gains.

The gains "greatly increased the weight of Sanaa [the Yemeni capital, under Houthi control] as a branch of resistance in the ongoing regional war," one of Iran's most conservative newspapers, Kayhan, wrote.

Supporters of the Iranian government have been holding nightly gatherings in major cities across the country since the US-Iran war began and this week, at the 200th such event, crowds chanted "you are my soul, O Yemen!"
The 'new Hezbollah?'

This was the kind of praise previously lavished on another "axis of resistance" group, Hezbollah. But Hezbollah's armed faction, degraded by recent Israeli attacks and the loss of their base in Syria, looks less intimidating these days.

And the Houthis now appear to be doing things that Hezbollah couldn't — for example, bringing down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet this week using a missile the group said it modified itself. Hezbollah has managed to shoot down large Israeli drones and has targeted fighter jets but never hit any.
Could the Houthis be taking Hezbollah's place as the potentially most important and possibly even more dangerous force in the "axis of resistance?"
The Houthis haven't had to fight Israel — they are too far away geographically.

"But I think they [the Houthis] have become more valuable than Hezbollah could ever be," says Farea al-Muslimi, a research fellow focused on Yemen at UK think tank Chatham House. "Of course, Hezbollah had decades of experience and was the one who built the Houthis' capacity over years. But the Houthis have now exceeded them."

The Houthis are "increasingly performing a similar strategic function for Iran [as Hezbollah] and in some respects a more useful one," confirms Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer at the School of Security Studies at King's College London.

"Hezbollah gave Tehran deterrence against Israel from Lebanon. The Houthis give Iran leverage over Saudi Arabia, Israel and global shipping," he told DW. "So I think their strategic importance to Tehran has risen sharply as Hezbollah has come under much greater pressure."

Al-Muslimi notes that Houthi leaders, including current chief Abdul Malik al-Houthi, were devoted fans of Hezbollah leader Nassan Hasrallah, killed by Israel in 2024 and seen as a hero because of his organization's part in forcing Israel to withdraw from Lebanon in 2000.

"You can see how he even tries to imitate Nasrallah in his speeches," al-Muslimi, who co-founded the Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies, told DW. "And now Abdul Malik al-Houthi has more leverage than Nasrallah ever had."

Nasrallah was once seen as "the fixer" for the "axis of resistance," he notes, a leader who acted as a conduit between the different factions, giving orders to Iran-supported fighters in Lebanon, Yemen and Syria.
Al-Houthi is likely moving into that role now, al-Muslimi believes, pointing to the fact that one recent attack on Saudi pipelines actually came from Iraqi axis members.
Iranian proxy or ally?
Unlike with Hezbollah though, there's still disagreement over exactly how much control Iran has over them.

A review of press by the Iraq-based outlet Amwaj showed that while Iranian media celebrated Houthi gains as a victory for Iran's "axis of resistance," Houthi-run channels were more focused on their own fight against Saudi Arabia, which has set up a blockade on Houthi-controlled territories.
Krieg believes the biggest difference between the Houthis and Hezbollah is autonomy.

"The Houthis… have their own leadership, ideology, domestic constituency and territorial project," he pointed out. "Tehran can enable them, arm them and benefit from their actions, but it cannot necessarily switch them on and off at will."

blocks.caption: The Houthis have not backed away from their hardline positions in the US-Israel-Iran war, which, one expert says, 'gives them a psychological advantage and makes them the heroes of the axis of resistance'Image: Khaled Abdullah/REUTERS

blocks.text: Other observers note that in the past, the Houthis moved ahead with certain military plans despite objections from Iran. Tehran has also denied having anything to do with this latest campaign.

But al-Muslimi isn't so sure. He says that over the past two years, the Houthis have come a lot closer to Iran. There are regular reports of Iran sending sophisticated weaponry to the Houthis. In July, sources inside Iran told Reuters news agency that Iranian leadership had discussed with the Houthis having them close off the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

"Even as Houthi leaders frame their actions in local terms, their alignment with Tehran appears to have tightened," Allison Minor, previously the US deputy special envoy for Yemen, said in Foreign Affairs magazine last week.
Can the Houthis be beaten?

The one thing everyone does agree on is that the Houthis will be hard to rein in. Past military campaigns by Saudi Arabia, the US and other countries have failed. Sanctions and economic pressure tend not to impact either because the Houthis don't operate within the international financial system.

The Houthis take a "zero sum approach," al-Muslimi explains. They collect taxes but don't pay salaries or provide public services; everything goes towards fighting. The group's founding father argued that contemporary Muslim societies were too "soft," and that poverty and hardship are a divine test.

blocks.caption: The United Nations say that fighting in Yemen has displaced at least 125,000 people since the start of September 2026Image: REUTERS

blocks.text: That's very different from Hezbollah: The Lebanese group also has a political branch at home, and offers social welfare services. It must also carefully balance relationships with other demographic groups in Lebanon.
The Houthis have none of those restraints.
"They don't care if the Israelis bomb the airport or the US bombs a hospital," al-Muslimi says. "It actually serves them very well because their ideology is all about martyrdom and sacrifice."
Which, he suggests, makes them potentially more dangerous than Hezbollah, especially for Yemeni civilians.
"They are a major international threat," he agrees, "but they're the biggest threat ever to the idea of a republic and citizenship in Yemen's history."

articles.title: Trump announces White House ban on CNN, other media outlets
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump announced an immediate White House ban on a number of news outlets, including CNN.

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks at the White House on Thursday. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·Breaking
U.S. President Donald Trump announced an immediate White House ban on a number of news outlets, including CNN.
U.S. president accuses outlets of reporting 'fiction and lies,' vows more will be barred
Trump, in a social media post, said MS NOW and Politico are also barred, adding, "other fake news media outlets to follow."

"Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report fiction and lies when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America," he wrote.
It is the administration's latest test of constitutional First Amendment protections.

It follows Trump's decision in February 2025 to keep Associated Press journalists out of the Oval Office, Air Force One and other events too small for a full press corps, in retaliation for the news outlet's decision not to follow his lead in changing the Gulf of Mexico's name.
The Associated Press filed suit and the case is ongoing.

Trump has long bristled at news coverage he sees as unfavourable to him and has a history of filing lawsuits against news organizations and lashing out at individual reporters in person or over social media.
Since returning to office, Trump has pursued legal action against The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, the BBC and other news outlets.
With files from The Associated Press

articles.title: Ryanair boss apologizes for calling other airlines 'rapists'
articles.summary: The airline CEO had used the term to describe other airlines with high fares. His comments were criticized by officials both in Ireland and the UK.

image.caption: O'Leary has been Ryanair's CEO since 1994 [FILE: March 3, 2026]Image: Kuba Steżycki/REUTERS

blocks.text: Ryanair CEO Michael O'Leary "sincerely and unreservedly" apologized on Friday for recent remarks in which he described other airlines as "rapists" because of their high fares.
O'Leary said 'careless' remarks caused 'considerable upset and offense'

"I have come to realize, however, that the word I used too carelessly has caused considerable upset and offense to a wide number of people, especially victims and survivors," O'Leary said in a video posted online.
It's a U-turn from earlier, when O'Leary refused to apologize for the comments. Dublin Rape Crisis Centre chief executive Rachel Morrogh said O'Leary trivialized rape with the remarks.
"Since I certainly did not trivialize the heinous crime of rape, I will certainly not be issuing any apology," O'Leary said last week.
O'Leary had originally made the remarks to journalists at Ryanair's company headquarters in Ireland.

blocks.caption: Ryanair is known for its cheap, no-frills flights around Europe [FILE: September 14, 2019]Image: Nicolas Economou/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: "You might find some people will choose not to fly with Ryanair — but you know they'll be overrun with the people abandoning Aer Lingus, Lufthansa, BA, and others desperate to get to Ryanair's low fares because they can't afford to fly with high-fare rapists around Europe," O'Leary said.
O'Leary's remarks met with backlash in Ireland, UK
O'Leary is one of Ireland's richest and most prominent businesspeople. His "rapist" remarks were met with criticism from leaders both in Ireland and the UK.

Ireland's Taoiseach Michael Martin said he was "disappointed" by O'Leary's comments and added the Ryanair chief "should just stand back and reflect and listen to the voice of women" regarding the issue.

Martin told RTE Radio One that rape is "an awful, awful violation of a person, which leaves a terrible trauma." However, the Irish leader of the centrist to center-right Fianna Fail party did not call on O'Leary to explicitly apologize.

Ireland's deputy prime minister, or Tanaiste, Simon Harris said O'Leary's comments were an "inappropriate use of language." However, Harris of the center-right Fine Gael party also did not explicitly call on O'Leary to apologize.

Laura Harmon, a senator belonging to Ireland's center-left opposition Labour Party, said O'Leary must apologize for the comments. "The casual use of the word 'rapist' to describe prices of his competitors is deeply shocking and could be traumatizing for any survivor of sexual abuse," Harmon said.
Fact check: Female politicians hurt by sexualized deepfakes
The UK's Transport Minister Heidi Alexander of the British Labour Party, in comments to LBC radio, said "Mr. O'Leary is often quick to share his considered thoughts with me and with the wider world."

"I would say that women who have been raped and who have been subjected to such appalling violence, I'm not sure they're going to be rushing to book tickets with him, let's be honest," Alexander said.
O'Leary had earlier made controversial remarks regarding obese and Muslim passengers. He had also floated a fee for using a toilet mid-flight and expressed climate denial.

articles.title: Rogue AI swarm used a University of Toronto link-shortening tool to communicate
articles.summary: A swarm of rogue OpenAI agents that hijacked a German website in the spring reportedly also used at least 10 other websites for unsanctioned communications earlier this year, including a…

image.caption: New graduates from the University of Toronto walk at the university’s St. George campus in Toronto in June 2025. Rogue OpenAI agents used more than 10 websites, including a University of Toronto tool, to communicate outside their assigned tasks. (Alex Lupul/CBC)

blocks.text: Canada·New

A swarm of rogue OpenAI agents that hijacked a German website in the spring reportedly also used at least 10 other websites for unsanctioned communications earlier this year, including a link-shortening tool at the University of Toronto.
U of T says there was no security breach or impact on the university's digital properties

A swarm of rogue OpenAI agents that hijacked a German website in the spring reportedly also used more than 10 other websites for unsanctioned communications earlier this year, including a link-shortening tool at the University of Toronto.
The university disabled the link shortener's use as a message board after learning that OpenAI agents may have used it, the university said in a statement to CBC News on Friday.
"OpenAI subsequently contacted the university about the possible activity by AI agents, which occurred in June," the statement said.

While the university said there was no security breach and no impact on its digital properties, reports of more rogue AI incidents come amid global concerns that OpenAI and other artificial intelligence companies are losing control of their own technology.

Reuters, which first reported the University of Toronto activity, used data from six sets of independent investigators to show that the agents' rogue activity was more widespread than previously disclosed — and, according to the investigators, probably wider still.

"It’s almost certain that there’s more going on here that we just don’t know about," said Andrew Yoon, a researcher with the California nonprofit CivAI. He told Reuters he tallied 18 previously undisclosed sites used by the agents between May and July. Investigators disagreed on the exact number of discovered sites, but all concurred it was more than 10.
Trump dismisses AI warnings as industry CEOs urge slowdown

On Sept. 4, researchers reported that a swarm of OpenAI agents hijacked a German-language wiki site and turned it into an improvised messaging platform for cheating on tests. The researchers told Reuters the agents left similar messages on the other sites, including U of T.

OpenAI has not publicly explained how or why its agents used third-party sites as improvised message boards, but the researchers who first identified the activity said it was likely because OpenAI had tasked the agents with answering a series of demanding research questions while permitting them only to scan the web for answers, not post anything.

Despite those restrictions, the agents still found ways to talk to one another by taking advantage of quirks that allowed users to make edits using non-standard commands, similar to how students forbidden from talking to one another during an exam can still share answers by scrawling notes on a bathroom stall.
Carney has called for international oversight

Mohit Rajhans of Think Start Inc., which advises businesses on AI adoption, told CBC News Network the duty of care lies with the tech companies to "come clean about how malicious some of this tech is."

He applauded Prime Minister Mark Carney's call for a global "technology stability" body to oversee AI safety, comparable to the international Financial Stability Board, though Rajhans said he's worried that any third party will be "bullied out of the conversation" by the half-dozen major players in Silicon Valley.

OpenAI did not directly address questions from Reuters about how many sites its agents used to communicate or say why it kept the activity under wraps for months. The company did not immediately reply to an interview request from CBC News.

items: OpenAI asks California court to dismiss lawsuits over Tumbler Ridge shooting
OpenAI flags 6 new examples of 'concerning' AI behaviour

blocks.text: The company announced Wednesday it would keep closer watch on "misalignment" — the industry term for when an AI system strays from the user's and developer's intent or fails to follow human values and safety rules. The company also released six previously unreported instances of rogue AI, but none that mentioned the university.

The company says it has not found any instances as serious as the so-called Hugging Face incident. In that case, around 1,200 agents tasked by OpenAI with working on problems build a covert message board where they collaborated to cheat on their tests and then tried to cover their tracks. About 700 of them ultimately hacked into online platform Hugging Face before they were discovered.
With files from Reuters

YouTube star also called on 'wealthy white' celebrities to match her donations

Ms. Rachel says she will be donating $1 million US to the Palestine Children’s Relief Fund (PCRF), matching the donation pledged by rapper Macklemore after he was ousted from Ed Sheeran’s U.S. tour over his pro-Palestinian remarks onstage.

The American YouTube star and educator, whose full name is Rachel Accurso, made the pledge in an Instagram post on Thursday, inviting "every wealthy white celebrity to match it and speak out against the genocide in Gaza."

"Over 20,000 precious Palestinian children have been killed and children continue to be killed every day," she wrote. "We have a moral obligation to use our privilege and platforms to protect children and human rights."

Accurso, whose YouTube channel boasts more than 21 million subscribers, became a global ambassador for PCRF last September. The children’s entertainer has been a vocal advocate for the protection and rights of children in Gaza, using her platform in recent years to draw attention to the humanitarian crisis there.
Macklemore, whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty, responded to the post by commenting, "Wowwww…. Love you so much."

The Can’t Hold Us rapper announced on Instagram on Wednesday that he would be donating the entirety of his $1-million net earnings from Sheeran’s tour to six organizations aiding the Palestinian people.

Macklemore was dropped as an opening act from Sheeran’s The Loop tour earlier this week after videos showed him saying "Free Palestine" repeatedly onstage to a cheering crowd and expressing solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza and the Israeli-occupied West Bank at a Sept. 4 concert.

items: Remaining supporting acts quit Ed Sheeran tour amid backlash over Macklemore ousting

blocks.text: In a speech at the second show on Sept. 5, the Seattle-born Grammy winner addressed Jewish audience members, saying, "criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, is in no way a criticism of you.
"My message is for peace — love for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect and equality."
His remarks drew a flurry of criticism from pro-Israel groups and prompted several venues in the U.S. to threaten to cancel the show if the rapper wasn’t removed.
Macklemore later said his removal from the tour was co-ordinated by American billionaire businessman and New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft.

In a statement shared with CBC News on Monday, Kraft, a staunch supporter of Israel, confirmed that he opposed Macklemore performing at Massachusetts' Gillette Stadium, which he also owns, stating that his stadium would "not provide a platform for hate speech." He added that Macklemore spread divisiveness through "selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas."

Following Macklemore’s exit, backlash against Sheeran came fast and furious, with many critics slamming the singer’s apolitical stance. The Shape of You singer shared a lengthy statement on his Instagram on Tuesday, explaining that Macklemore "coming off tour was the promoter’s decision, it was not mine."
He added that while he tried to "build a bridge," the venues remained resolute.

Sheeran wrote that he was "appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine," adding that the "suffering and pain caused on both sides is a human tragedy." But he defended his decision not to take a public stance.
"I have my personal views on this devastating conflict," he wrote in part. "Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn’t mean I don’t have them, and it doesn’t mean I don’t care."

Hours after Sheeran shared the statement, all of his remaining supporting acts announced they were quitting the tour, including Irish folk band Boega, who also announced they would no longer serve as Sheeran’s backing band for the remaining U.S. tour dates.
It means that the tour now has no openers. Sheeran’s next show is scheduled for Philadelphia on Saturday.
On Wednesday, Kraft announced that both he and Sheeran have each pledged $2 million US toward humanitarian aid in the Gaza region, following a public challenge from Macklemore to match his donation.
In a statement posted to the official Gillette Stadium account on X, Kraft said that Sheeran had contacted him before the public challenge.

"Ed called me and asked me to commit $2 million to match his donation to aid the region to fight this humanitarian crisis," he wrote. "Ed now plans to reach out to other venue owners and our goal is to continue to work together to build bridges."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kayla McLean is a web journalist with CBC News in Toronto. She grew up in Brampton, Ont., and received her bachelor of arts in media production at Toronto Metropolitan University. Before joining CBC in 2024, she worked as a breaking news reporter at Global News Toronto — covering everything from crime, sports, festivals and politics. She also reported for Global News's current affairs show, The New Reality, covering stories with a focus on racial equality and climate justice. She also previously held positions as a chase producer and writer for CTV News Channel.

articles.title: Why Europe has been absent from the great AI safety debate
articles.summary:
Though Europe has measures that address how consumers might encounter AI, technology will impact them if the worst scenarios bear

Europe’s dilemma over AI was rendered in stark terms this…

blocks.text: Europe’s dilemma over AI was rendered in stark terms this week. The head of the continent’s central bank, Christine Lagarde, said Europeans have two options: shun the technology and lose out on growth; or embrace it and become dependent on tools developed by the US and China.

The great debate over AI safety that has erupted in recent days threatens to make the choice moot. If the worst scenarios come to bear – and experts have differing views on this – then the technology will impact the continent regardless.

Europe has largely been absent from the highest levels of that debate, a result of the continent’s longstanding inability to produce a Silicon Valley-scale titan like Apple, Google or newcomer OpenAI. While it is a powerhouse in regulation, much to the White House’s chagrin, its lack of an Anthropic or Nvidia-sized frontrunner in the AI race has diminished its voice in the safety debate.

Ursula von der Leyen, a powerful political figure on the continent as president of the European Commission, the EU’s executive arm, addressed the issue this week by saying she will “invite the main frontier labs for a discussion on how we can support ongoing industry efforts to pace the frontier”.

Her remarks gained nowhere as much traction as Donald Trump and China’s dismissal of a slowdown. Without the support of Washington or Beijing, any sort of pacing is impossible – with our without Europe’s input.

Lagarde’s speech on Monday underlined the continent’s relative weakness. She asserted that Europe must develop its own AI technology and build more datacentres in order to nullify the threat of being cut off by the US or China.
If Europe invests in its own AI tech, said Lagarde, “the threat of being cut off loses its force.” Self-sufficiency would also give Europe a chance to develop its own answer to the AI safety crisis.

Margrethe Vestager, who clashed with the US tech industry as the EU’s former competition commissioner, co-authored a report this week – A Transformative AI Strategy for Europe – that echoed Lagarde’s warning. AI threatens to accelerate a development already affecting Europe, where citizens “are already bearing the economic and social consequences of decisions taken elsewhere”, she says.

Solutions to this, according to the report, include building more datacentres – the central nervous systems of AI – and also to ensure the continent is resilient enough to withstand “AI crises” like a powerful model slipping out of control.

Vestager said that Europe does have a voice in the safety debate through its EU AI Act, the rare piece of AI legislation that sets out requirements for developers of “high-risk” AI systems to report safety incidents and address risks like a cutting-edge model evading control.
But she adds: “Europe must … build its own AI to strengthen the ecosystem, retain talent, and inspire innovation.”

Vestager acknowledges that if there is an existential threat, it requires a global solution; one that does not hand power to the US and China. And that requires a different kind of supranational body.

“As for existential threats to humanity, we must first assess the actual level of threat – then act with urgency. The UN general assembly is an opportunity to address this. It is vital to move beyond the US-China rivalry narrative. There must be space for humanity between the egos of leaders like President Xi and President Trump.”

Frederike Kaltheuner, an adviser to the AI Now Institute, a research body, says that Europe is dependent on US technology in ways that will be hard to undo, from search engines to chips to datacentres. But the narrative that Europe is grievously behind in the race depends on a particular view of artificial intelligence aggressively promoted by American tech bosses.
after newsletter promotion

Because of their doomsday warnings, “we are exclusively talking about AI in a very narrow, specific kind of way – namely, the idea that there is such a thing as the AI frontier, which is getting better and better, and that access to the frontier is the most important thing that Europe needs for its security and economy.”

The reality of the market points at something else, she says: many companies are not adopting so-called “frontier models” – like ChatGPT and Anthropic – because of high costs and fears over what might happen to their data.

If this trend continues, Europe may not be so terribly positioned: the EU AI Act has a number of pragmatic measures which address how consumers might encounter AI on a day-to-day basis, legislating over matters such as labelling AI content, and the use of AI in medicine and hiring.

“Europe has a competitiveness problem, that’s true,” says Itxaso Dominguez de Olazabal, a policy adviser at EDRI, a European digital rights organisation. But US tech boosters are “blaming it on laws and protections, and have promised that deregulation will make European companies more competitive … in a race to the bottom to see if we can catch big tech”.

Nonetheless, the EU AI act is not viewed as model legislation for other countries or a vehicle for a global slowdown. Georgina Kon, a partner at law firm Linklaters, says the act is unlikely to be adopted as a global benchmark for several reasons, including criticisms of the heavy compliance burden, which has led to delays in parts of the act becoming active, and a narrow territorial focus on Europe. Those criticisms have also meant that lawmakers elsewhere have looked to differentiate their approach to AI legislation from the EU’s.
“The EU AI Act is not something that everybody else in the world feels constrained by, although many tech companies will of course want to sell to the EU,” she says.

Big tech still has a vast customer base in Europe. Kaltheuner worries that the doomsday narratives will push Europe towards dependency, encouraging it to adopt US AI models across the economy out of ill-defined fears over being left behind.

“There’s a vision of the future where Europe’s economy, its public sector, its education system runs on models and on infrastructure that is controlled by a very small number of companies that happen to be also in the US. This would be a sovereignty problem.”

articles.title: Ebola: DR Congo outbreak not slowing, MSF warns
articles.summary: Doctors Without Borders has warned against premature optimism amid the DRC's largest-ever Ebola outbreak. "The outbreak is not shrinking, it is moving," an MSF official said, entering new and more…

image.caption: Medical workers have tried to promote dignified burials that nevertheless minimize post-mortem transmission Image: Dieudonne Dirole/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Medical charity Doctors Without Borders (MSF) said on Friday that "the race to contain the Ebola disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is far from over."

MSF issued the comments after DRC's government and the World Health Organization (WHO) had both spoken of signs of slowing transmission in some places earlier this week, prompting some relatively upbeat headlines and coverage.
The outbreak, which was first declared in mid-May but likely started spreading several months earlier, is the largest in DRC's national history and the fastest-spreading on record anywhere.
Did Ebola start spreading before officials even knew?
What did MSF say about the outbreak and its spread?

MSF — which has around 1,700 staff in the DRC, most of them Congolese — warned that while the observed spread was slowing in the initial epicenter of Ituri province, the number of new cases being recorded had not fallen on a national level.
"Assuming the outbreak is under control because some Ebola treatment centers are admitting fewer patients would be a mistake," MSF's emergency coordinator in DRC Anthony Kergosien said.

"The outbreak is not shrinking, it is moving: South Ubangi has become the seventh affected province, while North Kivu now accounts for nearly half of all newly confirmed cases, with test positivity rising sharply in recent days," Kergosien said.

He added that undetected chains of transmission had already taken hold in the worst-hit areas, and said "the spread of the outbreak into new areas with even weaker preparedness and response capacities poses a serious risk."

blocks.caption: Incidental factors like the school year restarting this month provide new potential transmission risksImage: Dieudonne Dirole/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Which factors helped DRC's worst Ebola outbreak spread so fast?
The deadly virus has killed more than 3,500 people from more than 7,200 confirmed cases since the outbreak was declared in May, according to WHO figures.
Based on the recorded data, the quality of which is gradually improving with the passage of time, the 2026 outbreak is the fastest-spreading in history.

It's also the largest in the DRC's history, second in overall size only to the West African outbreak of 2013-2016. The West African outbreak needed around two and a half years to reach a caseload of more than 28,000, not four months to pass 7,000.
Congo's Ebola crisis: Fear, mistrust and a growing outbreak
Many of the cases have been concentrated in hard-to-reach areas in DRC's north and east long plagued by instability, poor health infrastructure and a series of armed groups.

Medical staff strikes have also contributed to problems fighting the spread, as have dearly-held funeral and burial traditions that pose the risk of post-mortem transmission as people bid their loved ones farewell.

The outbreak also involves a rare Ebolavirus strain, Bundibugyo, meaning that existing treatments and vaccines — several of which are prohibitively expense by the standards of the region anyway — were untested and of uncertain value against it.

articles.title: Toronto fans go wild for Hudson Williams. And the cast of his new show goes wild for Canada
articles.summary: CBC News was on the red carpet for the world premiere of Yaga — a new show with a cast packed with Canadian stars like Hudson Williams, Noah Reid, Carrie-Anne Moss and Clark Backo.

image.caption: Cast members of Yaga walk the red carpet for its Toronto International Film Festival premiere at the TIFF Lightbox theatre on Thursday. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
CBC News was on the red carpet for the world premiere of Yaga — a new show with a cast packed with Canadian stars like Hudson Williams, Noah Reid, Carrie-Anne Moss and Clark Backo.
Cast members of new Crave series show their love for Canada at TIFF
The cast of 'Yaga' is Canada down
When Hudson Williams touched down in Toronto on Thursday, King Street turned into a party.

Phone cameras were out. Fans went wild. Posters and selfies galore. Outside the TIFF Lightbox, some dedicated fans had even waited up to 12 hours just to catch a glimpse of the Heated Rivalry star and score a ticket to his premiere.
Williams was in town for a special in-conversation event and the premiere of his next project, Yaga, a sex-fuelled mystery series based on Slavic folklore that starts streaming in October.
Fans of Williams will be well-fed, too. He plays not one, but two, roles in the show.
Hudson Williams fans line up for hours at TIFF

Shot earlier this year on Vancouver Island, Yaga follows a private investigator called to a small coastal town to search for the missing young heir to a wealthy fishery family, only to uncover a darker web of secrets.

It has a cast packed with Canadian stars, including Noah Reid (Schitt's Creek), Carrie-Anne Moss (The Matrix), Clark Backo (Letterkenny), Sheila McCarthy and even original Anne of Green Gables star Megan Follows.
CBC News was on the red carpet for its world premiere at TIFF and although Williams didn't speak to the media, his co-star was asked if she had any advice for him.
Moss had a pretty simple answer: “He doesn't need it. He's doing great."
That set the vibe for the whole night. Yes, there was plenty of Hudson mania, but there was also an overwhelming sense of pride in the Canadian talent behind the show.
Reid, who stars as the private investigator with a fun, flirty change in tone from his role as Patrick on Schitt's Creek, shared his thoughts on the creative environment.
"There's a humility to the Canadian creative spirit that it's not ego-driven," he told CBC News.
"Everybody just wants to like, go in, do their best work, support each other, compete with each other in an effort to get the best product."
Backo, who stars alongside Reid as a local detective, agreed that the love for Canadian projects is "everything."
"I feel like people are making bets on Canadian shows that maybe they didn’t before," she told CBC News.
Yaga was born out of a play developed by Kat Sandler for Toronto's Tarragon Theatre in 2019.
When asked about being part of a project that's so unapologetically Canadian, Follows said it's "about time."

"Look at the talent, look at the stories, look at how unique and interesting and diverse and complex," she said, referring to the all-Canadian cast of Yaga and the flurry of shows coming out of the country.
"It's not enough to be a service industry. We have to be creating our own pieces across the boards in so many different iterations, right? So that's what's exciting."
Moss rounds out the Canadian cast, starring as a sultry professor in the thick of the mystery. Sandler reached out to her directly, making an offer she said she couldn't refuse.
"Being asked to do something is, first of all, an honour. And you know, you feel bad and you go, 'OK, I'll look at that.' And I love the material. And it was an easy yes."
Yaga premieres on Crave next month.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Griffin Jaeger is a reporter and producer with CBC's entertainment unit. He also formerly hosted and produced content for The National’s digital platforms. You can reach him at griffin.jaeger@cbc.ca

articles.title: Airport malaria in Germany remains infrequent
articles.summary: An outbreak of malaria at Frankfurt Airport this summer has raised alarm. Experts believe parasites probably arrived in a passenger's luggage. But with the onset of fall, the risks of contracting the…

image.caption: Malaria is only transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoesImage: James Gathany/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Eight people are known to have contracted malaria in the vicinity of Frankfurt Airport in central Germany since July; three of them have died. Those affected are mostly employees of the airport operator Fraport.

The Frankfurt Public Health Department believes the outbreak is due to "airport malaria," which occurs when a female Anopheles mosquito carrying the malaria parasite travels by aircraft to a country where the disease is not common from one where it is, bites a person and infects their red blood cells.

"We are dealing with a very rare occurrence, not a new frequent disease in Germany," said Achim Hörauf, the director of the Institute for Medical Microbiology, Immunology and Parasitology at Bonn's University Hospital (UKB), in a press release.
Several die from rare 'airport malaria' in Germany
Airport malaria is very infrequent

The last documented case of airport malaria in Germany before the current ones was in 2023, according to the Epidemiologisches Bulletin of the Robert Koch Institute (RKI), an online journal that regularly provides information on infectious diseases and public health.
Normally, those with the disease in Germany were infected elsewhere and brought it back during a long-haul trip.

But a mosquito can make its way to Germany as a "stowaway" if it was trapped in a suitcase or in clothing. Hörauf said that under certain circumstances, it might be able to survive in warmer areas of an airport.
Frankfurt cases are of dangerous malaria tropica
According to a UKB press release, the cases in Frankfurt involve malaria tropica, which is considered to be the most dangerous and potentially life-threatening form of malaria.

To contract the disease, a person needs to be bitten by a female anopheles mosquito infected with the Plasmodium falciparum parasite. This pathogen passes to the human and then attacks the red blood vessels.
"Simply put, it can lead to many small blockages in the blood vessels," explained Hörauf. "Depending on which organ is affected, various serious complications can arise."

Fluid can accumulate in the lungs, or neurological damage can result if the blood vessels of the brain are affected. Acute kidney failure is also possible. About 20% of those affected die if the disease is left untreated.
"If a diagnosis is made in time, there can be targeted treatment," Hörauf said. "If the disease is overlooked, however, it can very quickly take a severe turn."
At first, symptoms are not specific, resembling those of the flu: sudden high fever, chills, headaches and muscle pain. Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea are also possible.

blocks.caption: Those who live near Frankfurt Airport have been advised to seek medical help if they have any suspicious symptomsImage: Rene Traut/Rene Traut Fotografie/picture alliance

blocks.text: Frankfurt authorities tell public to seek advice in case of symptoms
The Frankfurt Public Health Department has advised anybody who lives or works near Frankfurt Airport to seek medical attention immediately if they experience any such symptoms.

Rapid diagnostic tests can provide evidence of malaria in human blood and then a blood test can help to confirm this. The RKI says treatment should take place at a hospital, which has expertise in tropical medicine.
As summer comes to an end and temperatures cool in Germany, particularly at night, the conditions are becoming less favorable for mosquitoes and malaria parasites.

However, experts warn that there could still be other cases of malaria in Germany despite the cooler weather. Plasmodium falciparum has an incubation period of seven to 15 days, so more than two weeks can pass between a mosquito transmitting malaria to somebody by biting them and the onset of symptoms. According to Hörauf, the biggest challenge is to ensure that people think malaria could be a possibility even if they have not traveled abroad.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Norval Morrisseau masterwork not seen for 40 years unveiled at Thunder Bay Art Gallery
articles.summary: After 40 years in storage, a rare masterwork painting by Ojibway artist Norval Morrisseau has been unveiled at the Thunder Bay Art Gallery in northwestern Ontario. The painting is on loan from EA…

image.caption: This masterwork by Ojibway artist Norval Morrisseau had been in storage for four decades, before it was unveiled at the Thunder Bay Art Gallery on Friday. (Marc Doucette/CBC)

blocks.text: Thunder Bay·New

After 40 years in storage, a rare masterwork painting by Ojibway artist Norval Morrisseau has been unveiled at the Thunder Bay Art Gallery in northwestern Ontario. The painting is on loan from EA Studios Calgary, and is described as "very spiritual" and "very powerful."
Rare, 'very spiritual,' 'very powerful' mural created in Jasper, Alta., on display until Jan. 3
Rare Norval Morrisseau masterpiece unveiled in Thunder Bay, Ont.
After 40 years in storage, a massive painting by Ojibway artist Norval Morrisseau has been unveiled at the Thunder Bay Art Gallery in northwestern Ontario.
The Morrisseau Masterwork painting, at roughly 6.7 metres long and just over three metres high, hadn't been viewed publicly since 1986.

It's on loan from EA Studios Calgary, which is collaborating with the gallery to mount the rolled, raw canvas from its collection on a stretcher — an auxiliary frame with expandable joints — for conservation.
The large Woodland Style mural depicts a gathering of adults, children, animals, birds and spiritual beings in a scene with natural elements.

“I’m really excited. I have to tell you, the first time I unrolled it with our contractors, it was very overwhelming, but in a positive sense," said Joseph Helmy, director of EA Studios Calgary. "This piece, it’s just very spiritual. It’s very powerful. It’s really hard to describe.
“This piece, I think, is going to really bring a lot of people together ...," Helmy said.

“From what I’ve learned through the stories that my father has shared and through the expertise of Mr. Jonathan Manovich, Norval’s paintings were created to tell his stories, but they were also created to bridge Indigenous and non-Indigenous people together — and that’s what I hope that this painting will do.”
Helmy’s family began their relationship with the artist in 1985 when his father, Galal, was recommended to sponsor Morrisseau’s work by Winnipeg art dealer Robert Checkwitch.

Helmy said the artist called and told his father he dreamt he was painting for him in the Canadian Rockies, where he resided in Jasper, which intrigued him and prompted him to book Morrisseau on a flight to Alberta.
Morrisseau continued to live and paint in a studio above EA Studios Calgary, which operated at the time out of the Maligne Canyon Tea House, during the winters until 1987.

“This piece was actually painted for my father and he actually never had this hung on the wall before,” Helmy said. It was shown only at a couple of Edmonton exhibitions and last shown in 1986, he added.
Displayed ‘where it all started’
The art studio has been working since 2025 with the Thunder Bay Art Gallery to unveil the artwork.
“We really have enjoyed working with them over the last two years to make this event happen,” Helmy said.
This piece has returned to the place where Norval was born, Helmy noted. He said he couldn’t think of a “better place to start showing this piece back to the public view again."

Morrisseau, who died in 2007 at age 75, is considered the grandfather of contemporary Indigenous art in Canada. He was from Bingwi Neyaashi Anishinaabek First Nation, also known as Sand Point First Nation, in northwestern Ontario.

“Many people associate Morrisseau with some of the larger works, Androgyny, for instance, at the governor general’s home, and when you see the Order of Canada inducted, that’s a Morrisseau piece behind it and that’s a huge epic canvas as well,” said Matthew Hills, the Thunder Bay gallery’s executive director.

“But … it’s a triptych, meaning there are three components of the canvas, and this is one large piece. So in many ways, we feel like this is the early period of Morrisseau starting to work bigger on more epic, larger canvases and really explore some of his artistic genius.”
It’s an entry point for the gallery to something that hasn’t been talked about in the last 40 years and hasn’t been examined, Hills said.
LISTEN | Mathew Hills: Giant Morriseau Painting :
Superior Morning7:48Mathew Hills: Giant Morriseau Painting
In addition to supporting the piece’s conservation, Hills said, the gallery can explore some of the art’s history. It can also share it in a territory and region associated with Morrisseau.
“We’re really happy to have this opportunity to show it off, and to do some conservation work on it and restore it to its full glory."
Hills said the gallery invites the public to come out and take a look. The Morrisseau Masterwork will be on view until Jan. 3.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Nicky Shaw is a reporter for CBC Thunder Bay. She graduated with a Bachelor of Journalism and a minor in Environmental and Climate Humanities from Carleton University. Aligning with her passion for covering global environmental and humanitarian issues, she has worked to develop in-depth multimedia content that shares the diverse experiences of people in Northwestern Ontario.

articles.title: Fact Check: False video alleges Berlin votes destroyed
articles.summary: A video claiming to show AfD postal ballots being destroyed has gone viral ahead of Berlin's September 20 election. DW Fact Check examines the footage, the accounts sharing it and how widely it is…

image.caption: Germany's postal voting system is a frequent target for disinformationImage: Caro Kadatz/picture alliance

blocks.text: Berliners will vote in state and district elections on September 20. In the days leading up to the vote, a video circulated on social media that allegedly shows a man opening postal voting envelopes and destroying ballots cast for the far-right party Alternative for Germany (AfD).

DW Fact check reviewed more than a dozen posts sharing the footage. The posts use similar captions, presenting the video as evidence of election fraud in Germany. Several have amassed hundreds of thousands of views on X.
How widely has the video spread? And is its reach driven by genuine public interest? Or is something else boosting its visibility? DW Fact check investigated the video and the accounts sharing it.
Claim: A video shows a man destroying AfD ballots in Berlin with a carpet knife.
One post sharing the footage claims:

"A video circulating in Berlin shows a man opening mail-in voting envelopes and destroying ballots marked for the AfD, while ballots for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's CDU are left intact. The footage appeared days after the AfD's landslide victory in Saxony-Anhalt. Berlin holds its state election on September 20."
The post had received about 327,000 views when DW Fact Check reviewed it on September 18.

blocks.caption: According to Berlin's state returning officer, the election papers shown in the viral video are not authenticImage: X

blocks.text: DW Fact check: False

At first glance, the ballot paper appears authentic. Its names and layout match those of the official ballot paper for the Spandau 2 constituency in western Berlin, which is publicly available online. However, there are several inconsistencies in the documents shown in the video.
Berlin's state returning officer, Stephan Bröchler, told DW that the documents shown in the video are not authentic election papers from Berlin.
Bröchler said the envelopes shown in the video did not match the official ones used for this election. Bröchler also noted that the way the envelopes are sealed appears suspicious.

According to official guidelines issued by Berlin's election authorities, postal voters receive a voting package containing a "Wahlschein," or a voter declaration that needs to be signed, plus two envelopes and the ballot papers for the elections. For the September 20 vote, Berliners receive two ballot papers: a grey-and-blue ballot for the election to the city-state House of Representatives and an orange ballot for their District Assembly.

In the video, however, the documents do not correspond to the official postal voting package. The person in the video opens a red envelope and removes a white envelope. The signed voter declaration is missing. Without it, a mail-in ballot would be invalid.
The person then takes out only the grey-and-blue ballot paper for the Berlin House of Representatives from the white envelope.

Although voters may choose to vote in only one of the two elections, it would be unusual for three envelopes in succession to contain only one ballot paper. However, the footage does not clearly show whether the second envelope is really empty.

blocks.caption: The orange Berlin ballot paper is missing in the video circulating onlineImage: Caro Kadatz/picture alliance

blocks.text: Another detail raises doubts about the video's authenticity: In the background, large grey bins allegedly containing postal ballots are marked with a version of Berlin's coat of arms featuring the Berlin bear.
Bröchler said such features were not used by Berlin's election authorities.
"Marking the ballot boxes with a Berlin bear is also unknown and uncommon here," he said.
Bröchler's conclusion is clear: "It can be ruled out that any actual Berlin election documents are involved. The video is clearly intended to discredit postal voting."
Has the video really gone viral?

One of the accounts that shared the video has previously come under scrutiny. An investigation by the Lithuania-based research organization Debunk linked the account to the so-called "Sprinter" network, a group of X accounts. The researchers identified what they described as signs of coordinated and inauthentic activity, including unusually high posting volumes, frequent account renaming and evidence of purchased followers. Debunk said the network was used to amplify pro-Kremlin narratives.

DW Fact check reviewed more than 15 other posts sharing the footage, many of them using nearly identical captions. Together, the posts had accumulated more than 3.2 million views by the time DW Fact check examined them.

The accounts sharing the video also showed several suspicious characteristics. Almost all of the 15 accounts examined exhibited at least one sign of potentially inauthentic behavior, including rapid follower growth, frequent username changes or limited evidence of normal user engagement.

One account, which presented itself as an independent media company based in West Asia, had more than 43,000 followers despite having been created only in April 2026. During that period, the account changed its username nine times.

On their own, these characteristics do not prove that the accounts are coordinated or that the video's engagement was entirely artificially generated. They do, however, show that the video's apparent reach should not automatically be interpreted as evidence of widespread, organic discussion on X.
A pattern seen before
The video resembles other false election-related claims that have circulated about Germany in recent months.
Fact check: Fake campaign about alleged division of Germany
Ahead of the September 6 election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, DW Fact check examined a video that similarly purported to show AfD postal ballots being destroyed. The claim was false.

Among other inconsistencies, all three crossed-out ballots shown in the footage carried the same name on the signed voter declaration. The envelopes had already been opened, and the ballots lacked a hole punch required for use with voting templates designed for blind and visually impaired voters.
DW Fact check has also investigated and debunked numerous other false claims targeting Germany's postal voting system.

Julia Smirnova, who investigates influence operations as a researcher at the Berlin-based Center for Monitoring, Analysis and Strategy (CeMAS), told DW that these similarities, together with the way the new video is being disseminated, indicate that it is "highly likely" to be part of the Storm-1516 influence operation.
German security authorities and researchers have attributed Storm-1516 to Russia.
The operation has previously used fabricated videos, forged documents and purported eyewitness accounts to spread false narratives about elections and other political issues.

In February 2025, Germany's Interior Ministry said it had indications that two fake videos alleging manipulation of AfD ballots were connected to the Storm 1516 campaign, citing similarities in their content and distribution.
Hundreds of fake posts target German elections

articles.title: 'Never giving up': Alberta separatist leaders say referendum vote won't end their fight
articles.summary: Premier Danielle Smith and her government expect next month's separation referendum to be the last word on the subject — but those fighting for an independent Alberta say no matter the outcome, the…

image.caption: Alberta separatists gathered at the Legislature in Edmonton on Aug. 29 for a protest organized by the Alberta Prosperity Project, a group whose leadership spurred the Stay Free Alberta citizen initiative petition. (Amanda Erickson/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Edmonton·New

Premier Danielle Smith and her government expect next month's separation referendum to be the last word on the subject — but those fighting for an independent Alberta say no matter the outcome, the fight goes on.
Advocates for an Independent Alberta say no ballot outcome will put the matter to rest
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Sep 18, 2026 1:50 PM EDT | Last Updated: 9 minutes ago
"We're never giving up," Jeff Rath, the lawyer for a group that helped organize an independence petition, said Wednesday in an interview.
"The logic of independence is such that we're not going home when this is all over.
"Do you think we're just going to stop advocating for a free and independent Alberta?"
Cory Morgan, an organizer with the Pathway to Independence group campaigning for separation, agreed: "That's a very significant movement on something that's looking for some very serious change."
Morgan said the grievances motivating advocates are still going to be there after the referendum.
"The issue doesn't go away, but it'll change its approach," he said.

items: Alberta separatists expect a win, regardless of numbers that say otherwise, poll suggests

blocks.text: Even on the pro-Canada side, there is doubt the issue will be put to rest after voting day.

Thomas Lukaszuk, who is steering the Forever Canadian campaign vying to keep Alberta a part of Confederation, said he doesn't put it past Smith to call a second, binding referendum even if a clear majority rejects separation.
"We're making sure that we have the contingency plans put in place to carry on [campaigning] if we have to. I hope we don't. I hope we put this behind us," Lukaszuk said earlier this week.
Voters head to the polls next month to answer 10 referendum questions. Nine of them focus on giving Alberta more elbow room on immigration and constitutional issues.
The final one asks if Alberta should stay in Canada or whether it's time to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.
The issue has roiled the province. Polls suggest a majority of Albertans want to stay in the country.
Smith has promised to vote to stay in Canada.
She has said she called the vote because of competing citizen-led petitions over whether to remain in Canada or leave.

items: Both sides of Alberta separation debate rally as momentum kicks up ahead of vote

blocks.text: Critics, including the NDP, say Smith has no mandate to roll the dice on Canada's future and that she is only doing so to mollify separatist hardliners in her United Conservative Party.
Keith Wilson, leader of the pro-independence group Let Alberta Decide, said a vote for separation is technically not a vote for separation, but a vote to hold another vote.

items: As Alberta separation vote approaches, both campaigns are banking on voter turnout

blocks.text: That means, he said, that regardless of the outcome, Alberta's intolerably subservient status in Canada continues. Central Canada has the majority of the population, he said, and therefore will continue to call the shots in Parliament.
"This vote won't resolve what's broken in Canada and won't fix how Albertans are treated poorly by Ottawa, so demands for fairness will continue," Wilson said.
'Ready to move forward'
Smith has said she expects the Oct. 19 vote to settle the matter.

As recently as this week, her office reiterated that in a statement following a surprising byelection loss by Smith's candidate to the Opposition NDP in what is normally a safe Calgary seat for her UCP.

"In five weeks, the referendum vote will be over, and we're confident Albertans will be ready to move forward and fight for a stronger Alberta within a united Canada," spokesperson Sam Blackett said in an emailed statement.
Alberta referendum campaigns heat up
Commentators on both sides of the political spectrum say disillusionment and dismay over Smith calling the referendum played a role in Calgary-Shaw voters punishing her party at the ballot box.
Smith's office disagrees, blaming right-centre vote splitting for the NDP win.
The loss could signal larger challenges down the road for the UCP given Calgary is viewed as critical to victory in the looming October 2027 general election.

Morgan said it's not just voters, but also UCP members that Smith needs to watch out for. He said Smith's embrace of citizen initiative petitions has activated a group of activists who hold significant sway over Smith's party.
"She's going to have to give them something to sink their teeth into or they're going to come after her," he said.
With files from Lisa Johnson

articles.title: Attorneys for Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs drop music mogul, alleging unpaid legal bills
articles.summary:
The musician is serving a 50-month federal prison term for prostitution-related offenses

Attorneys representing rapper Sean “Diddy”…

blocks.text: Attorneys representing rapper Sean “Diddy” Combs say they are no longer acting for the disgraced star in a dispute over months of unpaid legal bills.

The musician, who is serving a 50-month federal prison term for prostitution-related offenses, has become increasingly belligerent in recent months, causing “a total breakdown in cooperation and communication” with New York law firm Sher Tremonte, one of its partners, Michael Tremonte, said in a court filing.

The firm was representing Combs, 56, in a $100m civil defamation lawsuit stemming from his conviction last year in a sex-trafficking and racketeering case that also saw him acquitted of the most serious charges.

Combs, Tremonte said in the filing seeking to withdraw as counsel as reported by NBC News, “has not paid a substantial balance of attorney’s fees, costs, and expenses” stretching more than six months.

“The firm’s representation has been rendered unreasonably difficult by Mr Combs’s lack of cooperation, resulting in a breakdown in attorney-client communications and rendering Sher Tremonte incapable of continuing to provide effective legal services to Mr Combs,” the filing, in US district court in the southern district of New York, said.
For four of the months, it said, Combs has “declined to make himself available for timely, substantive and direct communications about his cases”.
In a statement provided by his representatives to the news outlet, Combs accused his lawyers of overcharging, and said that he fired them.

“I made the decision to switch lawyers because I won’t let anyone take advantage of me by overcharging me and running up bills that were never approved,” he said. “This is strictly a business matter, and any talk about unpaid fees is just part of our dispute over those unapproved charges.”
In an email to NBC, Tremonte rejected Combs’s claims and insisted his company had represented its client “zealously and very efficiently”.
“As stated in our court filings, we are withdrawing from representing him because he has not paid his long-overdue invoices and has become uncooperative,” Tremonte said.
“Any suggestion that we overcharged him is simply false.”

Earlier this year, prosecutors in Los Angeles said they were mulling filing new sexual assault charges against Combs, who is currently incarcerated at New Jersey’s Fort Dix federal correctional institution.
after newsletter promotion

Record producer Jonathan Hay has publicly accused Combs of “assault, sexual harassment, false imprisonment and infliction of emotional distress” during a 2020 collaboration relating to the estate of the late songwriter Christopher Wallace, better known as the rapper Notorious BIG.
Hay sued Combs and the Wallace estate for defamation in Los Angeles county superior court last year, and Wallace’s son, CJ Wallace, countersued Hay in an action in Florida.

In separate proceedings that gave rise to the payment dispute with Sher Tremonte, Combs is suing Courtney Burgess, a music manager who told a grand jury in 2024 that the hip-hop mogul gave him flash drives containing video of Combs sexually assaulting minors and fellow celebrities.

Earlier this month, TMZ reported, a judge allowed Combs’s case to proceed against Burgess, his lawyer Ariel Mitchell, and the media company Nexstar, which featured Mitchell on its NewsNation show vouching for Burgess’s assertions about the videos.
Combs has accused the pair of spreading “outlandish claims” and “wild lies” against him.

items: This article was amended on 18 September 2026. An earlier version wrongly stated that Combs sued record producer Jonathan Hay for defamation. Hay is the plaintiff.

articles.title: Earl Spencer doubles down on claims about ‘monstrous’ call with King Charles after Diana’s death
articles.summary:
Charles Spencer, Diana’s brother, claims the king told him ‘we’ll forget her soon enough’

Earl Spencer has doubled down on his bombshell claim that King Charles said of Diana, Princess of…

blocks.text: Earl Spencer has doubled down on his bombshell claim that King Charles said of Diana, Princess of Wales, “rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough” days after her death, saying he is telling the truth.

The alleged comments, revealed in Charles Spencer’s memoir, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, which is being serialised in the Daily Mail, prompted Buckingham Palace to issue an extraordinary statement suggesting Diana’s brother had misremembered events, saying “the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise”.
In an interview with the BBC, Diana’s brother stood firm in his recollection, telling Laura Kuenssberg: “I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said.”

blocks.caption: Diana died in a car crash in 1997, at the age of 36. Photograph: Simon Kreitem/Reuters

blocks.text: Responding to the palace’s statement, Spencer said: “Well, is he furious? Is he furious, or is he embarrassed?” When asked about the inference that his memory was coloured, Spencer said: “They’ve sort of smudged that one, haven’t they? They’ve said that recollections may vary.”
Spencer said the call was one of two he had with Charles in his lifetime and claims he told his friends and family members at the time about the comments “because it was so monstrous”.
On Wednesday, an extract from the memoir made the bombshell claim that Charles told Spencer days after Diana’s death that “rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough”.

The comments by the then prince were allegedly made during a heated argument over funeral arrangements. Spencer says the alleged comments reflected “his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death”, the Daily Mail reported.
Among other claims in the book are that Diana told a friend on the eve of her wedding to Charles that he said he was happy to marry her, but was not actually in love with her.

On Friday, the second extract from the memoir was published. Spencer writes Charles was “polite and formal” on the day of Diana’s funeral and says Prince Philip told him to look ahead while walking in unison alongside his nephews and former brother-in-law.
“It was hellish, entering that tunnel of grief, particularly because we were unable to put a face to it by looking at the individuals in the crowd,” said Spencer of the procession.

blocks.caption: From left: Prince Philip, Prince William, Charles Spencer, Prince Harry and King Charles, then a prince, walking in Diana’s funeral procession. Photograph: Jeff J Mitchell/AP

blocks.text: In the extract released on Wednesday, Spencer also claims he insisted to Charles that Diana would not have wanted her sons, Prince William, then 15, and Prince Harry, then 12, to walk in their mother’s funeral procession. In the end, her sons walked behind her coffin, which William later called “one of the hardest things I’ve ever done”.
after newsletter promotion

Spencer wrote that when one of Queen Elizabeth’s most senior aides told him in the days before the funeral that William and Harry would take part in the procession, he responded: “That’s not going to happen,” the paper said.

But minutes later he received a phone call from Charles, who insisted it should. It was during the ensuing argument between the two men that Charles allegedly made the comment, with Spencer reportedly writing: “‘Rest assured,’” he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough!’”
Spencer wrote that he was stunned by the alleged remark and took a few seconds to reply, writing: “‘I can’t believe you just said that,’ I said flatly, before hanging up.”
Swan Song is due to be published worldwide next Tuesday – in the UK by Penguin Michael Joseph, a division of Penguin Random House.
Four copies of the Dutch language edition were reportedly taken from a truck while it was en route from the Dutch publisher’s printers to their warehouse in the Netherlands.
Diana, who died aged 36 after a car crash in Paris in 1997, would have turned 65 on 1 July this year.

Buckingham Palace did not issue a fresh statement responding to the BBC interview, but on Wednesday a spokesperson said: “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss.”

articles.title: Zelenskyy holds inaugural 'Carpathian Eight' regional summit
articles.summary: Zelenskyy said the summit was a "significant beginning" of a movement to strengthen ties with its neighboring countries.

image.caption: Zelenskyy said the so-called 'Carpathian macro-region' has become one of the most reliable foundations of Kyiv's defenseImage: Vladyslav Musiienko/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday welcomed the leaders and representatives of Romania, Serbia, Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Austria and Hungary, to work on deepening cooperation. The European Union was also involved in the talks.
The summit took place in the western Ukrainian ski resort of Bukovel.
It comes amid increasing concern over Russia ramping up hybrid threats including sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation and potential drone incursions into NATO territory.
The meeting is also happening as overnight Russian strikes in multiple regions of Ukraine sparked fires, causing several deaths and injuries.
What is the 'Carpathian Eight'?

Dubbed the "Carpathian Eight,” the summit brought together nations such as Poland and Romania, who have been staunch supporters of Ukraine, along with others such as Hungary, Serbia and Slovakia, who have refused to provide Kyiv with direct military assistance.

Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram that the summit was a "significant beginning" of a movement intended to "further strengthen ties between our countries and create another strong element of cooperation at the EU level.”
The Ukrainian president added that the nations pledged to work together on security, energy, logistics, cross-border economic ties and support for local communities.
"The Carpathian macro-region has become one of the most reliable foundations of our defense. This is about strength that exists and will continue to exist," Zelenskyy added.
Ukraine secures nearly $4 billion in EU support
Zelenskyy said nearly 550 business representatives were expected to attend the forum and that investment ⁠and trade agreements worth €1 billion ($1.15 billion) would be signed.
"It's a ​good start: energy, logistics, infrastructure and cross-sector agreements," he said in a speech transmitted on Ukrainian TV.
As the summit kicked off, Zelenskyy announced in a Telegram post that Ukraine has secured €3.3 billion from an EU financial support package to strengthen Ukraine's defense capabilities.
The money included funds for the purchase of missiles and drones.

blocks.caption: Poland's Donald Tusk and Serbia's Aleksandar Vucic were among the leaders in attendanceImage: Vladyslav Musiienko/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Poland joins anti-ballistic missile coalition
During the summit, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced that his country had joined an anti-ballistic missile coalition with Ukraine and other allies.
"From today, Poland is part of this major project ... we agreed on ‌the ⁠forms ⁠and frameworks of this cooperation," Tusk said in a video posted on X.

The air-defense coalition was created in July between Ukraine and nine other European countries. It would include the joint development of a new anti-ballistic missile system to serve ‌as ​an alternative and cheaper solution to the US Patriot system.
Tusk also announced that ​Poland has prepared a new "significant" donation package for Ukraine, without giving further detail.

"I will be very consistent ⁠here. ​No one will change my opinion ​that Poland has to support Ukraine in its war ​against Russian aggression ... History ‌cannot divide us vis-a-vis Russia today," Tusk said.
Zelenskyy thanked Poland for the new aid package.
"Ukraine and Poland ⁠are strong ​neighbors, friends, and partners, and we have one common enemy," he wrote on Telegram.

articles.title: San Diego police investigate case of family of three found fatally shot in home
articles.summary:
Navy veteran David Voight, his wife, Amy, and their child were found dead as relatives report Voight was suffering from PTSD

Authorities are investigating what led to the tragic case of a…

blocks.text: Authorities are investigating what led to the tragic case of a family who was found fatally shot in their San Diego area home on Wednesday morning.

The San Diego police department identified the family as Amy Voight, 54, and David Voight, 56, and the couple’s 13-year-old daughter. The family died of gunshot wounds, police said, and investigators found a weapon in the residence.

Gerald Austin, Amy Voight’s father, told the San Diego Union-Tribune that his son-in-law had served in the navy as a officer in Iraq and Afghanistan, while his daughter worked with the Naval Criminal Investigative Service as a digital forensic examiner. He went on to say that his daughter adored David Voight, and that he believed the violence was driven by David Voight’s suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
Mary Austin, Amy Voight’s mother, said she had noted that David Voight’s symptoms had recently become more severe and that she and her husband urged their daughter to seek help for the veteran.
“You could visibly see there was something really wrong,” Mary Austin told Fox 5. “He was fidgety. You could tell.”

Gerald Austin said his daughter had sought help for her husband in recent days, but they were unable to receive services because they did not have an appointment, allegations the Department of Veterans Affairs denied.
The Department of Veterans Affairs said it could not comment on the case, citing privacy concerns, but that “what’s being alleged regarding VA services is not accurate”.
“All VA healthcare facilities offer same-day mental healthcare to all Veterans who request it,” said Quinn Slaven, the VA press secretary.
The couple and their daughter were discovered by a concerned neighbor on Wednesday morning, and all were pronounced dead at the scene.
The county medical examiner’s office will conduct autopsies to determine the cause and manner of death, police said in a statement.

Seven out of every 100 veterans will experience PTSD in their lives, according to the VA. The rate is higher among veterans who served in Iraq and Afghanistan at 29%. Deployment significantly increases the risk of PTSD, according to the VA.

articles.title: Warren Buffett steps down after six decades at Berkshire - 'Father Time always wins'
articles.summary: Since taking control in 1965, Buffett grew a struggling textile mill into a global conglomerate.

blocks.text: Warren Buffett has stepped down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, handing over leadership to his son Howard in the final chapter of a long-planned transition at the US business giant.

At 96, the world-famous investor will move into an advisory role as chairman emeritus and remain on the company board to offer his "judgement and perspective", according to a letter to shareholders, external.
The decision comes nine months after Buffett passed the chief executive role to Greg Abel, with his son, Howard, who has been a director since 1993, taking over non-executive board duties.
Known as the "Oracle of Omaha," Buffett built one of the most successful investment track records in modern history.
He took control of Berkshire Hathaway in 1965 when it was a struggling New England textile mill and turned it into a $1.1 trillion (£822b), global conglomerate.

Today, the business owns a wide range of well-known brands including GEICO car insurance, Dairy Queen, and BNSF railway system. It also owns large stakes in companies like Apple and Coca-Cola – a brand close to Buffett's heart, as he famously drinks five cans a day.
Buffett has made his mark through "value investing" – a strategy focused on finding companies with solid fundamentals, buying them at fair prices, and holding them for decades.
His annual letters to shareholders and festival-like annual meetings turned him into a leading mentor across the financial world.
Despite his retirement from the top board post, the change is considered an orderly passing of the baton rather than a sudden shock.

"The timing is right to complete the transition," Buffett wrote, noting he had recently celebrated his 96th birthday and the first birthday of one of his great-grandchildren, who is "moving a bit faster" than he is.
The company assured investors that day-to-day operations will remain steady.

While Greg Abel manages corporate strategy and capital decisions, Howard Buffett's main duty as chairman will be guarding the firm's "culture and values". A former farmer, philanthropist, and sheriff, the younger Buffett brings more than three decades of board experience to the role.
Buffett concluded his letter by saying it had been the "privilege of a lifetime" to serve as chairman, but acknowledged that in the end, "Father Time always wins".
