items: Kyle Alexander Aznar, the CEO of Aznar Shipping, is determined to break the generational curse that often affects family businesses by preparing to take the company public through an IPO.

The IPO aims to raise up to P737 million for fleet expansion and is part of Aznar's strategy to ensure the company's success for future generations, emphasizing professional governance and mentorship.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
As his family’s shipping legacy prepares to open itself up to the public, Kyle Alexander Aznar had an age-old curse on his mind.
“You know what they say, the third generation is the last generation,” the Aznar Shipping president and CEO told Rappler on Friday, September 18.

He was, of course, referring to the infamous adage that warns family fortunes rarely survives three generations. The first makes the money, second grows it, the third squanders what’s left. Gone, wasted, kaput.

The third-generation Aznar wasn’t about to let that happen. He was only 27 when he suddenly had to take over the family shipping business after his father died. Now 31 and at the helm, he sees one job as more important than simply making money.

“My main job is really to hand it over to the next gen,” Aznar told Rappler at the sidelines of his company’s H1 briefing. “We want our business to succeed — not just for my time. It’s really succeeding generations.”
His chosen way to keep the family ship afloat for another generation? Open it up to the public.

Aznar Shipping has filed for an initial public offering (IPO) that could see the Cebu-based company sell as many as one billion primary shares at an indicative price of up to P0.67 each, potentially raising P670 million in gross proceeds for the company. Another 100 million secondary shares could be sold through an overallotment option, bringing the total potential offer size to P737 million.

At this stage, everything still remains subject to book building and approval by the Securities and Exchange Commission and Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE). Aznar said the company is targeting a December listing, but stressed that he did not want to “jump the gun” on regulators.
Aznar is hardly the only old name sailing out of Cebu.

Cebu has long been one of the country’s biggest shipping hubs, producing generations of shipping families, from the Gothongs and Robles to the Cokaliongs and the Lims. The Aboitizes were once part of that club too, with Aboitiz Shipping eventually evolving into 2GO, now under the Sy family’s SM group. (READ: As Atlas Mining leaves by 2027, SMIC expects 2GO, renewables to fill gap)
But while many shipping businesses have remained private and closely held, Aznar sees public company governance as part of the antidote to the generational curse.

“Looking at the IPO process, the requirements, the standards that you are held to, it really coincided with my interest. That’s how I first started getting interested in it quite a few years ago,” he told Rappler.

The professionalization actually began before the IPO. Even before the company’s aspirations to go public, the shipping company already had independent directors sitting on its board. Aznar said he has been the only family member on the board for the past three years, surrounded instead by professionals whom he calls his mentors.
“I was just only 27 when I had to take over the company when my dad passed away,” he said. “I was humble enough to realize that I might not have all the answers, I might not always be right.”
That setup, he believes, has paid off.

blocks.caption: FINANCIALS. Aznar Shipping chief financial officer Dary Aran shares the company’s H1 2026 financial results. Photo by Lance Spencer Yu/Rappler.

blocks.text: Aznar Shipping’s revenue jumped from P59.2 million in 2023 to P223.9 million in 2025, when it booked P51.7 million in net income. In just the first six months of 2026, revenue reached P210.9 million while net income hit P53.2 million, already topping the previous full year.
The company currently operates nine vessels across four principal Visayas corridors, with cargo and rolling vehicles accounting for about 86% of first-half revenue.

The company wants to use IPO proceeds primarily for fleet expansion, with plans for newer vessels and, farther down the road, its own dry-docking facility. Aznar also said his company is not specifically hunting the customers of rivals.
“We’re not really eyeing specific players,” he told Rappler. “We’re following the market. We’re looking at complementary routes. We’re following our customers.”

blocks.caption: For GCash’s early private equity backers, record IPO will be ultimate payday

blocks.text: If Aznar wants to test whether investors believe the family business can survive another generation, he’s choosing a challenging time to do it.

Even before getting to the stock market, the shipping industry is contending with elevated fuel prices. Aznar said fuel is the company’s biggest operating cost, although its move toward larger vessels has helped protect margins because capacity has increased much faster than operating expenses. (READ: DOE sees ‘no signs’ oil prices will fall as excise tax relief goes on table)

“Our new vessel could probably carry three or four times the load of our previous one. But the operating cost is more or less the same,” he said. “That’s how we’ve kept our rates affordable. That’s how we’ve protected our margins as well.”

So far, Aznar said demand has held up despite the broader economic uncertainty. “Our numbers are good,” he said. “The demand is there. The volume is there. And I believe it’s the right time to expand.”
But the bigger uncertainty may be whether investors will be equally ready.
The PSE index remains below the 6,000 level amid worries over slow economic growth and broader market uncertainty, well below the roughly 7,800 level where it ended 2019 before the pandemic.
Then there’s the very large elephant potentially barging into the stock exchange just weeks ahead of Aznar: GCash.

Mynt, the operator of GCash, is targeting an October 20 listing for an IPO worth as much as P92.3 billion, dwarfing Aznar’s planned offering. Would there still be enough liquidity left in the market after the biggest IPO in Philippine history when Aznar comes knocking in December?
The young shipowner, for his part, offered an appropriately maritime answer to the uncertainty.

“Market conditions, they’re out of our control. They’re just like the sea. You can’t always hope for calm waters,” he said. “What you can do is really learn to sail in rough conditions.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: US wheat farmers navigate uncertainty amid drought and geopolitical chaos
articles.summary:
Some experts worry factors affecting wheat exports could push global food prices even higher than they are now

Wheat prices are at their highest level in three years, which means farmer…

blocks.text: Wheat prices are at their highest level in three years, which means farmer Merrill Nielsen should be getting more for his crops out of his 2,500-acre (1,010-hectare) Kansas farm.

Yet even as future prices for bread-type wheat are up 39%, Nielsen is unsure whether increased prices will raise his bottom line. The price of diesel fuel, which he needs to run his tractor, has hit record highs. Then there’s the erratic weather that made him lose his entire wheat crop in the spring, and drought has overtaken the southern Great Plains.

“We’re not looking to plant any more wheat than we probably normally would, or maybe we won’t even plant that much. I don’t know. Really, we’ll have to see what the weather does for us,” Nielsen said.

The combination of high costs, poor weather and geopolitics leave US farmers such as Nielsen with an uncertain growing season despite higher prices for their yields. It also leaves consumers, from millers and bakers to restaurants and grocery shoppers, at risk of feeling the pinch.

Droughts across the US and Europe have been shriveling harvests, and weather forecasts for a “super” El Niño this year means “there are some alarming signals” about the impact of weather on wheat crops, said Joao Lampreia, a market strategist at the Lisbon-based Freedom24.

The weather phenomenon, exacerbated by the climate crisis, causes warm waters to rise to the surface across the equatorial Pacific Ocean, along the coast of South America, and is known to imperil agriculture in the southern hemisphere significantly. Experts say wheat supplies in key exporting countries are at their second-lowest levels on record. Already, Australia’s wheat plantings are down 12% due to expectations of dryness and increased fertilizer costs.

The good news for farmers and consumers is that El Niño can also bring wetter conditions for the southern Great Plains in the fall and spring. During the last big El Niño in 2015 and 2016, the US set an all-time record-high winter wheat yield, said Mark Welch, an economist who researches grain marketing at Texas A&M University.

Even if the weather impacts turn out better than expected, recent Russian attacks on port facilities in the Black Sea, where one-third of the global wheat trade passes through, have also disrupted grain shipments. Black Sea farmers, who were some of the few global wheat exporters to experience a bumper crop, had just wrapped up their harvest before the attacks.
Because of the fighting, supply is largely inaccessible, which has pushed prices up, Welch said. But if Black Sea farmers and shippers can find alternative routes, prices will backtrack somewhat.
At best, about 35% to 50% of that wheat could find a way out, but it will take longer and cost more to get, Lampreia said.

Dan Basse, president of the agricultural market research company AgResource, worries the that combination of weather-damaged harvests and the impact of geopolitics on wheat exports could leave global food prices even higher than they are today. The United Nations’ Food and Agriculture Organization’s food price index, which tracks a basket of widely traded food commodities, was up 2.5% in August over a year ago, he said.

The spike in wheat prices “has tentacles that go far beyond the war between the Ukrainians and Russians”, Basse says. “The world needs more harvested acreage of every grain. All of this resonates in higher grain and food prices for the world looking forward.”

In the immediate future, US farmers will need to help make up the shortfall. Basse said he expected planted acreage for wheat this winter to expand about 10% more than last year as producers seek to capture higher prices.

But harvested acreage for wheat in the US has been at its lowest levels since 1877, as US farmers have found it more profitable to plant corn and soybeans rather than wheat. One year of high prices isn’t likely to change a structural decline.
Farmers will need higher production and strong values to benefit. “If it’s not an average yield or better, the breakeven cost really gets high very quickly,” Welch said.

And it’s unclear how much weather will continue to affect harvests. Vance Ehmke, a wheat-seed seller in south-west Kansas, said he’s been busy fielding more calls for seeds this year. But the weather in the southern Great Plains is now too dry for seeds to germinate and grow.
“If you get your wheat up, you’ve got 90% to 95% odds that you’ll harvest something. But if you can’t even get it up, I mean, you’re just screwed,” he said.
Prices will need to stay high to accommodate a surge in input prices, which have been exacerbated by ongoing trade wars. “We are the ones that get hurt by those policies,” Ehmke said.

articles.title: Avoid sharing videos, unverified info on Banga School shooting, DICT warns
articles.summary: The Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) on Friday called on the public not to share graphic videos and images, as well as unverified information on social media concerning…

blocks.text: Published September 18, 2026 6:59pm

The Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) on Friday called on the public not to share graphic videos and images, as well as unverified information on social media concerning the school shooting incident in Banga, South Cotabato.
“Let us respect the privacy and dignity of the victims and their families while allowing authorities to conduct a thorough investigation,” the DICT said in a statement.
The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) reported that at least six students were killed and 17 others were injured following the school shooting incident.
The Department of Education (DepEd) also expressed deep concern over the reported shooting incident at Banga National High School in Banga.
The DICT said it stands ready to provide assistance within its mandate and coordinate with concerned agencies should communications or technical support be needed.

“The DICT joins the Department of Education, local authorities, and the entire community in strongly affirming the need to protect our schools as safe spaces for learning and to uphold the safety, well-being, and dignity of every learner and educator,” it said.

“The DICT strongly condemns the reported shooting incident at Banga National High School in South Cotabato. Violence in and around educational institutions has no place in our communities, and the safety and protection of our learners, educators, and school personnel must remain a paramount concern,” it added. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Germany faces energy tax losses as EV sales rise
articles.summary: The rapid shift to electric vehicles in Germany is cutting fuel tax revenue. As EV sales surge, policymakers face growing pressure to find new ways to fund roads and transportation infrastructure.

image.caption: Germany's shift to EVs is reducing emissions while eroding fuel tax revenues, raising questions about future transportation fundingImage: DW

blocks.text: "People are moving away from gasoline and diesel," said Jens Boysen-Hogrefe, a tax and transportation expert at the Kiel Institute for the World Economy (IfW).
"The boom in electric cars triggered by high fuel prices is accelerating the transition in drive technologies that was already planned anyway," he told DW.
According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), sales of electric vehicles in Europe rose by nearly 30% in the first quarter of this year compared to the same period last year.
Norway is leading the way, with electric cars accounting for as many as 95% of all newly registered passenger cars in the country.

The agency's "Global EV Outlook 2026" reveals that EV growth rates in Asia-Pacific countries, excluding China, were even more remarkable, with sales in some regions rising by up to 80%. In Latin America, that figure was around 75%.
Fossil fuels remain a tax windfall

In Berlin, however, the boom in electric mobility has not been met with universal enthusiasm. That's particularly the case at the Ministry of Finance, as charging an electric car does not incur energy taxes, but only minimal electricity taxes.
Currently, a liter of diesel in Germany is taxed at 47.04 cents, and a liter of gasoline at 65.45 cents. On top of that, there is a carbon levy and a 19% value-added tax.
With gasoline priced at €2.10 per liter, taxes account for €1.14 of the total, meaning more than half of the pump price goes to the government, according to the ADAC motoring club.

The current fossil-fuel-based system, with its energy taxes, truck tolls and CO2 tax, is very lucrative for the government, said Boysen-Hogrefe. "The finance minister doesn't benefit much when people drive electric cars," he noted. "Quite the opposite."
Energy tax revenue in decline

"If the shift to electric cars takes place and nothing changes in the tax system, the road system will become a money-losing venture for the federal government," the tax expert underscored, predicting billions of euros in losses.
EU overturns combustion engine ban amid industry pressure
According to the Federal Statistical Office, revenue from the energy tax on diesel and gasoline fell from €37 billion ($43 billion) in 2016 to €33 billion ($38 billion) last year.
In 2022, a report by the scientific advisory committee to the German Transport Ministry projected that revenue from the energy tax would drop to as low as €5 billion by 2050.
Pressure to reform road funding

"The transition to electric vehicles has fiscal implications that have hardly been discussed so far," the report states. The expected tax shortfalls add to the costly subsidies for electric vehicles that are currently still necessary to drive the transition forward, it added.
In Germany, government incentives to purchase electric cars — amounting to several thousand euros per vehicle — were scrapped at the end of 2023.
However, electric cars are still exempt from vehicle tax through 2035. And companies that invest in electric cars continue to enjoy tax benefits.
In their report, the transportation experts advised the government not to wait until the tax deficit becomes so large that it is forced to act.
That's because "the lead time for such measures spans several legislative terms," they argued.
Boysen-Hogrefe said fiscal pressure could now increase. If people continue to buy electric cars in droves, "the government can't just shrug it off," he said.
How other countries are responding
Countries such as the United Kingdom and Norway have already come up with measures such as introducing new taxes.

In the UK, for instance, a levy on electric cars is set to take effect in April 2028. The so-called "Electric Vehicle Excise Duty" charges 3 pence (3.5 euro cents) per mile (1.6 kilometers) on fully electric cars and 1.5 pence on plug-in hybrids.
Since 2024, New Zealand and Iceland have required annual odometer checks for electric vehicles to calculate mileage-based fees.
Why big automakers are losing China

And in Switzerland, electric vehicle owners will be required to pay a road-use charge from 2030, either through a weight-based fee per kilometer or a tax on electricity purchased at charging stations.

Meanwhile, Norway, a trailblazer for electric vehicles, has restricted the VAT exemption for electric cars starting this year. It has also introduced a weight-based purchase or registration tax and tolls.
Are road tolls the answer?
In Germany, too, many experts are advocating for a passenger car toll to compensate for the shortfall in energy tax revenue while also taking road use more fully into account.
"The recommended policy option is a distance- and traffic-based toll," according to a recently published study by the University of Münster.
"If we realistically assume that policymakers will shy away from this step, the vignette solution is recommended," according to the report.
Under a vignette system, drivers pay a flat fee for road use over a defined period.
"If this, too, encounters insurmountable political resistance, the only solution left is to raise the motor vehicle tax," they concluded.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Early voting begins in midterms as campaign shifts focus to cost of living and Iran war – US politics live
articles.summary:
Campaigning or control of Congress is expected to ramp up as some states open early voting

Good morning, and welcome to our US politics live blog. The midterm elections are less than…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 18s agoTrump officials sending undocumented children to Texas sparks fears of mass deportation
20m agoEarly voting begins in midterms as cost of living and Iran war loom large

blocks.text: Trump officials sending undocumented children to Texas sparks fears of mass deportation
Alexandra Villarreal

The Trump administration has started sending a majority of undocumented children who came to the US alone and have new immigration court cases to Texas, where government facilities for them are unlicensed, their chances of getting a lawyer are low and advocates fear that “a deportation churn-out factory” awaits them, the Guardian has learned.

blocks.caption: Unaccompanied minors wait in Texas to be transported by the US Border Patrol after crossing the Rio Grande River from Mexico. Photograph: Go Nakamura/Reuters

blocks.text: Almost 80% of children in federal custody who arrived unaccompanied by a parent or legal guardian and who were placed in immigration court proceedings in July – and over 90% in August – have been funneled into shelter networks somewhere in Texas, a dramatic upswing from the months prior, according to analysis shared exclusively with the Guardian from researchers at the immigration data insights platform bklg.org.

This is understood to amount to a total of 925 children in the care of the Health and Human Services (HHS) department’s office of refugee resettlement (ORR) and in open immigration court proceedings based in Texas, with 651 sent there in July and August alone.
Early voting begins in midterms as cost of living and Iran war loom large

Good morning, and welcome to our US politics live blog. The midterm elections are less than two months away, but some states begin early voting today, marking the start of a crucial stretch of campaigning for control of Congress.

Virginia begins early in-person voting, while voters in Minnesota, Idaho and South Dakota can cast absentee ballots in person, as the campaign turns increasingly on the cost of living and the continuing war in Iran.

blocks.caption: The start of early voting comes at a time of deep angst among many US citizens about issues including rising gas. Photograph: Nam Y Huh/AP

blocks.text: High gas prices and low approval ratings are adding to the challenges facing president Donald Trump as Republicans head into the 3 November elections with their control of the House and Senate at risk. In its analysis of the US economy, the Wall Street Journal reports that mortgage rates are nearing 7%, consumer prices rose 3.4% in the year to August and gas prices are close to their highest levels since 2022.

“We are seeing what happens when a president launches a war of choice without anticipating the unintended consequences,” Aaron David Miller, a former adviser on Middle East policy to Republican and Democratic administrations, told Reuters.

Trump will take his case to the UN on Tuesday, where he is likely to present the Iran war as a victory despite having initially promised the military campaign would be over within weeks. The conflict has instead entered its seventh month, with Iran still able to disrupt regional shipping and the war putting further pressure on global energy prices.
In other developments:

items: The Trump administration has approved a potential sale of 48 advanced F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia, worth an estimated $24.3b. The Department of State said the propose sale “will improve Saudi Arabia’s capability to deter current and future threats by strengthening its homeland defense”. The move comes despite concerns from intelligence agencies that China could potentially gain access to, or steal, sensitive F-35 technology through Saudi Arabia, according to the New York Times. The newspaper reported:

blocks.text: double quotation markOne detailed report, issued months ago by the Pentagon’s Defense Intelligence Agency, raised questions about whether the Americans and Saudis would be able to secure sites with F-35 technology. It also raised concerns about the access that Chinese military personnel have to Saudi bases and the prevalent use by Saudi Arabia of Chinese technology in telecommunications infrastructure and defense installations.

items: Former staff members of the US Institute of Peace have asked a federal appeals court to prevent the Trump administration from carving the president’s name into the facade of its headquarters in Washington, which was renamed the ‘“Donald J. Trump United States Institute of Peace” last year. Lawyers for the institute’s ousted board members argued that engraving Trump’s name on the building would cause “irreparable harm” by undermining the organization’s independent mission.

The USIP dispute comes as another Washington cultural institution faces a court battle over changes under Trump. A federal judge has ordered the Kennedy Center to give 30 days’ notice before making any major physical changes to the building, including demolition as Trump has threatened. The president said the centre could be “ripped down” amid a dispute over plans to put his name on the building and a proposed $257m renovation. The center is currently closed due to what its Trump-backed leadership described as safety issues caused by age and structural deficiencies.

blocks.caption: Traffic cones keep cars from entering the driveway at the Kennedy Center in Washington, which was ordered to be closed for repairs by its board. Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/Reuters

articles.title: Dozens of suspected illegal miners die in Nigerian custody
articles.summary: Authorities linked the deaths to disease, but this has been disputed by intelligence reports and relatives of the accused.
articles.byline: Makuochi Okafor, Harry Sekulich, Wycliffe Muia

blocks.text: Thirty-seven people accused of illegal mining in north-central Nigeria have died in custody, local officials said.
Police have set up an investigation into the deaths, which the Nigerian Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) blamed on an apparent disease outbreak.
However, an intelligence report shared with AFP news agency suggested the group died because of overcrowding and poor ventilation inside the detention facility in Niger state.
"We believe they suffocated because there was no ventilation," the father of one of those detained told the BBC.
Abdullahi Dalhatu said his son had survived because he was near a small window.
"His friend slumped and fainted, and many others also collapsed."
His son described how detainees began collapsing in the heat of the overcrowded and poorly ventilated cell, his father said.
He said the detainees repeatedly knocked on the door for help but nobody opened it.
State governor Mohammed Umaru Bago called the deaths "sad and tragic" during a press conference on Thursday.
An NSCDC commander has been detained following the deaths, Bago added.
He declared three days of mourning and postponed the start of campaigning for elections scheduled for January.
Officials had arrested the group of young men on Tuesday for suspected illegal mining near Borgu, in the mineral-rich state of Niger. The region is known for small-scale gold mining.

Two days later, 37 people detained as part of the suspected unlawful operation were found dead inside the detention centre run by the NSCDC, a paramilitary agency responsible for protecting critical infrastructure and tackling crimes including illegal mining. It also assists police with internal security operations.
The NSCDC told the BBC that illegal mining was widespread in Niger state, where artisanal miners often operate in open fields.

Its spokesperson, Babawale Afolabi, said more than 50 people were arrested during an operation earlier this week. They had not been charged because profiling and documentation were still under way before the deaths, he said.
"Illegal mining in Niger is serious," Afolabi said.
The NSCDC had earlier said the detainees were possibly victims of a diphtheria outbreak, a serious bacterial infection that can be fatal.
But the agency's national headquarters later said the cause had not been established and would require medical and laboratory tests.
"The NSCDC wishes to clarify that reports attributing the deaths to any specific disease remain subject to medical and laboratory confirmation," it added in a statement.
Dalhatu told the BBC that security officers had been pursuing suspected illegal miners in the community for several days before making arrests.
He said relatives went to the NSCDC office seeking their release but were repeatedly told to return later. "Unfortunately, the following day we got the news that our children had died," he added.
One father told Nigerian media that his son had appeared healthy when relatives took him food the day before his death and called for an independent post-mortem examination.

Another relative, whose 17-year-old brother was among those who died, said the family had visited him during his detention and questioned how a disease could have killed so many detainees without apparently affecting their guards.
Post-mortem examinations are expected to help establish what happened.

Niger's police chief ordered an immediate investigation into "the unfortunate death of suspected illegal miners while in the detention facility of the NSCDC", spokesman Wasiu Abiodun wrote in a statement.
The victim's bodies have since been taken to the general hospital in nearby Minna for examination.
It is not clear yet whether any of the suspects had been charged.

Nigeria's constitution requires anyone detained on suspicion of a criminal offence to be brought before a court within a "reasonable time" - generally within a day where a court is available within 40km (25 miles), or two days in other cases, unless a longer period is considered reasonable.
The scramble for gold reserves dug up in illegal mines in Niger state has been blamed for fuelling criminal gang violence, according to officials and experts.
Much of the gold in the region is trafficked through global supply chains, a 2024 SwissAid report found.

articles.title: Women's football in Germany booming but still much to do
articles.summary: Women's football is growing rapidly, particularly in Germany. Nevertheless, equal pay and investment remain major talking points.

image.caption: Women's football in Germany has made strides in recent years, but still has work to do to improve its professional structuresImage: Grant Hubbs/STEINSIEK.CH/IMAGO

blocks.text: According to the German Football Association (DFB), investment in women's football by professional clubs has risen by 135% over the past six years. In addition, the number of girls in Germany who play the game has increased by about 30% since 2022.
Celia Sasic, the former Germany striker who has been in charge of diversity and inclusion at the DFB since 2022, has helped bring women's football more into the spotlight in the boardroom.
"We've focused on the issue and established new structures, so that there is now a separate department with its own sports director," the 38-year-old told DW.
"In my view, it's important that there are very clear responsibilities for the development and professionalization of this sport."

"I believe it's important that [women's football] is recognized within the licensed clubs. And it's becoming increasingly recognized, so the framework conditions need to be adjusted," continued Sasic.
"And we're seeing that if we provide the right framework for the game, there's huge growth potential there."

blocks.caption: Celia Sasic has been fighting for equality in women's football for years and wants better structures in the women's game in GermanyImage: Simon Hofmann/Getty Images

blocks.text: Numbers support growth of women's game

The most-watched football match featuring a German team in 2025 was the Women's European Championship semifinal between Germany and Spain. The match drew around 14.26 million viewers—and a market share of about 57.6%. By comparison, the men's game against Portugal in the Nations League semifinals drew around 10 million viewers.
Sasic, who was part of the German team that won the 2009 and 2013 European championships, regards this as a foundation to build on.
"This is incredibly significant for us as a society and in terms of our influence abroad," she said.
"There are women who play football, who play for us on the national team, and who inspire us so much that millions of us watch their games."
'Zidane was my hero'
Sasic is clearly proud of the recent progress. For a long time, women's football in Germany was not taken seriously.
"I had no choice; I had to look to men for role models," Sasic recalled.
"My biggest role model was Zinedine Zidane. I had posters of [Luis] Figo, [David] Beckham, and Michael Ballack hanging in my room."

Posters of women wouldn't have existed back then, but it's different now. These days, Germany captain Giulia Gwinn and players like Jule Brandt and Lea Schüller smile down from the walls of children's bedrooms, inspiring girls to dream of a great career in women's football.

blocks.caption: Support of the women's team has exploded in recent years in GermanyImage: Eddie Keogh/Getty Images

blocks.text: Further investment required to push women's game forward

Despite the boom, the financial gap between women's and men's football remains enormous, as figures from the DFB and the German Soccer League (DFL) show. While the 18 Bundesliga clubs spent €1.72 billion ($1.9 billion) on players and coaching staff alone in the 2024–25 season, the personnel expenses of the 12 Women's Bundesliga clubs most recently totaled just under €30 million — about 60 times lower.

Salaries also highlight how the professionalization of women's football is still very much in its infancy. In the 2023-24 season, a women's Bundesliga player earned an average base salary of around €48,000 per year. Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane is estimated to have earned €25 million during the same season.
This disparity is expected to narrow in the future.
"Football reflects our society—and thus also the gender inequality and the gender pay gap that we see in our society," former German Foreign Minister Annalena Baerbock told DW.

"Unfortunately, this gap in football is even wider in many countries than in other professions. But that is by no means set in stone," added Baerbock, who also served as the president of the United Nations General Assembly from September 2025 to September 2026.

"We know from the USA, the United Kingdom, Norway, and Spain that if you really want to invest in women's football, equal pay is an important part of that—especially when it comes to tournament bonuses."

blocks.caption: Annalena Baerbock believes change in terms of equal pay lies in the hands of football nationsImage: Eduardo Munoz/REUTERS

blocks.text: Young women need professional support
Celia Sasic currently sees significant progress when it comes to women's football, although it's still early days in the development process.

"Clubs must provide all the necessary resources to enable this development. Football pitches, medical care, a fitness facility, and a coaching staff must be available," said Sasic. "Investing in this ultimately makes the game much better, too."
Opportunities for young girls in terms of training also need to improve.
"It's a crucial step to have youth development centers where players are trained—not only athletically, but also professionally. These are essential factors for the success of the women's game."

blocks.caption: Bayern Munich offer some of the best training facilities in the country, but the aim is to improve all the facilities in GermanyImage: Jenni Maul/Eibner-Pressefoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Education and apprenticeship options must be available

A new DFB rule shows that even basic professional structures still need to be established. Only since the 2025–26 season have teams in the Women's Bundesliga been required to employ assistant coaches, goalkeeper coaches, and athletic coaches on a full-time, professional basis.

Sasic and women's football still have a long way to go, but the former player is determined to continue fighting for greater equality. The 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil is a great place to start, and Sasic is hoping for a successful showing for Germany at the tournament as this would likely give women's football another major boost—and bring broadcasters new record viewership ratings.
This article was adapted from German.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: No evidence Romualdez has stage 4 cancer
articles.summary: The lawmaker is reportedly suffering from illnesses such as sleep apnea, hypertension, diabetes, and major depressive disorder — not cancer

blocks.text: Claim: Following his arrest, medical findings confirmed that former House speaker Martin Romualdez has stage 4 cancer.
Why we fact-checked this: A YouTube channel named “News Update Files” uploaded a video on September 9 claiming that Romualdez has stage 4 cancer.

Text on its thumbnail reads, “Stage 4 cancer!? Romualdez paktay [sic] na!?” (Stage 4 cancer!? Romualdez is already dead!?). It shows Romualdez lying in a hospital bed with a detainee shirt draped over him.
The video’s title reads, “Kapapasok lang! Breaking news! Romualdez paktay na! Confirmed! Tamba merong stage 4 cancer pala!”
(Just in! Breaking news! Romualdez is already dead! Confirmed! Turns out Tamba has stage 4 cancer!)
As of writing, the video has drawn over 4,400 views, 230 likes, and 60 comments.

The facts: There is no court filing, public hospital record, or credible news report confirming that Romualdez has cancer, whether stage 4 or otherwise. The lawmaker’s medical conditions, as cited in reports, concern other health issues.

Romualdez was arrested on September 7 over a P7.44-billion plunder case linked to alleged flood control kickbacks. Authorities served the warrant while he was confined at Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City. Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said that at the time of arrest, Romualdez was suffering from a cardiovascular event, unstable blood pressure, and an anxiety attack.

Because of his condition, authorities processed Romualdez at his hospital bedside rather than taking him to a police station. He was photographed lying down, with the detainee shirt draped over him and the booking sign positioned above him. (READ: How Martin Romualdez avoided jail by going to hospital)

His actual documented conditions are cardiovascular and neurologic in nature, not cancer. In his own manifestation asking the anti-graft court Sandiganbayan for continued hospital confinement, Romualdez cited coronary artery disease, diabetes, and primary hypothyroidism, among other ailments.

The court ordered his transfer to the Philippine General Hospital (PGH), where an independent assessment found that Romualdez has chronic coronary syndrome, hypothyroidism, sleep apnea, anxiety, and major depressive disorder.
PGH Medical Director Dr. Gerardo Legaspi, however, said that these conditions are under controlled medication and that the lawmaker is in stable condition.

Behind bars: The Sandiganbayan subsequently ordered Romualdez’s transfer to the Quezon City Jail Male Dormitory in Payatas on September 14 following the PGH doctors’ examination. Romualdez remains alive and in custody, with his official mugshots being released the following day.

Romualdez is accused of receiving kickbacks related to the flood control corruption scheme. The case also involves former Ako Bicol representative Elizaldy “Zaldy” Co and two private individuals. Co remains at large, while Romualdez has pleaded not guilty during his arraignment before the Sandiganbayan on September 16. – Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Efren Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies at the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: Ombudsman probes 'ghost internet' scheme in government
articles.summary: The Office of the Ombudsman is investigating a “ghost internet” scheme involving the government"s Information Technology (IT) system allegedly rigged with substandard, if not fake software, Assistant…

blocks.text: Published September 18, 2026 6:19pm

The Office of the Ombudsman is investigating a “ghost internet” scheme involving the government’s Information Technology (IT) system allegedly rigged with substandard, if not fake software, Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavano said.

Clavano said that while the government pays billions of pesos for IT systems with very specific technical requirements, there are cases wherein the government is shortchanged due to lack of due diligence.

“Once the hardware, the machines, the routers are delivered and pass inspection, everyone assumes the software that's supposed to run on it is there as well. Nobody actually checks. And there comes the loophole. A contractor can install cheaper, outdated, or even fake software while still charging the government full price for the real thing,” Clavano said in a press conference.

“Because nobody verifies the software after the hardware is approved, the overpricing goes undetected. It only comes out when the systems break down, or when somebody finally digs deep enough to catch it, which is what our investigation is doing now,” he added.
Clavano then said that the investigation will center around the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT).

“Were the contracted sites actually installed, and are they working? Was the government billed for connectivity and services that were never delivered? Were the prices of hardware, software, and services reasonable, or were they inflated?” Clavano said.

“Who approved, certified, or released payment for projects that were not delivered? So that has entered into fact-finding, and we will update the public regarding the investigation on that matter as soon as possible,” he added.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Continue to hold firm on West Philippine Sea arbitral ruling, Carpio told Filipinos
articles.summary: Filipinos must keep on standing their ground in the West Philippine Sea amid the latest tensions between Manila and Beijing over the country"s exclusive economic zone.

blocks.text: Published September 18, 2026 6:11pm
Filipinos must keep on standing their ground in the West Philippine Sea amid the latest tensions between Manila and Beijing over the country’s exclusive economic zone.
“It is our obligation to protect that, not only for the present generation, but future generations,” retired Senior Associate Justice Antonio Carpio said.

This was after Defense Secretary Gilbert Teodor Jr. received a note from a Chinese official, reiterating China's rejection of the 2016 ruling of the Permanent Court of Arbitration in favor of the Philippines over the maritime claims, during an international forum.
Teodoro lashed out at China's claim in the South China Sea after he was handed the unsigned note

Carpio said Filipinos should never compromise when it comes to national territory and sovereign rights. In The Unsinkable Spirit, a three-part documentary that narrated how generations of Filipinos have defended the West Philippine Sea from China’s aggression through diplomacy and commitment to international law, Carpio said that the work ahead is an intergenerational struggle.
He further said that the previous generation already laid out the foundation by winning the arbitral ruling but that it still not enough.
“The Constitution, in the end, only promises the inheritance. Each generation still has to go out and hold it,” Carpio said.

On July 12, 2016, the Hague-based Permanent Court of Arbitration ruled that China's sweeping claims over nearly the entire South China Sea had no legal basis under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), in a case brought by the Philippines in 2013.

For geopolitical analyst and professor Chester Cabalza, the ruling is considered Filipino First in its purest constitutional form. The idea of Filipino First is often associated with late President Carlos Garcia and his economic policies in the 1950s and was eventually embedded in the 1987 Constitution.

“Our fisherfolk feed the Filipinos and if they could not fish, how could they feed us? The award was decided in their favor in the most concrete way available: Filipino fisherfolk have the right to fish in the West Philippine Sea,” Cabalza argued.

“A Filipino fisherman, inside a Filipino exclusive economic zone, exercising a right the Constitution reserved to him exclusively — and a state under a written obligation to make that right real,” he said.

Supreme Court spokesperson Camille Ting explained that the Filipino First policy requires the state to give preference to qualified Filipinos when granting rights, privileges and concessions involving the national economy and patrimony.

The strength of this policy was already proven some 30 years ago in a case between the Manila Prince Hotel and the Government Service Insurance System. Ting said “the policy is self-executing, meaning it can be enforced directly without an implementing law.”
“National patrimony is not limited to the country's natural resources. It also includes the Philippines' cultural heritage and other assets that form part of the Filipino identity,” Ting said.

Meanwhile, amid the still ongoing tensions, Cabalza emphasized that the theme right now, for many nations around the world, is strategic autonomy which means that a nation can stand on its own, even if it has treaty alliances. He noted that it was a Filipino idea to sue China and not because it was dictated by some ally.
“If we do not protect the Filipino First concept, it is so easy for major powers to just intrude in our homeland,” Cabalza said.

Philippine Coast Guard commandant admiral Ronnie Gil Gavan, for his part, insisted that Filipinos should always keep in mind the victory of the arbitration despite continued efforts from China to say otherwise.

"The law has remained to be the great leveler in the relationship amongst countries, big or small. We are equal insofar as the law is concerned. And it has remained to be the best friend of weaker countries,” he said. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Ombudsman flags DICT, begins fact-finding for ‘ghost internet’ projects
articles.summary: The 'ghost internet' projects deal with government contracts where hardware and related software are bought by the government, but the software installed may be either outdated or fake, leading to…

blocks.text: The 'ghost internet' projects deal with government contracts where hardware and related software are bought by the government, but the software installed may be either outdated or fake, leading to project overpricing
MANILA, Philippines – The Office of the Ombudsman announced in a press briefing on Friday, September 18, that it was conducting a fact-finding mission on what it called “ghost internet” projects.

The “ghost internet” projects deal with government contracts where hardware and related software are bought by the government for billions of pesos, but the software installed within the devices purchased may be either outdated or fake, leading to project overpricing.

Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavano said during the briefing, “Once the hardware — the machines, the routers — are delivered and passes inspection, everyone assumes the software that’s supposed to run on it is there as well. But nobody actually checks, and there comes the loophole.”

“A contractor can install cheaper, outdated, or even fake software while still charging the government full price for the real thing. Because nobody verifies the software after the hardware is approved, the overpricing goes undetected,” Clavano added.
It is only found out when systems break down or when somebody digs into the matter further. The investigation, Clavano said, will center around the DICT and will seek to answer four basic questions.

items: Were the contracted sites actually installed and are they working?
Was the government billed for connectivity and services that were never delivered?
Were the prices of hardware, software, and services reasonable or inflated?
Who approved, certified, or released payments for projects that were not delivered?

blocks.text: Clavano also said the scope of the investigation will deal with entirety of contracts related to DICT initiatives, but did not specify particulars as the fact-finding process is ongoing.

The Ombudsman, in the same press briefing, confirmed that graft complaints are now pending against members of the Villar family due to allegations related to PrimeWater Infrastructure Corporation. – Rappler.com

articles.title: World View with Marites Vitug: Inside the fight against POGOs

blocks.caption: World View with Marites Vitug: Inside the fight against POGOs

blocks.text: Rappler editor-at-large Marites Vitug speaks to former PAOCC officials Winnie Quidato and Winston Casio about their book, The Rogue Compound: POGOs, Human Trafficking, and the Fight to Reclaim the Philippines
Bookmark this page to catch the discussion on Friday, September 18, at 6 pm!

MANILA, Philippines – Scam compounds linked to Philippine offshore gaming operators (POGOs) have become a major organized crime problem in the country, with human trafficking, online scams, and other criminal activities converging in the same operations.

Former Presidential Anti-Organized Crime Commission (PAOCC) officials Winnie Quidato and Winston Casio draw on their experience dismantling scam compounds in their new book, The Rogue Compound: POGOs, Human Trafficking, and the Fight to Reclaim the Philippines.

On Friday, September 18, Rappler editor-at-large Marites Vitug speaks to Quidato and Casio about how scam compounds took root in the Philippines, the challenges law enforcement faced in going after them, and what it takes to dismantle these criminal networks.

Quidato is a retired police officer with decades of experience in intelligence work. He spent three years working to dismantle scam compounds as PAOCC deputy executive director. Casio, meanwhile, is a crime analyst and educator who served as PAOCC spokesperson.
With the Anti-POGO Act now in place, do POGOs still operate underground?
Catch the interview on Thursday at 6 pm! – Rappler.com

articles.title: Australian man accused of murdering Thai teenager and putting body in suitcase pleads not guilty
articles.summary:
Simon Peter Carman appeared in a Pattaya court on Friday charged with killing Tunchanok Donhomla

An Australian man accused of murdering a Thai teenager and putting her body in a suitcase…

blocks.text: An Australian man accused of murdering a Thai teenager and putting her body in a suitcase pleaded not guilty on Friday in a hearing in the seaside resort city of Pattaya, a court official said.

Simon Peter Carman, 45, was arrested in June after 17-year-old Tunchanok Donhomla was reported missing in Pattaya City, about 150km south-east of Bangkok. A suitcase containing her body was found shortly after.
Police said she died of suffocation.
Carman appeared on Friday at Pattaya provincial court, where he pleaded not guilty to all charges, a court spokesperson said.
He had been charged with murder, concealing a body and taking a minor for indecent purposes. The next court date was set for 12 October.
Police previously said CCTV footage showed him entering a condominium in Pattaya with the girl in the early hours of 25 June, and leaving that evening carrying a large black suitcase.
In a police interrogation video shared online by Thai media, Carman has said he was acting in self-defence because the girl was threatening him with a knife.
The case put the spotlight on Pattaya, which is popular with foreign tourists for its beaches and nightlife, but also has a reputation for sex tourism.

articles.title: Louisiana firefighters find feline native to sub-Saharan Africa while responding to house fire
articles.summary:
The African serval, illegally enclosed in the back yard, was subdued and transferred to an animal welfare facility

Louisiana…

blocks.text: Louisiana firefighters responding to a small house blaze found a wildcat native to sub-Saharan Africa illegally enclosed in the back yard, and an animal welfare agency is now seeking to place the creature in an appropriate environment, according to officials.

Firefighters investigating a report of a minor fire at a home in the suburban New Orleans community of Marrero on Tuesday spotted the cat in question – an African serval – behind the residence in a chain-linked enclosure resembling a cramped baseball batting cage, a spokesperson for the local animal protection services said.

A statement from Jefferson protection and animal welfare services (JPaws) said its director, Michelle Brignac, and humane department supervisor, Victoria Clark, joined firefighters at the scene after they were summoned there. Local laws require an exotic animal permit to legally keep a serval as a pet, and the owner of the home at the center of the case did not have such a document, JPaws spokesperson John McCusker told the Guardian on Thursday.

blocks.caption: An African serval cat being transported after being found in an enclosure in the back yard a of a home. Photograph: John McCusker, JPaws

blocks.text: The statement said Brignac and Clark therefore “subdued the hissing serval and wrangled it” into a transport carrier from its 9ft-by-9ft (7.53-sq-meter) cage that McCusker likened to “a dog kennel”. Brignac and Clark then brought the serval to the JPaws facility in the nearby community of Harvey, according to the statement from the agency, which also shared vivid photographs of the wildcat.

Beside their black spots, svelte physiques and striking facial features, servals are known for their ability to leap as high as about 7ft (2 meters) in the air. So McCusker said JPaws gave the serval an entire room to itself while the agency sought an appropriate refuge for the wildcat, which was born in captivity but whose natural habitat is African grasslands.
Servals share some similarities with domesticated cats that make them immensely popular as pets, including their affinities for grooming themselves, purring, yowling and stalking potential prey.

Nonetheless, they are not easily sustained pets, JPaws’ statement maintained. Servals in captivity do not have the physical space and stimulation needed to engage in normal, healthy behaviors, and they endure chronic stress as a result, the agency’s statement said.

They mark their territory, become aggressive as they mature, cannot be fully house-trained and destroy furniture, and they have been known to barge through walls and doors, according to JPaws. Experts also say servals require a diet and specialized care beyond what house cats need, making them a major responsibility.

JPaws’ statement said the agency would explore having the serval held temporarily at New Orleans’ Audubon zoo. A zoo spokesperson, however, said the institution did not plan to take the serval in and understood JPaws was looking into another arrangement, the details of which were not immediately available on Thursday.
The Marrero serval was the latest of several indicators of the wildcats’ growing popularity, a boom driven in part by social media content creators showing them in videos online.

blocks.caption: Servals mark their territory, become aggressive as they mature and cannot be fully house-trained. Photograph: John Mccusker/John McCusker, JPaws

blocks.text: Cases involving servals have also tended to generate widely read news headlines in North America.
That happened in Ohio in 2023, when officials in the Cincinnati area captured an African serval named Amiry that was spotted in a Cincinnati neighborhood tree and later tested positive for cocaine.

In late 2025, a search for an African serval that escaped a Pennsylvania wildlife center culminated in heartbreak after a motorist fatally struck the wildcat, as Philadelphia’s NBC News affiliated reported.

blocks.caption: The Marrero serval was the latest of several indicators of the wildcats’ growing popularity. Photograph: John Mccusker/John McCusker, JPaws

blocks.text: And the news outlet People reported on authorities in the Canadian city of Vancouver returning an African serval to its owners after it escaped and nestled under a neighbor’s porch in June.

The British Columbia province to which Vancouver belongs had just banned keeping exotic cats such as African servals as pets. But, People reported, the owners of such cats were given until the beginning of May 2027 to apply for permits to legally possess them.

articles.title: Iranian actor Laheh Marzban faces severe threats after Venice film festival speech
articles.summary: Marzban, who won a best actress award for her portrayal of a woman held hostage by her father in Falling House, has received condemnations from authorities after dedicating her prize to ‘the women…

blocks.text: An Iranian actress who won the best newcomer award at the Venice film festival has come under severe attack from the country’s authorities and state media after highlighting the plight of women in Iran in her acceptance speech.

Laleh Marzban last Saturday won the best actress award in the Orizzonti sidebar competition for emerging talent, for her role in Mohsen Gharaei’s Falling House, a film revolving around three generations of women who are incarcerated in their own home by the family’s father.

At the awards gala, Marzban dedicated her prize to “the women of my country who have paid the highest price for even the smallest measure of freedom”. Speaking in Farsi, she added that Iranians were experiencing some of the most difficult days of their lives but should not lose hope.

On Thursday, the Supreme Council of the Cultural Revolution, a conservative-dominated government body appointed by Iran’s supreme leader, issued a statement condemning Marzban’s speech as “presenting a one-sided narrative of Iran’s proud society”.

Referring only to “recent statements and behaviour made at the Venice film festival”, it said reducing Iranian women to “the stereotypes desired by western circles […] is not in line with the awareness-raising mission and social commitment of art”.
The statement has come on the back of a raft of similarly worded attacks in state-affiliated Iranian media, some of which called for the actress to be disciplined by the regime.

Zahra Chekhmaghi, a journalist and presenter associated with the Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB), called Marzban “a two-faced person, […] self-interested, hypocritical, despicable and miserable”, while another IRIB-affiliated media personality, actress Zhila Sadeghi, criticised Marzban for not dedicating her speech instead to the children killed in a US missile strike on an elementary school in Minab on 28 February.

On state TV IRIB, a Qu’ran expert said the actress had been “deceived by the enemy” and called on the government to not let her work in Iran. Another news agency, Student News Network (SNN), urged the ministry of culture to not let Marzban back into the country.

The Iranian reaction to Gharaei’s film and Marzban’s speech appears to mirror the pushback against another film that premiered on the Lido this year, Guardian-produced documentary NAZA, about Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza.

Prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu said this week he would seek new laws allowing Israel to strip citizenship from people who “smear” Israeli soldiers, escalating a campaign against NAZA’s directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.

Gharaei’s Falling House thematises the collapse of traditional patriarchal family structures in Iran, and men’s efforts to keep them in place by force. Marzban plays twentysomething Ensi, who announces to her family her plans to leave the country and pursue a modelling career in Turkey. In a desperate effort to assert his authority, her father Rashid (Farhad Aslani) locks Ensi and the other female members of the household in their rooms.

Asked after Falling House’s Venice premiere how the film would be received in Iran, Marzban said: “This question is very important for me as an actress, and as all other women in Iran, whether they be doctors, artists, whatever profession women can perform, we can only make one step at the time, one step towards our objective,” she said.
“I have made my small part. I have given my contribution. I really hope many other people can make small steps towards our common objective.”

articles.title: Senators should take public transport once a week --Win Gatchalian
articles.summary: Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said Friday senators should experience commuting via public transportation at least once a week to better understand the situation faced by commuters.

blocks.text: Published September 18, 2026 5:47pm
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said Friday senators should experience commuting via public transportation at least once a week to better understand the situation faced by commuters.
“That's the only way we will feel and see the needs of our constituents. In fact, dapat kaming mga senador gawin rin namin 'yun to be honest about it,” he said.
(That's the only way we will feel and see the needs of our constituents. In fact, we senators should do the same to be honest about it.)
Gatchalian made the statement during the Senate hearing on the Department of Transportation’s (DOTr) proposed 2027 budget.
He asked Transportation Secretary Giovanni Lopez if the agency’s policy requiring top management to commute once a week is still being implemented. Lopez said he continues to follow the policy.
“Hindi ko pa po binabawi. Ginagawa ko pa rin po. That's once a week...As a matter of fact, we just don't publish it po,” Lopez said.
(I haven't taken it back yet. I'm still doing it. That's once a week...As a matter of fact, we just don't publish it.)
“But to be honest, hindi ko alam kung ginagawa po ng aking mga kasamahan. That's something I cannot check anymore. Pero at least po ginagawa. I have to ask them,” he added.
(But to be honest, I don't know if my colleagues are doing it. That's something I cannot check anymore. But at least it's being done. I have to ask them.)
Gatchalian praised the practice that allows government officials to personally see and experience the challenges faced by commuters.
For Gatchalian, the practice is inspiring.

“I would encourage you and your top management to continue that policy para lang makita natin 'yung totoong situation ng public transportation sector natin. Ako, na-inspire ako doon to be honest about it kasi nakita ko 'yung puso ninyo para sa mga commuters natin. Importante rin 'yun,” he said.

(I would encourage you and your top management to continue that policy just so we can see the real situation of our public transportation sector. I was inspired to be honest about it because I saw your heart for our commuters. That's important too.)

“Hindi naman kailangan mag-Facebook o mag-live o ano.Hindi naman kailangang ganun eh. I think part of the experience and part of the job 'yun. So, sana mag-guilty 'yung mga...nagpaparinig ako. Hindi kayo tine-check ni Secretary pero mag-guilty na lang kayo,” he added.

(You don't have to go on Facebook or go live or anything. You don't have to do that. I think that's part of the experience and part of the job. So, I hope those who are listening to me will feel guilty. The Secretary is not checking you, but you should feel guilty.)
In September last year, Lopez ordered the agency's road and rail officials to take public transportation once a week to better understand the concerns of commuters.
The memorandum aims to implement effective transportation projects and programs, as these officials will experience what daily commuters have to deal with.—AOL, GMA News

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Poa remains VP Sara’s counsel, defense spokesperson in impeachment trial
articles.summary: Lawyer Michael Poa serves as Duterte's legal counsel and defense team spokesperson in her impeachment trial. He stepped down as the Office of the Vice President’s spokesperson in 2024.

blocks.text: Claim: Lawyer Michael Wesley Poa has vacated his post as Vice President Sara Duterte’s spokesperson.

Why we fact-checked this: The claim was posted on September 9 by the Facebook page “Balita at Kaalaman,” which has more than 219,000 followers. The post has reached over 1,800 reactions as of writing.
The post, labeled as “breaking news,” reads, “Atty Michael Poa binitawan na ni #SaraDuterte after kawawain sa harap ng publiko. Grabe ginagawa sayo niyang praning na amo mo atty.”
(Sara Duterte dropped Atty. Michael Poa after being humiliated in public. That paranoid boss of yours is really putting you through a lot, attorney.)
Two other posts, uploaded on September 2 and 7 respectively, mention that Poa has resigned as Duterte’s spokesperson.

A YouTuber by the channel name “Mike Cervera Vlog” also posted a live stream commentary on August 29 with the title “Atty. Michael Poa nag resign na?!” As of writing, it has reached over 180,000 views and 400 comments.
The posts circulated following reports on September 9 that Duterte appointed lawyer Paolo Panelo as the new spokesperson for the Office of the Vice President (OVP).

The facts: Poa already stepped down as Duterte’s spokesperson on November 5, 2024. However, he remains Duterte’s legal counsel and her defense team’s spokesperson in her impeachment trial. He himself confirmed this in a message to the media on the day Panelo’s appointment was announced.
In a September 10 interview on Bilyonaryo News Channel, Poa clarified his role as he addressed social media speculation that he had been replaced or removed from Duterte’s team.

In November 2024, Poa said the OVP pre-terminated his consultancy contract as spokesperson, describing the move as a “mutual decision.” He added that he could not fulfill his contract as spokesperson because he deemed it difficult to face the media without losing objectivity. At the time, Poa was a resource person in a House panel probe into the OVP’s alleged misuse of funds.

In appointing Panelo as its new spokesperson, the OVP said he will “serve as the official point of communication, representing the views and positions of the Vice President and engaging with the media and public on relevant matters.”
Prosecution’s hostile witness: On September 1, Poa temporarily stepped aside as counsel and spokesperson for the Vice President’s defense team to take the witness stand in the impeachment trial.
He became one of the prosecution’s hostile witnesses, called to testify on Article I of the impeachment articles concerning Duterte’s alleged misuse of confidential funds.

During the trial, Poa faced questions around the use of P112.5 million in confidential funds of the Department of Education (DepEd). In his testimony, Poa said that during his time as DepEd undersecretary and chief of staff, he prepared the agency’s response to the 2024 Commission on Audit findings on DepEd’s use of confidential funds.
However, he said that he was unaware that Duterte’s security officer Colonel Dennis Nolasco handled the funds.

He clarified that his involvement in the confidential funds issue only began when he received the audit memorandum, and that he relied on other officials’ reports to respond to COA’s inquiries on the use of the funds. – Lourence Angelo Marcellana/Rappler.com

articles.title: Andrew Hastie says AI advised him to reply ‘congratulations!’ to man who planned to end life with assisted dying
articles.summary:
Liberal MP speaks of AI’s shortcomings as cyber chief tells inquiry the tech is needed to fend off ‘highly capable malicious cyber actors’

  • Get our

blocks.text: When a man with a terminal illness wrote to his local MP Andrew Hastie, telling him he planned on ending his own life with voluntary assisted dying, Microsoft Copilot suggested Hastie reply with “congratulations!”, “great to hear from you” or “that is wonderful news!”.
Hastie shared the episode at a parliamentary inquiry on Friday to underline the shortcomings of the American-run software as he called for AI run by Australians.
The hearing offered the some of the most detailed explanations of the Albanese government’s desire to bring Anthropic and OpenAI to Australia, in the face of calls to slow them down or shut them out.
The defence establishment told the inquiry that cutting the companies out could be catastrophic.
Abigail Bradshaw, the director general of the Australian Signals Directorate, said her agents needed advanced AI every day to fend off “highly capable malicious cyber actors”.

“If a digital adversary has access to newer, more capable models than we do, they may be able to identify and exploit vulnerabilities in systems and networks before we can identify them,” Bradshaw said.
But Australia’s top cyber-intelligence agency is “entirely reliant” on US-housed processing and would “dramatically” lose capability if cut off in a conflict, Bradshaw said.

The defence department’s chief AI officer, Chris Crozier, said the government was already trying to keep its tech needs local, contracting Google to build a series of interlinked datacentres spread across the country and disconnected from the US.
“Somebody can’t wake up and have a bad day and decide they’re going to turn it off,” Crozier said.
“We do not want to be using AI tool sets that are located offshore … we want the compute, we want the application, we want the data, we want the decision making, all based in Australia.”
Bringing big tech into the country would make the job much easier, he said, and not just by allowing the army to protect and maintain its datacentres.
The Office of AI, set up in the prime minister’s department, said bringing firms under Australian law would make it easier for local law enforcement to combat threats on the platforms.
Tight conditions on access could also materially improve Australia’s chances of using and defending itself with the best AI tools in the world, the inquiry heard.
“We will get more assured access, earlier access, more detailed technical access, and better integration with technical experts at the frontier,” Bradshaw said.
These would be assured by strict requirements on any top developers looking to train models in Australia, such as demanding government oversight and early access to advanced models, she suggested.

blocks.caption: The Australian Signals Directorate chief Abigail Bradshaw. Photograph: Mike Bowers/The Guardian

blocks.text: The government is already planning to set the rules for companies that come here. It is consulting on standards that would force AI companies to report issues and breaches and potentially reserve some computational power for local research.
Large datacentres will have to engage with communities, build away from schools and homes, and underwrite new renewables in most states.
after newsletter promotion
Another pillar of the standards – copyright law – is yet to be settled, with AI developers refusing to train models here without law reform.

A proposal to give the companies access to everything Australians create online by default sparked a wave of backlash from creatives, who say the companies could pay for local licensing deals to access Australian content.

But Jenna Priestly, the assistant secretary at the attorney general’s department, on Friday confirmed looser copyright laws would also affect AI access to foreign-made content distributed in Australia.
She said the companies wanted to train models on “maybe billions” of pieces of information and claimed it was practically “impossible” to make deals with every rights holder.

“As Australia’s copyright framework protects not only copyright material that’s Australian in origin, but worldwide, I think it is a fairly large number that [companies] would need to go and strike deals with,” Priestly said.

The Greens senator David Shoebridge, who is among those fighting calls for copyright reform and demanding a pause on AI development, on Friday said Labor had refused him a seat on the inquiry committee.

Labor ministers have spent the week meeting with OpenAI’s vice-president, and Anthropic’s special envoy Jeff Bleich, who this week suggested Australia had just months to bring in effective regulation.

The attorney general’s department told Friday’s hearing the shape and timing of any copyright reform was yet to be decided. But the prime minister’s department said Anthony Albanese wanted draft laws on the broader AI standards by the end of 2026.
Australia’s chance for influence on and special access to the models could be at risk by a delay, Bradshaw said.
“Decisions around training are a matter of urgency,” she said. “I think it is inevitable that those providers will look at other places to locate.”

articles.title: Oktoberfest 2026: Everything you need to know
articles.summary: This year, AI will be used to manage overcrowded situations. Find all the numbers surrounding the fest — including the price of water!

image.caption: Oktoberfest attracts millions of visitors every yearImage: Wolfgang Maria Weber/IMAGO

blocks.text: On Saturday, September 19, at noon, Oktoberfest will once again open with the ceremonial tapping of the keg, during which the mayor of Munich drives a tap into the first wooden barrel of beer and calls out "O'zapft is," a Bavarian phrase that translates to "It's tapped."
His call will be followed by 12 gunshots, a signal that lets all festival tents know that they can start serving beer.
More than 6 million people are expected at the world's largest Volksfest, which runs this year through October 4.
Oktoberfest: What to know about 'the best party in Germany'
Expanded security measures to prevent overcrowding
The festival grounds are enormous: Oktoberfest takes place on Munich's Theresienwiese, a 34.5-hectare site roughly the size of 48 soccer fields.
But crowds can swell, especially on weekends — sometimes to dangerous levels.
Last year, officials had to temporarily close the entrances.

One reason is that nearly all 38 beer tents operate in two or three reservation shifts. When one group of guests leaves and the next arrives at the 14 large tents — which each accommodate several thousand people — huge numbers of visitors end up trying to enter and exit at the same time.
That's how, on one Saturday afternoon at last year's Oktoberfest, the crowds became so dense that movement temporarily came to a standstill. The crush caused some visitors to panic.
To prevent that from happening again, the city of Munich has overhauled its security plan for this year's festival.
Twenty-six new cameras, in addition to 56 police cameras, will monitor the grounds, while an AI system will analyze visitor flows and issue alerts if areas become overcrowded.

blocks.caption: Around 300,000 people were at Oktoberfest simultaneously on the second Saturday of the festival in 2025Image: Frank Hoermann/SVEN SIMON/picture alliance

blocks.text: A newly established coordination center is also intended to improve communication between security agencies and event organizers.
Organizers and police have drawn up a plan to defend against drones over the grounds, though no details have been disclosed.
In addition, 600 police officers will be deployed on site.
Oktoberfest is famous worldwide, but most visitors are local
Oktoberfest may be known around the world as an international tourist attraction, but most of its visitors don't travel very far to get there.
A study commissioned by the city of Munich last year found that the festival remains overwhelmingly regional.

blocks.caption: Statistically speaking, two international guests sit at every 10-person table in the festival tentsImage: Maryam Majd/REUTERS

blocks.text: In 2025, 41% of visitors came from Munich, another 25% from the surrounding area and 9% from elsewhere in the region. In all, three-quarters of Oktoberfest's roughly 6.5 million visitors came from Bavaria. Another 4% came from elsewhere in Germany.

About 21% of visitors — roughly 1.35 million people — traveled from abroad. Americans made up the largest group of international visitors, accounting for just under 20% of the total, or more than 270,000 people. Italians were next, at just over 13%.
Beer prices rise again
Cannabis is banned throughout the festival grounds.

Alcohol, on the other hand, is available in whatever quantities visitors are willing — and able — to pay for. A Mass, the traditional 1-liter mug of beer served at Oktoberfest, costs between €14.80 and €15.90 ($17-$18.25) this year, only slightly more than last year.
A liter of table water comes in at a hefty €11, although the grounds also have several free drinking water fountains.
Visitors planning to enjoy one of Oktoberfest's many rides would be wise to stay relatively sober. Tickets cost anywhere from just under €5 to €14.

Germany's traditional fairground culture was officially added to the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2026, and that tradition remains very much alive at the 191st Oktoberfest. According to organizers, about 90% of the festival's more than 130 fairground operators can trace their roots back to the 19th century.
The festival remains decidedly traditional when it comes to payment, too: Many vendors still accept cash only. Visitors caught without any can withdraw money from ATMs on the grounds.
Dirndl or lederhosen for Oktoberfest?
Then there's the question of what to wear.
Bavarians who take pride in doing things properly generally show up in local traditional dress.

blocks.caption: Traditional garb can be seen at the annual breweries' paradeImage: Felix Hörhager/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The dirndl is the traditional dress worn by women and girls, which consists of close-fitting bodice with a low neckline, a blouse worn under the bodice, a wide high-waisted skirt and an apron.
Men wear lederhosen, the traditional leather shorts or knee-length breeches with suspenders.

For those who are not Bavarian, lederhosen and dirndls are certainly an option, but they're by no means required. Munich's event marketing department, Simply Munich, advises first-time visitors to consider renting traditional garb rather than buying it.

Be aware that locals find cheap imitations of traditional dress off-putting, as Simply Munich points out: "If you want to avoid wry looks, steer clear of Seppl hats, 'leather pants' made of cloth and garish mini plastic dirndls. With jeans and a checkered shirt, you'll definitely be more suitably dressed."
This article was originally written in German.
