articles.title: Weather tracker: Thunderstorms hit Spain as Japan braces for typhoon
articles.summary:
At least one person dead as stormy weather causes severe flooding in Barcelona and Valencia

Intense and slow-moving thunderstorms broke out on Wednesday afternoon across parts of eastern…

blocks.text: Intense and slow-moving thunderstorms broke out on Wednesday afternoon across parts of eastern Spain, bringing some severe flooding and killing at least one person.

Storms first struck over the Castilla-La Mancha regionduring the afternoon before passing over Spain’s east coast, becoming very slow-moving and continuing overnight. Torrential rainfall, strong winds and large hail were reported in Valencia and Barcelona, causing widespread flooding in both cities. Weather stations west of Barcelona recorded some of the highest totals with more than 100mm (4in) of rain falling in the space of a few hours, and locally 70mm in just 30 minutes in the early hours of Thursday morning. Cars and roads were submerged, and flights were cancelled across the region.

Wednesday’s La Liga fixture between Levante and Athletic Club had to be postponed due to flooding at the Estadio Ciudad de Valencia. On Thursday rescuers found the body of a man near Olivella, west of Barcelona, after his car was swept away in the waters. Spain’s east coast is susceptible to extreme rainfall during the autumn months, as experienced in 2024, when devastating flash floods killed more than 200 people in Valencia. With the Mediterranean Sea reaching record temperatures, this is providing extra fuel and moisture to thunderstorms, making flooding more likely.

In New Jersey in the US on Sunday, the Racefaster half marathon was disrupted due to extreme rainfall and a partly submerged course. Runners had to wade through chest-deep waters at times as 50mm-100mm of rain fell. Despite the flooding, 250 people managed to finish the race. Flooding was also reported to the north-east in Connecticut and Rhode Island, where up to 190mm of rain was recorded in a 36-hour period.

Tropical Storm Dujuan, currently over the open west Pacific Ocean, will move north-west on a track towards Japan over the coming days. It is forecast to intensify into a category one typhoon on Friday. The joint typhoon warning centre is forecasting that Dujuan will skirt past the southeast coast of Japan, potentially affecting Tokyo and the surrounding areas.

articles.title: ‘We have something that will kill Elliott’: Icac questions former Labor councillor over message
articles.summary: Sharangan Maheswaran denies message he received about NSW minister was related to work for fugitive property developer

blocks.text: A former Labor councillor says he had a “common interest” with a conservative Liberal operative, but denied that a message he received about damaging the reputation of NSW Liberal minister David Elliott was related to political work for a fugitive property developer, an inquiry has heard.

Sharangan Maheswaran told the Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Friday that a message sent to him by lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood claiming “We have something that will kill Elliott” did not relate to work by Greenwood’s company Beckington for Jean Nassif.
Maheswaran, who is no longer a councillor, was a lawyer to property developer Nassif and became an executive at his company, Toplace, in September 2020.

Icac is examining whether Liberal figures Greenwood, Charles Perrottet and Christian Ellis anticipated receiving $2m in prohibited donations from Nassif in exchange for political outcomes, including damage to the career of former NSW Liberal minister and centre-right faction member David Elliott, who had opposed Toplace developments. Greenwood, Perrottet and Nassif have denied that Nassif paid for political outcomes.
On Friday, Dwyer took Maheswaran to a message Greenwood wrote to him in February 2020 in which he said: “We have something that will kill Elliot.”

Maheswaran replied: “Your ears must be ringing. I just picked up the phone to let you know that I’ve got something decent, and the SMH [Sydney Morning Herald] is going to fire up re [centre-right Liberal MP Alex] Hawke this week off the back of an ALP bill to ban developers.”
Dwyer put it to Maheswaran that the messages showed he shared “a common interest with Beckington in terms of damaging the reputation of David Elliott”.
Maheswaran said he “had a common interest with Mr Greenwood in relation to the Hawke faction of the Liberal party”, but rejected the suggestion the messages related to work by Beckington for Nassif.
When he was asked if Nassif had told him that Elliott had objected to Toplace proposals, Maheswaran said “this is a new invention by Mr Nassif”.

Dwyer asked him if he “seriously contend[ed] to the commission that Jean Nassif never told you that David Elliott was objecting to his proposals”, asking if Maheswaran was suggesting that Nassif had lied to the commission.

Maheswaran said: “His complaint, up to 2025, as I understood it, was that Mr Elliott was backgrounding against him to the media and to various public officials and government officials, but it wasn’t specifically related to any planning process.”

Asked again if Nassif had lied, Maheswaran said “absolutely”. He was shown a draft statutory declaration he sent to a lawyer in 2022 in which he wrote that Nassif had spoken to Elliott about his opposition to a Toplace developments.
Dwyer put it to Maheswaran that he was “happy to assist him [Nassif] with the political outcome he was seeking, which was to get rid of Mr Elliott”.
“I don’t think that was an objective that Mr Nassif was seeking at that point in time,” he responded.

The inquiry heard that Maheswaran came to know Nassif through his daughter Ashlyn Nassif, who was sentenced to a six-month community corrections order earlier this month after pleading guilty to providing false or misleading information to obtain a $150m construction loan from Westpac.
Maheswaran said he was subcontracted to do work for Toplace through Ashlyn Nassif and her sister Evelyn Helou’s law firm EA Legal in late 2019, through another company, Anwalt Pty Ltd.
after newsletter promotion
But he took issue with Dwyer’s suggestion that he and Anwalt were one and the same.

He said: “That’s nonsensical from a corporation’s perspective, from a commercial perspective, from any sort of understanding of contractual law, I’m sorry, Dr Dwyer, I’m speaking in terms of as I understand the world.”
“No problem,” replied Dwyer. Under questioning, Maheswaran accepted that he was the only shareholder and employee of Anwalt at the time.
Dwyer said: “So the only person doing any actual work was you, correct?”
“At that point in time, yes,” said Maheswaran.

Maheswaran told the commission he was paid $1.4m by Toplace between 2020 and 2023, but said he had not disclosed that he was a close associate of a property developer when he nominated for council in 2021, which Dwyer said was required by law.

Icac is investigating whether Maheswaran and fellow Labor Strathfield councillor Karen Pensabene engaged in conduct towards former mayor Matthew Blackmore in a way “that involves the dishonest or partial exercise of their official functions and/or a breach of public trust, including conduct which could involve blackmail” and possible breaches of the Surveillance Devices Act.

When Icac announced its public hearings, Maheswaran told Guardian Australia: “I have every confidence that my actions will be regarded by the public and by any fair tribunal to be lawful and entirely in the public interest.”
On Friday, the inquiry heard that Pensabene had been excused from her summons for medical reasons.
The inquiry continues.

articles.title: ‘We demand the truth’: Olga Tokarczuk and JM Coetzee lead calls for proof of life of disappeared Eritrean writers
articles.summary:
More than 180 writers sign letter renewing calls for information on 12 authors detained incommunicado since 2001 crackdown on free speech by Isaias Afwerki

More than 180 writers have signed…

blocks.text: More than 180 writers have signed a letter to Eritrean president Isaias Afwerki calling for proof of life for 12 writers arrested in 2001.

Nobel laureates Olga Tokarczuk and JM Coetzee join prominent writers including Colm Tóibín, Elif Shafak, Isabel Allende, Ben Okri, Yann Martel, Kamila Shamsie and Tsitsi Dangarembga in signing the letter dated 18 September, marking 25 years since a government crackdown on the independent press. “Within days, Eritrea’s free press and the nation’s independent voices were systematically crushed,” opens the letter.
It lists 12 writers who have been held incommunicado since 2001, including the poet Amanuel Asrat and playwright and journalist Dawit Isaak.

“The families of these writers, the Eritrean people and the global literary community have been met with a painful and unlawful silence,” continues the statement. “To withhold all information regarding their health, location, and survival is a violation of international law and an act of cruelty.”

Along with Asrat and Isaak, the other writers named in the letter are Dawit Habtemichael, Fessehaye “Joshua” Yohannes, Mattewos Habteab, Medhanie Haile, Sahle “Wedi-ltay” Tsegazeab, Said Abdelkadir, Said Idris “Abu Are”, Seyoum Tsehaye, Temesgen Ghebreyesus and Yousif Mohammed Ali. Six of the writers were profiled in the Guardian in 2015.
The letter, signed by 188 writers in total, calls for “immediate, verified proof of life for all arbitrarily detained Eritrean writers and critics”.

Other signatories include Andrei Kurkov, Anthony Doerr, Chloe Aridjis, Lauren Groff, Lemn Sissay, Maaza Mengiste, Madeleine Thien, Margaret Busby, Max Porter, Philippe Sands, Preti Taneja, Tice Cin and Viv Groskop.

“Mr President, Eritrea’s future must be built with its brightest minds, not based on their suppression,” the letter adds. “No writer or journalist should be disappeared for peacefully expressing their views.”
Eritrea operates as a repressive dictatorship under Afwerki, with no national elections held since independence in 1993.
“We remain in solidarity with our missing colleagues, and we will not cease our efforts until they are free,” the letter concludes.

PEN International will attempt delivery of the letter at the Eritrean embassy in London at 10am on Friday. Earlier this year, the organisation launched a petition, open to the public, which also calls for proof of life.

“Twenty-five years is an unbearable length of time for any family to live without knowing whether a loved one is alive,”, said Burhan Sönmez, president of PEN International. “These writers have not disappeared from our memory. We will continue to speak their names, and we will continue to demand the truth about what happened to them.”

articles.title: At least one dead and multiple injured in Philippines school shooting
articles.summary: At least one person is believed to have died and several injured after the shooting in Banga in Mindanao province.

blocks.text: A shooting at a high school in southern Philippines has left at least one person dead and several injured.
The incident happened on Friday afternoon at Banga National High School in South Cotabato, in Mindanao province.
Local media and officials have reporting conflicting casualty figures. The identities of the shooter and the victims have not been confirmed.
The Department of Education said in a statement that it was "deeply concerned by the reported shooting incident".

"Our immediate priority is the safety and well-being of our learners, teachers and school personnel," the statement said, adding it was coordinating with authorities to verify the incident and provide necessary support.
"We urge everyone to remain calm and refrain from sharing unverified information as authorities continue their investigation."

South Cotabato Governor Reynaldo Tamayo told reporters earlier that one person died and four people had been hospitalised. He did not give details on the identity of the shooter, nor did he indicate the shooter was among the dead or injured.
Local media have been reporting much higher casualty figures, citing other Philippine authorities.
Classes have been suspended "in all levels in the entire municipality of Banga" due to the shooting, the Banga disaster management authorities said in a statement.
The Philippine Red Cross said it has deployed medical teams to help out in the aftermath of the shooting.
Police are at the site investigating the shooting, local media reported.
Gun crime is not uncommon in the Philippines, which has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in the region - though school shootings remain rare.

In June, three students were killed and more were injured after their peers opened fire at a high school in central Philippines. Investigators believed the deadly shooting had been motivated by a "grudge" over bullying.

The Department of Education expressed deep concern and is ready to offer psychological support as investigations continue into the shooting.

MANILA, Philippines – At least five students, including the alleged perpetrator, were wounded and have been hospitalized after a gun attack at the Banga National High School in South Cotabato on Friday, September 18, according to Governor Reynaldo Tamayo Jr.
“Lima ang affected na kabataan: apat ang naging biktima at isa ‘yong suspek. Ang suspek ay nagbaril din ng kanyang sarili after niya binaril ‘yong apat,” Tamayo said in a video statement.
“Ngayon ay nando’n lahat sa ospital pero medyo delikado ang kalagayan ng iilan sa kanila,” he said.
(Five minors were affected: four victims and the suspect. The suspect also shot himself after he opened fire. Now, all of them are in the hospital, but some of them are in critical condition.)
The police investigation is still ongoing.
Tamayo said the incident was an “isolated case,” and authorities have sent the students home to “control their emotions.”

“Sa ngayon, manatili lang tayong kalmado. Alam kong mabigat ito sa munisipyo ng Banga at sa mga magulang na nandito, pero wala tayong choice kung hindi pakalmahin muna natin ang ating mga sarili,” he said.
(For now, we must remain calm. I know this is a serious issue for the municipality of Banga and the parents here, but we have no choice but to calm ourselves for now.)

In a statement, the Department of Education (DepEd) said it was deeply concerned by the reported shooting incident, adding that its immediate priority was the safety and well-being of students, teachers, and school personnel.
It said it is ready to provide psychological first aid and mental health and psychosocial support.
“We urge everyone to remain calm and refrain from sharing unverified information as authorities continue their investigation,” the DepEd said.
In June, three students were killed after their two schoolmates opened fire at the San Jose National High School in Tacloban City.
In August, two students died in the shooting incident at Ateneo de Zamboanga’s junior high school campus in Zamboanga City, including the alleged shooter himself.
This is a developing story, and will be updated. – Rappler.com

articles.title: [OPINION] BARMM post-elections: Building a coalition that needs to govern
articles.summary: A healthy parliamentary democracy requires a credible opposition. The BFP should resist the temptation to create an oversized coalition simply to eliminate opposition.

blocks.text: After generally peaceful and democratic parliamentary elections, the region now faces a different — and perhaps more difficult — political challenge: how to govern after the votes have been counted.

Based on unofficial results, four political parties out of 13 appear poised to cross the 2.5% threshold for regional political party representation. The Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP) leads with 16 party seats, followed by the Moro Islamic Liberation Front-led United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) with 15, the clan alliance under the Bangsamoro Grand Coalition (BGC) with 8, and the Bangsamoro People’s Democratic (Raayat) Party with 1.

For the 32 district representatives, incumbent chief minister Abdulraof Macacua of BFP won in Maguindanao del Norte while MILF chairman Ebrahim Murad’s son, Mansor, won the seat in the Special Geographic Area. BFP won a total of 13 district seats, UBJP had 10, and the Adiong-led local party SIAP of Lanao del sur got six. Three other local parties got one seat each.

The six elected sectoral seats all went to the UBJP, thus affirming the sectoral and territorial dominance of the MILF’s UBJP. Two representatives from the indigenous peoples in BARMM were elected by them prior to September 14.

Overall, the 80-member parliament is now comprised of the following: a total of 30 seats for the BFP, 29 seats for UBJP, and 19 seats for the clan-led political parties. This parliament will govern for the next five years.

Many analysts would always equate the BARMM to the national government’s interests which is a given. The Bangsamoro Organic Law ties those interests due to national security risk management, natural resource management, devolution imperatives, and political economy. But that is another matter to discuss.

The numbers in votes tell only part of the story. No party has a majority. And that means the first elected Bangsamoro government will have to be built through coalition, negotiation, compromise, and trust. It also should not lead to a super majority coalition where there is no credible opposition.
What is needed is for a coalition to govern and not just forming a government. The former is difficult, the latter is easy.

With no party dominating the elections, the arithmetic is straightforward. The transition party incumbent BFP’s 30 party seats are not enough to govern alone. An alliance with the UBJP’s 29 seats would produce a dominant majority. But that would leave out the clan-led political parties which is critical for governance.
This is where the real politics begins.

The Bangsamoro parliamentary system was designed to encourage representation and negotiation. Unlike a presidential system where the executive derives a separate electoral mandate, a parliamentary government depends on the ability of political forces inside Parliament to construct a stable governing majority.

A government that survives by one or two votes on every major issue will be unstable. The new governing coalition should be dominant enough to survive disagreements, defections, political shocks, and difficult budget negotiations. The objective should be a stable parliamentary majority, not merely the minimum number needed to elect a chief minister.
Coalition governments inevitably require some distribution of executive responsibility.
But there is a danger. If Cabinet positions become rewards for delivering votes, the new government could reproduce the worst features of traditional Philippine politics.

The BFP-led coalition should instead adopt three principles: representation, competence, and accountability. Coalition partners should have meaningful representation in government. But ministers must also be competent to manage public institutions.

With the elections of the chief minister happening on the first day of convening parliament, a coalition government needs to be formed prior to that. In reality, the incumbent government under the BFP can initiate the formation. The goal should not merely be to find 41 votes to elect a chief minister. The goal should be to build a majority that can govern for five years.

But the first substantive agenda in coalition negotiations would be a governance agenda for a coalition government. The BFP could propose a Bangsamoro Governance Compact 2026–2031, signed by coalition partners before the election of the Chief Minister. The compact could establish a common agenda around on peace, development and governance.
This would shift coalition formation from “What position do I get?” to “What government are we going to build?” That distinction is crucial.
There is another delicate issue. The electoral transition should not be interpreted as the end of the MILF’s political relevance. The Bangsamoro Parliament itself is a product of the peace process.

The presence of former MILF leaders and representatives associated with the movement inside the elected political system is therefore not an anomaly. It is part of the transition from armed struggle to democratic politics.

blocks.caption: No single party gets majority of first-ever elected Bangsamoro Parliament

blocks.text: The challenge is to institutionalize that transition.

The most consequential negotiation may be between the BFP and UBJP. With 30 party seats between them, the two parties could form the nucleus of the next government. But the relationship would carry a significance beyond parliamentary arithmetic. The UBJP represents a political tradition deeply connected to the Bangsamoro peace process and the transition that produced the BARMM.

A BFP-UBJP coalition could therefore symbolize an important political transition: from the politics of the peace process to the politics of democratic parliamentary government, without abandoning the gains of the peace process itself.
The two should not be framed as competing sources of legitimacy. The Bangsamoro needs both.

The future government can draw legitimacy from the peace process, the ballot box, and the communities represented by elected district and sectoral leaders. The challenge is to bring these sources of legitimacy together. That would be a genuine measure of the success of the peace process.

The new parliament is likely to include representatives associated with powerful political families and local networks, including the Adiongs, Ampatuans, Gandamras, Hatamans, Mangundadatus, Midtimbangs, Sinsuat, etc.
These representatives should not automatically be dismissed as “clan politicians.”
They represent real constituencies. Their voters have concerns about roads, schools, hospitals, agriculture, fisheries, livelihood, security, local government, and access to public services.

The question is not whether these representatives have local political interests. Of course they do. The question is how those interests are incorporated into a transparent regional development agenda. The new government should establish transparent criteria for allocating public resources, while giving district representatives a legitimate role in setting regional priorities.

Representation must also mean geographic balance. The Bangsamoro is geographically and politically diverse. The composition of the executive should reflect this diversity. This is especially important for communities that historically have felt distant from the regional government like the Special Geographic Area carved out from the North Cotabato Province. A coalition government that promises inclusion but remains concentrated around the region’s established political centers will quickly lose credibility.
There is another important principle. Not everyone should be brought into the government.

A healthy parliamentary democracy requires a credible opposition. The BFP should resist the temptation to create an oversized coalition simply to eliminate opposition. This is what happened at the national level that should not be replicated.

An opposition can strengthen government. It can expose weaknesses, question expenditures, scrutinize appointments, challenge policies, and force ministers to explain their decisions. A Parliament in which everyone is part of the government risks becoming a Parliament where nobody is accountable.

The ideal arrangement is therefore: a broad governing coalition, a legitimate opposition, strong parliamentary committees, and active civil society. That is how parliamentary democracy becomes more than an institutional design. It becomes a political culture.

The 2026 parliamentary election should ultimately be judged not only by whether it was peaceful. It should also be judged by what happens after the election. The most important question of all: can the government be seen, felt, and deliver tangible improvements in the lives of ordinary Bangsamoro?. – Rappler.com

Tom Villarin is a political science professor at the Ateneo de Manila University. He served in the 17th Congress as Akbayan Party List representative. He also was former local government undersecretary under the Noynoy Aquino administration.

articles.title: Deepfake doctors peddling bogus cures are becoming more convincing — and very little can be done to stop them
articles.summary: Physicians warn AI-generated ads featuring the likenesses of prominent doctors are scamming patients out of their money, putting Canadians’ health at risk and eroding public trust. Yet there’s still…

image.caption: B.C. Provincial Health Officer Dr. Bonnie Henry, shown on a smartphone screen during a news conference in February 2021, is among the prominent Canadian physicians being "deepfaked" on social media. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: During the COVID-19 pandemic, B.C. Provincial Health Officer Dr. Bonnie Henry became a familiar face across the country, appearing regularly at news conferences and in media clips.
Then her face and voice started popping up somewhere else: in AI-generated videos on social media, where her likeness was used to peddle supposed health products, including a prostate treatment.
"It really scared me initially, because it was so easy for people to make it look like I was saying things that were just not true," Henry recalled in a recent interview with CBC News.
Known as deepfakes, the online ads are "disturbing," she added, "because you know that people are taking things that are real and distorting them."

items: As more teens turn to AI for emotional support, experts say it's no substitute for human connection

blocks.text: Henry is far from the only prominent Canadian physician whose likeness has been faked in questionable social media ads — and who has found little recourse.

Dr. François Marquis, chief of intensive care at Maisonneuve-Rosemont Hospital in Montreal, said he's heard from multiple patients and colleagues that videos featuring his likeness — all selling a range of pills or products — keep popping up on Facebook.

"This time I'm selling something that is supposed to fix your joints," he said, referring to the latest AI-generated ad. "And what is getting bolder is, now I'm offering $1 million if you're not a satisfied customer."
Canadian doctors selling meds online? Those are AI deepfakes

Marquis and other physicians say these videos are scamming patients out of their money, putting Canadians' health at risk, and eroding public trust. Yet there's still no clear method to get deepfake videos taken down, multiple doctors agreed.

items: He runs a secret AI slop empire from Vietnam. Here’s how we found him

blocks.text: "A few years ago, when this started to happen to me, nobody had any policies, nobody knew what to do," said Henry, who eventually filed cease and desist letters to multiple parties in hopes of combating the wave of deepfakes using her voice and face.
But she says her complaints are still hitting roadblocks today.

"I think our organizations — whether it's police services, whether it's universities, whether it's employment organizations — they're not really prepared yet to support people who are going through this," she said.
Don’t fall for this deepfake scam using AI-generated images of doctors, Quebec physicians warn
Scams 'only going to get more convincing'
The term "deepfakes" refers to a digital likeness of a real person, including their facial movements and voice, created by AI.
The videos have exploded online in recent years and the quality has dramatically improved, too, making fake videos of politicians, celebrities or physicians increasingly tough to spot.
One study found up to 50 per cent of people couldn't distinguish deepfakes from authentic videos about scientific subjects — and that was three years ago.

items: Will rogue AI development mean the end of humanity? Experts weigh in
AI 'fearmongering' could harm Canada’s rare opportunity, says top CEO

blocks.text: "It's only going to get more sophisticated," warned Timothy Caulfield, a researcher and professor focusing on health law and science policy at the University of Alberta.
"These kinds of scams — and that's really what they are — are only going to get more convincing."

While there's no major Canadian research yet on the prevalence of doctor deepfakes on platforms like Facebook and TikTok, a 2024 report in the British Medical Journal noted they're increasingly common in the U.K., while American policymakers are considering a bill — dubbed the "NO FAKES Act" — to combat the growing trend of AI deepfakes in the U.S.
Canadian physicians say more research and recourse is needed here as well, alongside public education to help patients avoid getting scammed.
New AI deepfakes law 'too little, too late' for Halifax woman
Concern over fake drugs, dangerous health advice
Marquis recalled a victim of one deepfake scam who came looking for him in the ICU, wanting his money back for pills that were never delivered.
"It was very sad, because that person invested hundreds of dollars in those pills and never received anything," he said.

items: Why are AI leaders calling for a slowdown?
Why are there suddenly so many data centres planned in Canada? Your questions answered

blocks.text: Marquis's bigger fear is patients ordering and consuming fake drugs, or following false advice to stop their medications.

Despite those risks, he routinely struggles to get deepfake videos taken down before new ones pop back up — even though he's flagged them to social media platforms, Quebec's medical college and the police.
"Basically I was told that there's nothing they can really do," he said.
He lost $3,000 after falling for a fake Carney ad pushing for crypto
Canada lacks 'co-ordinated response'

As part of an effort to clamp down on deepfakes and other AI-related security issues, the federal government has in recent years taken measures such as expanding the Canadian AI Safety Institute and introducing legislation to combat non-consensual sexualized deepfakes — dubbed the Protecting Victims Act — and AI-generated electoral misinformation.
Anyone who may have been a victim of cybercrime can file a police report or contact the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre, a federal bulletin from 2024 noted.
CBC News has contacted Science and Economic Development Canada for comment on how it is tackling medical deepfakes, specifically.

items: Canada's AI strategy aims to make health data more accessible. How will it protect privacy?

blocks.text: Dr. Fahad Razak, an internist at St. Michael's Hospital and Canada Research Chair in Healthcare Data and Analytics at the University of Toronto, said there still isn't a "co-ordinated" response to the problem across Canada.

"And what makes it very challenging is that a lot of the media we consume in Canada is not generated in Canada," he added. "We don't have enforcement mechanisms and the ability to save and filter out content from certain parts of the world."
Fact check: Ads on Facebook link to Carney deepfakes
Videos selling products can be 'red flag'
For now, much of the onus to spot and avoid deepfake scams falls on the public.
"I think that any time content is being pushed to you and they're selling a product, that should be a major red flag," said Caulfield.

That's even more true for Canadian doctors supposedly selling health drugs or treatments, since provincial and territorial medical colleges enforce strict standards, noted the Canadian Medical Association (CMA) in an awareness post earlier this year.

items: Quebec physicians warn of deepfake scams using their likeness to sell medications

blocks.text: "Although the precise rules vary, the intent is clear: doctors cannot publicly endorse health products in ads, on social media or in interviews," the CMA stated. Those products are defined by Canada's Food and Drugs Act as any regulated drugs, biologics, medical devices or natural health products.
Razak encouraged people to be highly skeptical of any videos featuring a doctor selling medical goods.
"If you think about your own physician experience, how often is a physician pulling out a drawer of material and trying to sell you something?" he said.
"That's not how our health-care system works."

articles.title: Starbucks workers in Hamilton hope to tackle wage, customer harassment issues in negotiating 1st contract
articles.summary: A group of Hamilton Starbucks workers who joined United Steelworkers this month aims to address issues including harassment by customers and an unclear wage structure as they prepare to negotiate…

image.caption: Workers at the Starbucks on 112 King St. E. in Hamilton voted to join United Steelworkers earlier this month. (Justin Chandler/CBC)

blocks.text: Hamilton

A group of Hamilton Starbucks workers who joined United Steelworkers this month aims to address issues including harassment by customers and an unclear wage structure as they prepare to negotiate their first collective agreement, the union and a worker told CBC Hamilton.
Downtown workers joined United Steelworkers this month, among union shops at Starbucks in Ontario
A group of downtown Hamilton Starbucks workers has unionized in an attempt to address issues including harassment by customers and an unclear wage structure, the United Steelworkers union (USW) says.

Employees at the Starbucks by Gore Park reached out to USW to join and voted in a process supervised by the Ontario Ministry of Labour in early September, local USW co-ordinator John Catto told CBC Hamilton.
This is at least the sixth Starbucks location in Ontario to organize with USW, Catto said Wednesday. The union also represents Western Canada workers with the coffeehouse chain.
In May 2025, USW announced shops in Ajax, Kitchener-Waterloo and Toronto had negotiated their first collective agreements.

items: 5 Starbucks shops in Ontario ratify first collective agreements

blocks.text: "We felt that without [a union] we didn’t really have a voice," one of the Hamilton workers said in an interview Thursday.
CBC is not naming them out of concerns speaking out will negatively impact their employment.
The worker, a barista at the 112 King St. E. location, has been with the company for several years.

The barista said they reached out to USW about unionizing because they remembered hearing about a Kitchener store joining, and thought it would be the worker's best shot at tackling workplace issues that employees felt managers weren't addressing.
USW's news release said the workers raised issues including:

items: Health and safety concerns, particularly about harassment from customers.
Unclear time and attendance rules that could lead to dismissal.
A lack of recognition of seniority and limited opportunities for longtime employees.
Corporate changes focused on higher prices and increased volume that affect workers.
A need for a clear wage structure and benefits that don't change when Starbucks shifts its approach to business.

blocks.text: Company success 'starts and ends' with workers
CBC Hamilton asked Starbucks to respond to the workers' concerns.

In an emailed statement Tuesday, spokesperson Mary Franssen said the company's success "starts and ends" with its employees. In July, the company reported $9.3 billion in revenues for the 13-week period ending on June 28, 2026.

"We respect the right of all partners to make their own decisions regarding unions, whether they favour or oppose representation, and will continue to work together to make Starbucks the best job in retail."
Franssen didn't directly address the issues in the union's news release.

In August, Starbucks Workers United, a union representing what it says is more than 12,000 baristas in the U.S., called for a public boycott of the store until the workers there, calling for higher wages and better working conditions, get a contract.

items: Hamilton café Democracy closes suddenly, laying off workers months after unionization

blocks.text: The newly unionized Hamilton workers don't yet have dates for negotiating a collective agreement, Catto said.
He hopes to meet with the workers soon to help get that process started.
USW will reach out to other unionized Starbucks locations to learn from their contract negotiations, Catto added.

The Hamilton barista said it has been awkward between employees and managers at work since the Starbucks in the city organized, but they're hopeful a collective agreement can improve conditions and raise the bar at other locations.
"I see this as being able to be a beacon of hope for other stores," they said.
They also said customers have congratulated the workers on unionizing.
Unionized shop in B.C. closed 3 years ago
In 2023, Starbucks closed its only unionized shop in Vancouver.

USW brought a complaint before the B.C. Labour Relations Board. In February 2025, the board found the company had legitimate reasons to shut down the Vancouver location, but found Starbucks wrongfully made "threats of adverse consequences" against a union-supporting employee.
Catto said that to his knowledge, no Starbucks workers have lost their jobs for unionizing with USW in Ontario.
In recent years, employees at similar workplaces to Starbucks have unionized in Hamilton, including at Coven Market and the café Democracy.
Democracy closed in December, and workers raised questions about the timing.
The Hamilton barista said they think any worker curious about organizing their workplace should reach out to a union and ask about the process.
Catto agreed.

"I've been a unionized worker for 30 years or so," he said. "The union dues that I pay have been worth every penny. If anybody's employer is not treating them in a manner that is fair or treating them without dignity and respect, then you probably need a union."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Justin Chandler is a CBC News reporter in Hamilton. He covers stories of all kinds from places including picket lines, court rooms, council meetings and research labs. Justin has a special interest in how public policy affects people, and loves a quirky human-interest story. Before CBC Hamilton, he worked for TVO and on a variety of CBC teams and programs. He co-hosted Radio Free Krypton on Met Radio.

articles.title: At first, Rick Hansen fought the idea of a wheelchair. But then it became a vehicle for his freedom
articles.summary: At first, Rick Hansen saw his wheelchair as a symbol of limitations, eschewing what would eventually help propel him around the globe and shatter the true barriers: stigma and a world designed for…

image.caption: Rick Hansen and his wife, Amanda, share some of the private moments from the Man in Motion Tour 40 years ago, which propelled the issue of accessibility to the forefront. (Tessa Lloyd/Rick Hansen Foundation)

blocks.text: The Current

At first, Rick Hansen saw his wheelchair as a symbol of limitations, eschewing what would eventually help propel him around the globe and shatter the true barriers: stigma and a world designed for the able-bodied. When he overcame that, it became a vehicle for his freedom and advocacy.
40 years ago, Hansen wheeled himself around the world, shattering stigma and raising $26M
LISTEN | An interview with Rick and Amanda Hansen:
The Current25:45Rick and Amanda Hansen reflect on the “Man in Motion” Tour

At first, Rick Hansen saw his wheelchair as a symbol of limitations, eschewing what would eventually help propel him around the globe and shatter the true barriers: stigma and a world designed for the able-bodied.
Instead, he often used crutches and leg braces to get around after he was paralyzed from the waist down at 15 when he was thrown from the back of a pickup truck in rural B.C.

“I had this stigma about it and I tried to avoid it with everything I possibly could,” he said of his wheelchair in a recent interview with The Current. “It was one of my greatest handicaps at that time."
Eventually, he realized the issue was not his legs. Nor was it the wheelchair.

“It's coming from, usually, your mind and your heart and the precepts that you have,” he said. “You try to remove them and redefine them so that you're liberated and free … and you now see the wheelchair as your vehicle for mobility and freedom.”

When he set out on the Man in Motion Tour on March 21, 1985, what he was most determined to do, he says, was to showcase the athleticism and power that still lived within his body and inside others with disabilities.

On May 22, 2027, 40 years will have passed since Hansen finished that tour, wheeling across 34 countries and 40,000 kilometres to raise $26 million. A film documenting that 26-month journey premiered at the Toronto Film Festival this week, Man in Motion: The Rick Hansen Story, with the final screening on Saturday.

Not only did his wheelchair take him around the world, Hansen has said his epiphany about it shifted his advocacy primarily to making spaces accessible, rather than on walking again, though the Rick Hansen Foundation has contributed heavily to spinal cord research.

That acceptance distinguishes Hansen from other high-profile people with spinal cord injuries, like Christopher Reeve; in a Globe and Mail interview in 2010, Hansen told the publication that the hope of walking unassisted one day is not the thing that drives him.
"My life is full," he said at the time.
The making of the man in motion
While many Canadians are familiar with Hansen’s legend, the film unearths the private moments from that time and how the physical and psychological toll caused the B.C.-born athlete to doubt himself.
The first moment of reckoning came as Hansen faced the brutal foothills of California’s Siskiyou Mountains. He already had tendonitis in wrists, and it was only Day 2.

"I was like, literally, completely filled with fear, uncertainty, and I needed some big time support,” he said. “That summit was, like, the first massive challenge. And I knew that if we could get up that one, maybe, maybe, maybe there was some hope."

That support arrived in the form of his physiotherapist, Amanda Reid. She had already helped him recover from a dislocated shoulder in April 1984 after he crashed going 80 km/h test-driving a new wheelchair he wanted to use on the tour.
Hansen said she quickly became the person he turned to for encouragement.
“With each passing mile, I grew more and more fond of her and eventually was in love with her,” he recalls.
They both acknowledge the tour tested their relationship.

But by the time the team returned to Canada in 1986, public support had picked up. This was before social media, Hansen reminds Current host Matt Galloway, so they were relying on "snail mail and carrier pigeons."
That buoyed the couple and the team itself.

As they moved through New Brunswick, Hansen proposed and the pair would be married the next year. They now have three daughters and five grandsons and have continued their advocacy work through the Rick Hansen Foundation, which funds spinal cord research and has also developed a accessibility certification for public and private buildings.
And it was Amanda who talked him through one of the most challenging and remarkable moments on the journey: the Great Wall of China.

In his mind, Hansen says he had pictured wheeling up the Great Wall as a symbol of his journey — but they arrived to find 103 stairs he would have to navigate. He recalls not wanting to get out of the van and have his supporters see him being carried.

But Amanda said she "was quite blunt" and told him there were people with disabilities waiting for him, that his team had been “carrying [him] since the beginning” and that this was another example of their support.
Hansen says he agrees that while he was the one in the wheelchair and the face of the campaign, his journey was that of a team.
Rick Hansen scales the Great Wall of China

For every moment where Hansen was able power through 13 hours of wheeling each day, in rain, up mountains and alongside angry drivers, there were others — like the Great Wall — that reminded him exactly why he was doing this.

He would be invited to give a speech, and there would be steps to get onto the stage. In hotel rooms, he would have to crawl across the floor to get through spaces his wheelchair could not. And the ensuite washrooms were almost never accessible, he said.

“The world was built not for people with disabilities, it was built for an average person,” he said. “So this was the beginning of what I think is a global movement, you know, where hundreds of millions of people say, ‘That's not good enough. We're building a society for all of us.’”
'He inspired all of us,' says Rick Hansen about his basketball teammate Terry Fox.
Terry Fox

During his journey, Hansen had a touchstone that kept him going on the hardest days. Inside the support van, was a small statue of Terry Fox, with whom Hansen became close friends after playing wheelchair basketball together.

“When you think about quitting, you think about, well, 'Terry wouldn't have quit,'” Hansen said, his voice quavering. “Get out of the motor home. Get into the cold steel chair. Put on the wet slimy gloves. Push out again."
He paused.
“See how far you can go [but] don't make the decision here," he said. "Terry's inspiration was, was there with me through the entire journey — and is today.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Laura Fraser is a senior writer and editor with CBC Radio and is based in Halifax. She writes about justice, health and the human experience. Story ideas are welcome at laura.fraser@cbc.ca

articles.title: Japan raises interest rate to new 31-year high to curb rising prices
articles.summary: Central banks around the world have hiked rates as high energy prices are pushing up inflation.

blocks.text: Japan's central bank has raised its main interest rate to a fresh 31-year high as it continues to move away from decades of ultra-low borrowing costs and as the country faces increasing economic pressures.
In a widely expected move on Friday, the Bank of Japan (BOJ) increased the rate from 1% to 1.25% - a level not seen since 1995.
It comes as major central banks around the world are hiking rates as higher energy prices caused by the Iran war are helping to push up inflation.
On Wednesday, the US Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate for the first time in over three years, while the European Central Bank also increased its borrowing costs earlier this month.
The BOJ has been raising the rate since 2024, when it stood at minus 0.1%. It has now hiked rates six times in the last two and a half years.
Since then the bank has been steadily putting up the rate as it tries to reach a level similar to other major economies.
When a central bank raises rates, known as tightening monetary policy, the country's currency usually becomes stronger as it makes the it more attractive to traders.
"One of the world's last sources of ultra-cheap money is disappearing," said market analyst Lale Akoner from investment company eToro.
Japan is facing several economic challenges including a persistently weak yen, rising prices and a shrinking workforce.
Official figures published on Friday ahead of the BOJ announcement showed that inflation eased slightly last month.
Core inflation fell to 1.7% in August from 1.8% the previous month but remains close to the bank's 2% target level.
While Japan's inflation rate is not high by international standards, rising prices are a relatively new development in the economy.
Until recently the country had experienced very low inflation or deflation - falling prices - for around three decades.
Global oil and gas prices have risen this year as the Iran war caused major disruptions to shipments through the key Strait of Hormuz shipping route.
Japan is particularly vulnerable to those supply interruptions as it is heavily reliant on energy from the Middle East.
The country's currency has also been under pressure in recent months.
In August, Tokyo and Washington confirmed that they had jointly intervened to halt a slide in the yen after it fell to a fresh 40-year low.
The coordinated intervention was the first since 2011, when both countries took action together to weaken the yen after the devastating earthquake and tsunami that hit eastern Japan.
Both Japan's Ministry of Finance and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said at the time that they would not hesitate to conduct more joint interventions in the future.
Bessent has also been ramping up pressure on the BOJ to raise interest rates to help support the yen, calling on its Governor Kazuo Ueda to "do the right thing".
"If [the yen] remains weak despite higher rates, the resulting inflation pressure could force the BOJ to tighten faster than markets or Japan's government would like," Akoner said.

articles.title: Japan raises interest rates to 31-year high to curb impact of rising prices
articles.summary: Increase from 1% to 1.25% follows US Federal Reserve and European Central Bank tightening monetary policy

blocks.text: Japan’s central bank has increased interest rates to a fresh 31-year high as it attempts to combat high global inflation linked to the war in Iran.
The Bank of Japan voted to raise its target interest rate from 1% to 1.25%, the highest level since 1995.

The move meant the BoJ joined the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank in tightening monetary policy this month, as central banks attempt to curb the impact of rising prices, linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
The Bank of England on Thursday voted to leave UK interest rates on hold at 3.75% but warned they could soon rise amid the fallout from the Iran war.

The BoJ has been raising rates since 2024, when it lifted its base rate out of negative territory. It has been under pressure to raise borrowing costs as the yen weakened steadily against the dollar this year, to levels that prompted policymakers to intervene to stabilise the currency. The Japanese currency weakened about 0.7% against the dollar on Friday.
The vote to raise rates was not unanimous – with two board members dissenting to the increase.

“The tone of the statement, along with two dissenters for the decision to raise rates, leaves lingering doubts that Japan’s central bank will be cautious in tightening monetary policy further,” ⁠Fred Neumann, the chief Asia economist at HSBC, said.
“While back-to-back hikes appear unlikely, investors will look for clues as to whether officials are prepared to raise interest rates again in December.”

The drop in ​the yen helped the Nikkei stock market index to rise nearly 2%, while the Japanese two-year government ‌bond yields, which are most sensitive to ‌monetary policy expectations, fell four basis points to 1.82%.
European stock futures slipped 0.35%, indicating a lower open.

Prashant Newnaha, a senior rates strategist at TD Securities, said the BOJ reiterated its concerns that underlying inflation could deviate upwards from its 2% target, but “we don’t see a smoking gun supporting a back-to-back hike ‌in October”.
He said: “We stick with our call for rate hikes roughly every quarter with the next 25 basis points hike in December.”

articles.title: VAR's mission creep a problem for football
articles.summary: After a decade of use, questions around VAR in football are louder than ever. Has the technology strayed too far from its remit?

image.caption: How much technology is too much? VAR appears to have strayed too far from its original missionImage: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Another domestic football season is underway and already, in mid-September, the shortcomings of technology in sport are at the center of the discourse once again.

The video assistant referee (VAR) is perhaps the most discussed technology in modern sport. While video replays have been in use for years in sports like American football, rugby or cricket, it has only been a decade since the International Football Association Board (IFAB), the highest regulatory authority in the sport, approved the use of VAR.

With artificial intelligence (AI) reportedly reaching dangerous levels of development and technological optimization of people's lives at an all-time high, it is perhaps a pertinent time to consider the use of technology in sport. Has it finally evolved from a supporting role to an all-powerful, game-altering one?

"The idea behind VAR was that technology could reduce human error while leaving the referee in charge," Susmit Gulavani, an assistant professor in AI and machine learning in sport at the University of South Carolina, told DW.

"Over time, however, VAR has expanded in both its use and its influence. The introduction of newer technologies, such as AI-assisted Semi-Automated Offside Technology (SAOT), has made it an increasingly central part of decision making. While these advances have improved the precision of offside decisions, they have also raised expectations that technology should deliver perfect outcomes," he said.

"That is where the sense of "mission creep" comes from. VAR is now expected to resolve almost every contentious decision, even though many incidents, such as fouls or handball decisions, still require human interpretation."

That pursuit of perfection often leaves fans waiting and confused, and it breaks up a game that is fast and fluid. The World Cup this summer was evidence of that. And yet, if anything, the technology looks like it is finding more ways to embed itself into the sport.
VAR in the Bundesliga under the spotlight
It has been nine years since VAR was introduced to the Bundesliga.

After the World Cup, German officials confirmed that VAR will also be allowed to have a say in second yellow cards and corner kicks in the Bundesliga. Granting technology additional powers did not go down well with organized fan groups in the country though, who launched a coordinated campaign calling for VAR to be scrapped in August this year. The broad message was that the technology has "robbed football of its joy" and that it was time to put the cameras back in the box.

This is particularly significant in Germany, where many fans are club members and therefore have genuine influence over the actions of their club and the governance of the game. Jochen Drees, the head of VAR operations in Germany, has however argued for refining the technology rather than removing it – a natural tendency, according to Gulavani.
VAR mission creep a symbol of technology's power
"VAR is a useful example of a broader societal pattern. As technology becomes more capable, we increasingly rely on it, but we also have to decide where its role should begin and end," he said.

"The appeal is understandable because AI can significantly improve efficiency and productivity. Tasks that once took hours can often be completed in minutes. At the same time, this expansion raises important questions about privacy, transparency, accountability, environmental costs, and where human judgment should remain central."
Is AI the better referee?
What will technology in sport look like in the future?
Sport without this technology is unlikely. Business, recruitment and event management are already finding ways to be more efficient thanks to the introduction of AI and other technologies.

As for VAR, perhaps a different system is required. At the U20 men's football World Cup last year, challenge cards, as seen in the NFL for example, were trialed. Coaches could ask for situations to be reviewed, reducing the interference of constant replays and slow-motion assessments. Reportedly, trialing of the approach, officially called Football Video Support (FVS), continues but it is likely seen as a cheaper alternative to the expensive VAR rather than a replacement.
"The key is to treat technology as decision support rather than decision replacement," Gulavani said. "

AI and technologies like VAR are good at processing large amounts of information quickly and consistently, but they cannot fully understand the context, intent, or nuance that many sporting decisions require. Human referees are still needed to interpret the Laws of the Game and exercise judgment in situations where there is no objectively 'correct' answer."

A return to a previous era seems unlikely, but the challenge is familiar. Can sport find a way to return technology to a supporting role rather than one that governs it to such an extent that it removes human engagement and emotion? If it can, perhaps those ripples will be felt beyond the white lines of sporting arenas.

articles.title: Organized crime and drug-related deaths rise Germany
articles.summary: Presenting its annual report for organized crime, the German police said that cocaine was a danger for the state and society, and that the cases of money laundering had increased.

image.caption: There were more drug-related deaths in Germany in 2025 than in the previous year Image: Fabrizio Bensch/REUTERS

blocks.text: "We are experiencing a flood of cocaine in Germany," German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, from the Christian Democrats (CDU), said earlier this week as a new police report was presented. "We are experiencing a record number of drug-related deaths. We are seeing children being exploited as criminals."

Standing alongside Dobrindt, Holger Münch, the president of the Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), and Hendrik Streeck, the German government's drug and addiction commissioner, presented findings described as alarming.

blocks.caption: Holger Münch, Alexander Dobrindt and Hendrik Streeck presented the organized crime report this weekImage: Annette Riedl/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Last year, 10 tons of cocaine were seized, two thirds of that amount in German ports. And 2,150 people lost their lives because of drug use, 13 more than in 2024.

Profits generated from drugs by international organized crime networks are often invested in real estate to conceal their origin. Münch said that 195 cases of money laundering, amounting to almost €1.4 billion (ca. $1.6 billion) had been investigated in 2025.
"They [the criminals] use their considerable financial clout to bribe and to exert influence," he said. "And they launder the money and funnel it into the legal economic system."
He added that the most widely used drug was cocaine and that it posed a threat to the state, the economy and society as a whole.
'There is blood on every gram of cocaine consumed for pleasure'
"It is not only the state that is being damaged," said Streeck. "Above all, it is people who are being damaged."
About 83% of the drug-related deaths concerned men, whose average age was 41.
"They are all customers of a market that deals in deadly substances and is driven by violence, environmental destruction, extortion and exploitation," said Streeck, who trained as a doctor.

He insisted that there should be zero tolerance for those who profited from addiction and zero indifference to those suffering from it. His focus is on preventative measures, which include a public awareness campaign about the impact on health and the environment.

He explained that in some countries, rainforests were being cleared to make way for cocaine production. Streek pointed out that toxic substances used for processing the drug, such as kerosene or battery acid, ended up in the soil and water. Farmers and their families were blackmailed. He lamented the fact that cocaine had become more popular in Germany.
"There is blood on every gram of cocaine consumed for pleasure," the drug and addiction commissioner stated.
Cocaine, Crime, Cartels: Can Europe fight back?
Digitalization of drugs trade
Streeck added that the situation had changed significantly in recent years and the market had gone digital.
"Dealers are no longer on the street corner; they're on the phone. For example, people can order so-called 'cocaine taxis' [cars that deliver drugs to any location] via QR code," he said.

"What is particularly alarming is that criminal groups are recruiting minors through social media or gaming platforms," he added. "Organized criminals look for recruits in the places where young people spend their free time."

Münch noted that this development posed a particular challenge for German and international law enforcement agencies. He said that, more and more, the cliched image of organized crime — discretion, isolation and closed structures — was a thing of the past. The fact that people can purchase criminal services on the dark web represents a paradigm shift, according to Münch: "It's not just a question of who commits a crime, but of who ordered it, who financed it, who is profiting from it?"
Moreover, there is a suspicion on the part of investigators that state actors are increasingly involved in opaque crime activities, launching attacks as "hybrid threats."
Münch said that "money laundering, corruption and violence can contribute to social destabilization."
Risky business: European dock workers helping drug cartels

In 2025, there were about 600 investigations into cases of organized crime in Germany, which has been the average for the past five years. The German police considers one of its major successes to be the shutdown of the Archetyp Market, an online drug marketplace on the darknet. Its administrator was arrested in June 2025. He had overseen the sale of cocaine, heroin, cannabis and other drugs, amounting to 250 million. When the platform was shut down there were 3,200 registered sellers and 612,000 customer accounts according to the police.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: South Korea will not send military to support US war on Iran, defying Trump pressure
articles.summary:
Seoul resolves recent speculation over sending military to strait of Hormuz, saying ‘there won’t be deployment that would involve or enter war’

South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, has…

blocks.text: South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, has said he will ⁠not deploy the military to the ⁠Middle East in a way ​that could draw the country into conflict, resisting calls from Donald Trump to support his war in Iran.
“There won’t be deployment that would involve or enter war. I can tell you that very clearly,” Lee said at a ⁠news conference on Friday. “We won’t deploy military assets in any form to that end.”

However, Lee added that he was reviewing whether to play a greater role in safeguarding navigation in the region. South Korea maintains a naval presence off the coast of Somalia as part of an anti-piracy mission.
“[It] is also clear that we must do the minimum as other countries do to ​protect our commercial shipping and crude shipments, and also the safety of ‌our people,” he said.

Trump has criticised Seoul for what he called insufficient support for the Iran war ‌and scaled back major joint military drills by the two countries’ armed forces this summer, a move that unsettled the US ally.
South Korea’s government has been reviewing a ‌possible military deployment to the Strait of Hormuz, although the idea is proving unpopular domestically.

Asked about progress in reaching an agreement with the US on Seoul’s US investment commitments under its trade deal with Washington, Lee said concern over the commercial viability of the package was the main sticking point.
Lee said there were elements that were difficult for Seoul to accept, but that the two sides were nearing an agreement.
South Korea committed last year to invest $350bn in US manufacturing in return for Washington lowering tariffs on Korean imports to 15%.
Seoul this week postponed ‌a parliamentary briefing on the investment plans, which is expected to take place next week instead.

The South Korean president also said it was possible that a meeting could take place in the coming months between Trump and the North Korean leader, Kim Jong-un, but many factors needed ​to align for that to happen.
“What’s clear is that President Trump wants talks, and I want him to as well, and we’re continuing coordination to make dialogue between the North and the US possible,” he said.

North Korean state media has so far remained largely silent on the repeated calls from Trump for such a meeting. Trump has been pushing aides for a meeting with Kim as soon as the autumn, the Wall Street Journal has reported.

articles.title: Indonesia gets its first aircraft carrier amid debate over cost and military ambitions
articles.summary:
The gift from Italy has sparked fierce debate among defence analysts and opposition politicians who question its true cost and purpose

Indonesia has received its first aircraft carrier, a…

blocks.text: Indonesia has received its first aircraft carrier, a former Italian warship that the government says will strengthen the archipelagic nation’s maritime security and disaster response capabilities.

The 41-year-old former ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi, with capacity for short takeoff and vertical landing aircraft and helicopters, arrived Friday morning at a naval base in North Jakarta’s Tanjung Priok port, where it was welcomed with a military ceremony.

Italy in March agreed to give the carrier, which was retired in 2024, to Indonesia in a move aimed at boosting Italy’s broader defence engagement with the south-east Asian country. Italy is seeking deals on submarines and aircraft, and gifting the carrier to Indonesia also saves it the cost of decommissioning the ship.

blocks.caption: Indonesia’s first aircraft carrier, the ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi (C), arrives at Tanjung Priok port in Jakarta. Photograph: Mast Irham/EPA

blocks.text: The transfer would make Indonesia only the second country in south-east Asia with a carrier in its fleet. The first was Thailand’s HTMS Chakri Naruebet, which was commissioned in 1997 after being procured from Spain along with carrier-capable AV-8S Matador jump-jets.

The carrier will be formally commissioned into the Indonesian Navy next week as the KRI Gajah Mada, named after the famed 14th-century Majapahit-era military leader, whose campaigns and vision of a unified archipelago have made him one of Indonesia’s most celebrated historical figures.

Defence development was one of the top priorities for president Prabowo Subianto’s administration, as he has advocated an expansion of the military through the purchase of submarines, frigates, fighter jets, missiles and pushed for more defence cooperation with various countries.

But the Garibaldi acquisition has sparked a fierce debate among defence analysts, economists and opposition politicians who question whether Indonesia needs an aircraft carrier at all and whether the government should be spending millions of dollars to refurbish and operate an ageing warship while facing mounting fiscal pressures at home.

Indonesia’s finance ministry approved $450m in financing for the aircraft carrier program in 2025. However, some lawmakers have warned the overall bill could be far higher. TB Hasanuddin, a member of parliament’s Commission I, said the cost of retrofitting the carrier alone could reach 16tn rupiah (about $900m).

blocks.caption: The aircraft carrier ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi sailing near Bangka Belitung island.  Photograph: Indonesian Navy 2nd Fleet Command Public Relations Office/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Unlike major naval powers that use aircraft carriers to launch fighter jets far from home shores, Indonesia views the vessel as a mobile command centre and support hub for helicopters, drones and maritime operations across its thousands of islands.

Speaking during a disaster management meeting early this month, Prabowo said the vessel would help authorities combat forest and peatland fires that regularly blanket parts of south-east Asia with hazardous haze.

Prabowo said the carrier could accommodate up to 10 medium-sized helicopters, including aircraft with capabilities comparable to the Black Hawk and Mi-17, and could carry large quantities of water and be deployed to areas with large numbers of fire hotspots.

He also outlined plans to operate drones from the ship and use it as a mobile platform that could be rapidly deployed to help in the event of natural disasters, which are common in Indonesia, a nation that sits in the Pacific “Ring of Fire.”

blocks.caption: The through-deck aviation cruiser class ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi docks in Indonesia. Photograph: Mast Irham/EPA

blocks.text: Operating a carrier is extremely costly, however, and experts have questioned whether Indonesia’s leadership has thought through whether one is necessary for the country’s defence or disaster-relief needs.

The acquisition comes as Indonesia’s economy faces growing fiscal pressures. Prabowo’s government has been funding a free nutritious meals program – which has been tainted by multiple food poisoning incidents – and other costly initiatives while economists have warned about slowing growth, weaker state revenues and widening budget constraints, prompting closer scrutiny of major government spending projects.

blocks.caption: Experts have warned that operating a carrier is extremely costly. Photograph: Indonesian Navy 2nd Fleet Command Public Relations Office/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “The plan to acquire the Garibaldi must be based on genuine operational needs and our ability to operate it, rather than being driven by pride or other considerations,” said Muhammad Fauzan Malufti, of the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

He said policymakers must weigh not only the vessel’s acquisition and modernisation costs, but also the Navy’s ability to sustain its operations, including personnel, maintenance, fuel, weapons systems and supporting infrastructure.

Fauzan said the government should be transparent about those considerations, particularly given the vessel’s age. He cited Thailand’s carrier as a cautionary example, saying it has spent much of its service life in port because of operational and budget constraints.

“The bottom line is that this should not be forced. Otherwise, the benefits could be outweighed by the costs,” Fauzan said. “The money might be better spent on other priorities, such as increasing the number of frigates in the fleet.”

blocks.caption: Indonesian defence minister Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin on the ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi. Photograph: Mast Irham/EPA

blocks.text: Military analyst Khairul Fahmi of the Institute for Security and Strategic Studies said aircraft carriers are not a priority for Indonesia, which is focused on preventing adversaries from operating freely in the country’s territorial waters.
“Indonesia has a greater need for submarines, frigates and asymmetric weapons systems to protect its maritime sovereignty,” he said.

But he added that if Indonesia is seeking to position itself as a major maritime nation, “an aircraft carrier can be both a symbol of national power and a multifunctional platform capable of supporting a wide range of military and non-military missions.”

articles.title: Why US plan to sell F-35 warplanes to Saudi Arabia is controversial
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia has lobbied the US for years to buy F35s, the world's most advanced fighter jet.

blocks.text: Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois, a Democrat, opposed the sale on Thursday.
He warned "it could put the crown jewels of American military technology within reach of the Chinese Communist Party".
Other Democratic lawmakers and some American defence officials have raised similar concerns about giving F-35s to Saudi Arabia.
They said Riyadh might share the sensitive technology with China under a security partnership between the two countries.
The state department said in announcing the deal on Thursday that it would support US "foreign policy and national security objectives".
It said the deal would improve "the security of a major non-Nato ally that is a force for political stability and economic progress in the Gulf region".
"The proposed ⁠sale of this equipment and support will not alter the military ⁠balance in the region," the state department added.
Trump has a close relationship with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited the White House last November.
The two also met in May last year in Riyadh, where a $142bn arms sale was sealed – described by the White House as the "largest defence sales agreement in history".
The latest proposed sale announced to Saudi Arabia would include 48 F-35s, which are built by the arms company Lockheed Martin.
This would place the country on a level with Israel, which currently has a fleet of 50 jets.
However, Israel's ministry of foreign affairs announced in May, external that it would procure another F-35 squadron.
This deal would double the size of Israel's F-35 fleet to 100, according to the Jerusalem Post, external.
Just one of Lockheed Martin's F-35A jets costs about $82.5m.
Congress has previously questioned arms deals with Riyadh after the murder of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi in 2018.
Former US President Joe Biden's administration considered supplying F-35s to Saudi Arabia if Riyadh would normalise its ⁠relations with Israel, but that diplomatic effort faltered.
The proposed sale comes as the Saudis are engaged in fighting with the Houthis, an Iran-backed armed group that controls much of western Yemen.
The Houthis have recently seized control of swathes of Yemen's Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed pro-government forces.
The Saudi crown prince has personally pressed Trump to take military action against the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, the BBC's US media partner.
But Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, the sources said.
Additional reporting by Sareen Habeshian

articles.title: Zara Larsson criticises White House for using her song in deportation video
articles.summary: The White House removed Larsson's Midnight Sun from one of its reels after the artist called the clip "dehumanising".

blocks.text: Swedish pop star Zara Larsson has condemned the White House for using one of her most recognisable songs in a social media reel.

The clip used Larsson's Midnight Sun in a video appearing to show immigration enforcement raids. The song has since been removed from the post, but the video is still visible on the White House's TikTok feed.
The video is captioned "never ending deportations", riffing on Larsson's lyrics "never-ending midnight sun".

In a three-minute reaction video posted on social media, Larsson described the clip as "dehumanising", joining a growing list of singers, including Sabrina Carpenter and Ariana Grande, who have told the Trump administration to not use their music.
The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.
The reel splices together multiple videos of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, as well as other US law enforcement personnel, handcuffing men and putting them into vehicles.
Larsson reposted part of the original clip, which then cuts to a selfie video of her using her fingers to hold an 'L' shape against her forehead.
In the reaction video that has already clocked up more than 4.2 million views on TikTok, she tells her followers the White House video is "so dehumanising".
Larsson continues: "These people in this video – they're real people."
"The vast majority of these people who are undocumented are regular people with jobs and they're just trying to have a better future".

"It's so crazy how everything is so memefied and so 'ha-ha-ha'," she says, accusing the White House of using her song to sow "division", despite the lyrics reflecting a connection between people and nature, according to Larsson.
Earlier this year, Larsson condemned a video of President Donald Trump dancing at various events overlayed with her hit Lush Life.
White House social media accounts have been forced to remove various songs from their feed following interventions from artists.

Taylor Swift's seasonal track August disappeared from a reel shared by the Trump administration in August, while one of Olivia Rodrigo's songs vanished from a video after the singer condemned its use for what she called "hateful propaganda".

Sabrina Carpenter and Ariana Grande have also warned the Trump administration in separate incidents to not use their music in social media content after the White House posted videos featuring their songs.
