articles.title: Almost 50 dead in Nigeria after drinking alcohol suspected to contain methanol
articles.summary:
Drinking locally made alcohol is common in Nigeria, especially in rural areas where it is more affordable and poorly regulated

At least 48 people have died and about 100 others are receiving…

blocks.text: At least 48 people have died and about 100 others are receiving treatment in southern Nigeria after consuming a locally brewed alcoholic concoction suspected to contain methanol, officials said on Thursday.

Banji Ajaka, Ondo state’s commissioner for health, said the cases had been reported in the Odigbo and Irele local government areas. A total of 182 people are believed to have been affected and some are being treated in the hospital, he said.
“I took like two shots and I went out on Friday. On Saturday, I noticed that I could not see,” 32-year-old Sola Adebayo told the local TVC News channel from a hospital bed.
Drinking locally made alcohol is common in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country, especially in rural areas where it is more affordable and poorly regulated.

“This thing happened rapidly. Once they consume, depending on the quantity, the kidneys will pack up, the eyes will go, the brain will be damaged,” Ajaka told The Associated Press, speaking about the drink.

Ondo state police spokesperson Abayomi Jimoh said in a statement that 15 people were arrested in connection with the incident, including one allegedly “involved in the production of substances suspected to contain methanol and is currently assisting the police with investigations.”
Locals told the AP they suspected a popular herbal drink with high alcohol content, known as “Monkey Tail,” was mixed with methanol, causing the deaths.

A trader who sells the concoction in Odigbo, speaking on condition of anonymity for fear of being arrested, told the AP there are two versions of Monkey Tail: an original, safe version, and another version which is unsafe.
Local media reports said the first death was reported nearly two weeks ago.

Nigeria’s National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control is now enforcing a nationwide ban on alcohol in sachets and small plastic containers, which it said are easily accessible to children and young people.

articles.title: US court sentences ex-Syrian official who ran notorious ‘punishment wing’ to 60 years
articles.summary:
Samir Ousman al-Sheikh, part of Bashar al-Assad’s regime, was in charge of Adra prison where prisoners were tortured

This article contains descriptions of torture.

A US…

items: This article contains descriptions of torture.

blocks.text: A US federal court in Los Angeles sentenced a former Syrian government official who ran one of the country’s most infamous prisons to 60 years in prison on Thursday – the most significant punishment handed to an official of ousted president Bashar al-Assad’s regime by a foreign court and to a defendant present in person.

Samir Ousman al-Sheikh was the head of the Adra prison, on the outskirts of Damascus, between 2005 and 2008, when he oversaw an underground “punishment wing”, known as “Wing 13”, in which prisoners and regime opponents were interrogated and tortured as he watched through surveillance cameras. A federal jury convicted al-Sheikh last March of having tortured prisoners and then lying about it in US immigration forms.
“The conduct was heinous, unimaginably cruel and almost unspeakably violent and brutal,” said Hernan D Vera, a US district judge, before delivering the sentence.
Al-Sheikh’s legal team and the justice department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Following al-Sheikh’s conviction, Bill Essayli, first assistant US attorney, had said in a statement that the case showed the US “is not a refuge for criminals – especially criminals who engage in the brutality of the kind this defendant inflicted on his victims”.

Al-Sheikh, 73, who also served as governor of Syria’s Deir Ez-Zour province in 2011, at a time of violent regime crackdowns against protesters, moved to the United States in 2020, obtained a green card and applied for US citizenship. He was arrested in July 2024 at Los Angeles international airport on immigration fraud charges and prosecutors later added four-torture related charges.

He is the first al-Assad regime official to go to trial in the US and the highest ranking regime official to be tried anywhere in the world in person. Al-Assad was ousted by a lightning rebel offensive in December 2024 which toppled the regime in just 11 days.

Since then, Syria’s new government has held a number of in absentia trials for former regime officials in connection to crimes committed during the country’s years-long civil war, which killed about half a million people and displaced half the country’s prewar population of 23 million. In August, a court sentenced al-Assad and his brother Maher to death for crimes against humanity and war crimes, but the two men have been in Moscow since the regime’s collapse.
Other factions in Syria’s civil war have also been accused of abuse of detainees, including insurgent groups and the US-backed, Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces.

During al-Sheikh’s nine-day trial, several victims and witnesses testified. They described guards folding prisoners into car tires, restraining and beating them. Some they said, were cuffed by their wrists to pipes on the ceiling, beaten with cables, and left suspended for extended periods of time.

Others testified that they were placed on a device known as a “magic carpet,” which consisted of two large wooden panels with hinges in the middle onto which guards strapped prisoners, forcing the panels together to cause excruciating pain. One victim recalled al-Sheikh himself stomping on the device. Another testified he was subjected to the “magic carpet” as punishment for writing a letter of support to a political prisoner and also forced to wear a red jumpsuit assigned to prisoners designated for execution, leading him to believe he was going to die.

“[Al-Sheikh] chose to serve the ruthless, repressive Assad regime in Syria throughout his professional life, including for four years as the warden of Syria’s largest prison,” prosecutors wrote in a sentencing memo. “[He] knew that what he was doing was wrong. Nonetheless he ordered and participated in the torture of his victims because he had the power to do so and because he thought he would never be held accountable.”

Several victims and witnesses also submitted written and video testimonies to the court ahead of the sentencing, in which they spoke of being haunted and traumatized by their experiences two decades later.
“I still hear the screams of others begging for mercy,” said one of the men, Nidal Shikhani.
“Even though 20 years have passed, I still live in the prison of my memory,” said another, Sultan Abdul Malek. “I suffer from sudden panic attacks and constant anxiety.”

His brother, Khaled Abdul Malek, who was taken to “Wing 13” twice during his four years at Adra prison, spoke of the physical and psychological scars he was left with, including chronic back pain and mobility problems.
“My son Battal asks if he could ride my back and with a heart wrung with pain, I am forced to tell him I [am] no longer strong enough to carry him,” he said.

Several witnesses also submitted testimony on al-Sheikh’s behalf, speaking about his age and frailty as they asked the court for leniency. More than 50 people sent letters of support to the court, describing him as “a person of integrity, compassion, and generosity to his family and community”, his attorneys wrote.

Prosecutors had asked the court for a minimum sentence of 80 years; al-Sheikh’s attorneys had called for a five-year sentence, citing his poor health and noting that he was willing to be deported to Syria.

“Whatever moral weight this case carries in the broader arc of history – however much the world, or the victims, or the public might wish the sentence to ‘send a message’ – that desire cannot be the foundation of a just sentence,” the defense team wrote in a memo to the court.

“This case sends a message both to the new government of Syria and to other victims that justice is possible,” said Ela Matthews, an attorney at the Center for Justice and Accountability, which represented several victims. “The transitional justice process that is happening in Syria needs to continue to evolve and bring individuals like this to account, but in the US this sends a message that the rule of law is still functioning and that these types of cases are possible.”

articles.title: 'This is our company': Nigerians show off oil wealth after share-buying frenzy
articles.summary: Many Nigerians buy their first ever shares - in the oil refinery owned by Africa's richest man, Aliko Dangote.

blocks.text: Every Nigerian is now an oil magnate.
At least that is what the social media memes would have you believe as investor fever hits the country.
Nigerians have been eager to have a piece of the energy business that was built up by the country's – and continent's – richest man: Aliko Dangote.
More than four billion shares in his giant oil refinery – representing just over 3% of the company - went on the market on Monday in Africa's biggest-ever sale of its kind.
The minimum purchase was 10 shares for about $4 (£3) and despite this only representing a miniscule portion of the firm, many are now celebrating and joking about their new-found (part-)owner status.
One popular social media video has a Nigerian narrating how he stopped a speeding Dangote company lorry driver, telling him not to be reckless with company property.
Other memes show investors trying to phone up Dangote to discuss business matters.
And the term "Yangote" – a pun in the Hausa language essentially meaning "we all have a share now" - has been trending on social media.
On the first day of the Initial Public Offering (IPO), investment apps crashed as they could not handle the high demand.
Bamboo, which runs one of the most popular investor tools here, later apologised, saying: "We know we let you down."

Public affairs analyst Jamil Ubah said he had rarely seen Nigerians as excited about something as this. He argued that it fed the dream that it could lead to greater riches for a population that is often battling to make ends meet.

"I think the hope for the common man is that his money will grow into something big, and don't forget this is coming at a time when many are struggling as the economy is not doing great," he told the BBC.
Dangote wanted this to be "the people's IPO" with drivers, cooks, cleaners and servants having the chance to be part of something big.
And they took him at his word.
Twenty-five-year-old clothes seller Idris Lawal Musa made his first-ever stock exchange purchase and told the BBC he was happy after investing 21,000 naira ($16; £12) in 40 shares.
"It is no longer Dangote but 'Yangote', the company belongs to us now," he said while laughing.
But he may make a quick sale.
"I am a trader by profession and when I see that the shares have increased in price I will sell," he noted.
The popularity also reflects a growing investment culture among younger Nigerians who have embraced mobile trading platforms, cryptocurrencies and digital savings products.
But fear of missing out may have also pushed some to get into the investment business.

In the build-up to the IPO, social media platforms were awash with financial conversations. People shared subscription guides, debated valuation metrics and encouraged friends and family to participate.
But amid the frenzy, experts have warned that there are risks – shares can go down in value, as well as up, meaning people could lose some, or all, of their investment.
Financial analyst Shuaib Uwais said prospective investors should avoid thinking of the IPO as a guaranteed route to wealth.

He urged people to consider a number of factors that could impact the refinery's future performance, including disruptions to crude oil supply, operational challenges, regulatory changes and fluctuations in demand for refined petroleum products.
"If for any reason the company experiences difficulty in sourcing its raw materials, there could be challenges," he told the BBC.
Nevertheless, the IPO has given people the chance to be part of this home-grown success story.

Dangote's sprawling refinery on the outskirts of Lagos, which began operating two years ago and now processes around 700,000 barrels of crude a day, has transformed the fortunes of Nigeria's oil sector.
Until recently, Africa's largest crude oil producer had no refining capacity and had to import the finished product. Now the Dangote refinery is feeding much of the domestic demand.
But for Dangote, the share offer is about raising cash to fund the growth of the business, something that the country's mini-magnates may now be able to get behind.

articles.title: New wild cat species discovered - with only one known living member
articles.summary: A spotted wildcat long mistaken for relatives has been identified as a new species in Bolivia.

blocks.text: Only one confirmed living member of the species is known - a cat in a rescue sanctuary in Bolivia - but scientists believe others exist.
It was this 10-year-old cat, nicknamed 'Tigrino', that set scientists on the path to discovery.
Bolivian scientist Dr Nogales-Ascarrunz was volunteering at the sanctuary when she noticed the cat looked unusual.
It had been found in the forest by a local resident, who initially thought it was a domestic kitten. As it grew older, however, it became clear that it did not behave like a house cat.
Dr Nogales-Ascarrunz had heard of other sightings of small wild cats in the dense forests of the country's Yungas region, but these had not been investigated by scientists.
To solve the mystery, she joined forces with other researchers from around the world to investigate the family history of tiger cats, using DNA from living animals and museum specimens.

"There's so few records or pictures, no individual in a museum, so it was hiding because nobody was looking," said Eduardo Eizirik, a conservation geneticist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil.

The study, published in Current Biology, external, uncovered further surprises, suggesting there are five rather than three tiger cat species, including the newly described Tilcaya cat (Leopardus tilcayo) of Bolivia.

articles.title: YouTube star Ms Rachel to match Macklemore’s $1m Palestine aid donation
articles.summary:
Educator talks of ‘moral obligation’ and urges ‘every wealthy white celebrity’ to make similar donation

YouTube star

blocks.text: YouTube star Ms Rachel has said she is matching rapper Macklemore’s $1m donation to organizations supporting Palestinians, calling on other public figures to follow suit.

Macklemore, who was fired as the opening act on Ed Sheeran’s tour after saying “Free Palestine” on stage at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium, pledged to donate the entirety of his earnings from Sheeran’s tour to several organizations focused on the Palestinian people.
Ms Rachel, whose full name is Rachel Accurso, wrote on Instagram: “Over 20,000 precious Palestinian children have been killed, and children continue to be killed every day.”
Accurso said her donation would go to the Palestine Children’s Relief Fund.
“We have a moral obligation to use our privilege and platforms to protect children and human rights,” she wrote.

Accurso, a children’s entertainer with over 21 million YouTube subscribers, has been vocal about the hardships Gaza’s young people face amid the war with Israel. She encouraged “every wealthy white celebrity” to match her donation.
Accurso is the latest public figure to back Macklemore, after he was dropped from Sheeran’s Loop tour for remarks he made at a 4 September concert about the plight of the Palestinian people.
“Free Palestine! I want those words to be loud and clear, so that people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them,” he said during a two-minute speech.

Macklemore’s words prompted a flurry of criticism from Israel-aligned groups. The singer Pink also called on Macklemore to be removed from the tour, and referenced a 2014 incident where he wore a costume decried for bearing resemblance to Jewish caricature. Macklemore apologized for the costume at the time.

Pink expanded on her position in an Instagram post, saying she was not speaking on behalf of the Israeli government, but rather wanted to advocate for Jewish concertgoers who may have been alarmed by the rapper’s remarks.

Macklemore directly addressed Jewish audience members at a second tour date on 5 September, saying: “Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you. My message is for peace, love; for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect and equality.”
Sheeran has maintained the decision to fire Macklemore was led by stadium owners, including Gillette Stadium and New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft.

Sheeran wrote on Tuesday on Instagram: “I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn’t mean I don’t have them, and it doesn’t mean I don’t care. Nor does it mean I don’t support causes in my own, personal way.”
Kraft and Sheeran are both donating $2m each to Palestinian relief funds, Kraft said Wednesday, although it is unclear which organizations their funds will support.
Four supporting acts, among them American singer Finneas and Danish pop band Lukas Graham, have quit the tour in solidarity with Macklemore.

articles.title: New cat species identified in Bolivia for first time in more than a century
articles.summary:
New species of wild cat was discovered in Bolivia’s Yungas forest and is smaller than the average domestic ⁠cat

A diminutive wild cat that inhabits Bolivia’s ⁠cloud forest has been…

blocks.text: A diminutive wild cat that inhabits Bolivia’s ⁠cloud forest has been identified as a previously unknown species, marking the first time a new living cat species has been formally named and described in more than a century.

The cat, called Tilcayo by local communities, is part of a group called tiger ⁠cats found across much of South ⁠America. It was found in Bolivia’s ​lush Yungas forest, a mountainous region where forests are often covered by clouds and surrounded by high humidity, according to researchers. It measures about 18in (46cm) long and weighs about 3lbs (1.4kg), making it smaller than the average domestic ⁠cat.
Researchers used genetic data to confirm that the cat is a new species, and gave it the scientific name Leopardus tilcayo, retaining its local name.

“Its fur is light brown ... with irregularly shaped rosettes across its body,” said Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, a National Geographic explorer and one of the authors ⁠of the study describing the newly identified species published on Thursday in the journal Current Biology.

Little is yet known about the cat’s biology and lifestyle. Remains of small rodents in scat ​samples suggest they may form part of its diet, while camera-trap evidence indicates it ‌could be more active at night, Nogales-Ascarrunz said.

Tiger ‌cats are so-called cryptic species, meaning they cannot easily be distinguished merely by appearance, said evolutionary biologist and study co-lead author Jonas Lescroart of the University of Antwerp in Belgium.
Tiger ‌cats previously had been considered a single species, but genetic studies decades ago suggested the existence of multiple species.
Referring to the new species, Lescroart said: “Our information at this moment is limited to the two live individuals that we examined, and a small number of camera-trap records.”
One of the live cats is a 10-year-old male that now lives in the Senda Verde Wildlife Sanctuary after being kept by a local family in their home.

Observing the Bolivian cat drew interest because “its characteristics did not match the descriptions, most of them based on Brazilian cats,” Nogales-Ascarrunz said. “This made us wonder: what tiger cat do we actually have in Bolivia?”
The team analysed DNA from 38 cats sampled across several South ‌American countries, including eight museum specimens. The study found that tiger cats are in fact five genetically distinct species.
“We never expected this Bolivian tiger cat to be a separate species, and no one had ever proposed it as a different animal, subspecies or otherwise,” Lescroart said.
Genetic analysis suggested ​that the Tilcayo lineage separated from other tiger cats about 1.4m years ago.

“The more differences in their DNA, the longer the time that we estimate those lineages to have been physically separated,” Lescroart said, adding that such a gap is generally considered a species-level divide in cats.

The research team also described a new tiger cat subspecies in Peru’s Yungas, naming it Leopardus tigrinus antisuyo after Antisuyu, the region of the old Inca empire that included the area it inhabits.
The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) red list tracking the status of species currently treats ⁠tiger cats as two “vulnerable” species with declining populations.

The researchers have shared their findings with the IUCN, whose upcoming review will assess ​the five lineages separately. That could give a more accurate picture ​of risk, Lescroart said, and species such as the Tilcayo ​could be considered endangered when assessed on their own.
The need for a clearer assessment is particularly acute in the Yungas, one of the ​region’s most threatened ecosystems.

The mountain forests ‌face growing pressure from deforestation, agricultural ​expansion, human-caused fires and mining, Nogales-Ascarrunz said. ​Restoring forest patches damaged by fires, protecting remaining native forest and maintaining connections between habitats are urgent priorities, Nogales-Ascarrunz added.

“Showing the general public that even in a flagship group such as cats ... there are still new species to be discovered may transmit an important message,” said Eduardo Eizirik, an evolutionary biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil and senior author of the study. “There are many undiscovered species out there in the world, and they are at risk of disappearing before we even discover them.”

articles.title: Why Canadians are ready for closer ties with Europe
articles.summary: People the BBC spoke to are excited by the prospect of working and studying in the EU, a suggestion Carney made this week.

blocks.text: Watch: 'A better opportunity' - Canadians on a closer alliance with Europe
Miriam Levin-Gold likes Prime Minister Mark Carney's idea of Canadians being able to live and work in the European Union under proposed closer ties with the trade bloc.
"I think that's great for young people to explore different parts of the world and work in different places and have different experiences," the commuter told the BBC in Toronto.

Canadians woke up to news of Carney's speech to the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Thursday morning, welcoming the EU's ambition for Canada to become its first "associate member" as he urged closer co-operation on defence and energy.
"We should deepen our people-to-people ties, allowing our youth to live, work and study where they want on either side of the Atlantic," the PM said.
Carney told MEPs that Canada and Europe were "stronger together" in the face of "geopolitical rupture".

But before Canadians start packing their bags, "associate member" status does not currently exist within the EU and could take years to implement, given that all 27 EU member states would have to approve such an arrangement.
Nevertheless, people the BBC spoke to were excited about the potential prospect of working and studying in the EU as news of Carney's speech spread.
Miriam Levin-Gold is excited about potentially greater opportunities for young Canadians to be able to explore the EU
Alex Nash, from Montreal, said closer ties would clear away the obstacles of work visas and permits.
"It would certainly be really nice for that to be easier, more convenient and to be able to visit more easily," she said.
Canadian social media has lit up with the topic.

One person on a Facebook group, A Canadian Outlook, said they would love the opportunity for their grandchildren to study at European universities for better rates. Another woman said it would make it much easier for the home she already owns in France.
"Snow birds are going to love it," another person said, referring to Canadians who head to warmer locations for winter.
The sentiments hint at dissatisfaction in Canada over bilateral tensions with the US.
Growing up in Canada, David Jardine thought of the US as not just a neighbour, but an epicentre of culture and cool.
"I remember wanting to go and visit New York all the time," he told the BBC after finishing his overnight shift, not far from one of Toronto's most iconic buildings, the CN tower.
But he's become a lot more sceptical in the light of US President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada and rhetoric about annexation.
"I would say I think not only does it make more sense to associate closely with Europe, it's a place that I would rather be associating with given the way things are these days," he said.

blocks.caption: Image caption, David Jardine and Alex Nash hope Carney's news means there will be fewer obstacles to spending time in Europe

blocks.text: David Jardine and Alex Nash hope Carney's news means there will be fewer obstacles to spending time in Europe
Maggie Stainton, who manages local pub C'est What in Toronto's St Lawrence Market district, became emotional when she spoke about Canada's frayed ties with the US.
"It's too volatile with the United States," she said. "I feel that there's some stability in Europe."
For decades, America has been a cultural centre of gravity that is difficult to avoid, with many Canadian actors working in Hollywood and Canadian radio stations playing US music.
"I think we're forced to feel more American simply by the influences that we have," Stainton added.
"However, I think deep down, I definitely I lean towards feeling more European in my ideas and ideals."
These views were echoed by many other people the BBC spoke to in the centre of Canada's biggest city.
Carney, who used to lead Canada and Britain's central banks, was elected on a promise that he would not only take a tough stance against Trump, but broaden Canada's economic horizons.
Up to 72% of Canadian exports are to the US, and the ongoing trade tensions have spurred Ottawa to seek closer ties with other nations.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Maggie Stainton is disappointed by the frayed relationship with the US

blocks.text: Maggie Stainton is disappointed by the frayed relationship with the US
The EU, in many ways, would seem a natural fit. Over half of Canada's population reported having European origins, according to the last census, which was taken in 2021.

A recent Abacus Data survey conducted before Carney's speech found that 80% of Canadians say the country should deepen strategic cooperation with the EU, and over half feel closer to Europe than America.
However, details of Carney's proposed plans for greater ties with the EU are scarce.
A pair of opposition Conservative MPs have called on him to elaborate on what he and the bloc plan to work towards.

"It could be a concrete, meaningful proposal. Or it could be just words and vibes," said Adam Chambers, MP for Simcoe North in Ontario, during an interview with the BBC on the eve of Carney's speech on Thursday.
Chambers alluded to the existing Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (Ceta) between the EU and Canada, highlighting that it still awaits ratification by multiple EU nations.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ahmed Khalil hopes ties with Europe brings in more money to Canada in light of tensions with the US

blocks.text: Ahmed Khalil hopes ties with Europe brings in more money to Canada in light of tensions with the US
And while deepening ties with Europe would be welcomed by many Canadians, there is still a sense that the country's relationship with the US - however strained - must not crumble.
"I grew up here. I've been here 40 years in Canada, in Ontario, and America's always been the neighbour," says Ahmed Khalil.
Building bridges with Europe makes sense, he said: "I think it brings in more money for Canada and more culture, brings Europeans over, probably solves a lot of problems."
But Canada shouldn't forget its southern neighbour, added Khalil.
"I think both are equally valuable to us," he said. "Both are equally valid."
With additional reporting by Madeline Halpert and James Fitzgerald

articles.title: This Olympic river has 500 crocodiles in it - but that's not the main concern
articles.summary: Queensland's Fitzroy River has been selected for the 2032 Games, despite concerns over the course - and its inhabitants.

blocks.text: The annual rowing regatta for schools in the Australian state of Queensland usually passes off without too much attention.
Each year more than 600 of the state's most promising teenage rowers battle it out on the crocodile-inhabited Fitzroy River, in the city of Rockhampton.
"We've never had any media wanting to attend here," Anthea O'Loughlin, head of Rowing Queensland, tells the BBC.

But this year is different. In six years' time, the 2032 Brisbane Olympics and Paralympics are set to stage rowing and canoe sprint events in this very stretch of water, which has just passed a technical assessment and been endorsed as safe and fair for athletes.

While sightings of saltwater crocodiles on the river – which number around 500 and can grow to four metres (13ft) long – are not uncommon, state government files going back more than 40 years record no attacks by the reptiles on humans.
And while influential figures at last month's World Rowing congress in Amsterdam made occasional references to "safety", the presence of the reptiles was not their chief concern.

"Fairness" is what's been raised with British Rowing's chief executive Tom Solesbury – a reference to the tidal river's natural bends and currents, which many in the rowing community say make it unsuitable for elite competition.
Drew Ginn, who has won three Olympic gold medals for Australia in rowing, told BBC Radio he had concerns over potential flooding and "fairness and integrity" at the venue.
"Personally, I'm not fearful of the Australian animals but I've never had a crocodile near me," he said.
"I'm sure I'd row faster, I'm sure all the athletes would row faster. That's on the list of concerns, I don't think it's the highest priority in concerns but it was certainly cited very early on."
The German rowing body's president Moritz Petri said athletes had also questioned the sustainability of holding the event some 600km (373 miles) from Brisbane.
But the "so-called impediments" got short shrift from the most senior politician in Queensland, state premier David Crisafulli, who reached for less diplomatic language.
"Let's be honest, let's scratch beneath the surface and call it for what it is," he said days after the Amsterdam meeting.
"It is a group of interstate and overseas elites who are trying to bully their way because they don't want to go to regional Queensland and that's not right."
Rowing chiefs contacted by the BBC before Thursday's decision declined to comment directly on Crisafulli's "elites" remarks.
But both Petri and Simon Wickham, chief executive of Rowing New Zealand, said their concerns had nothing to do with regional or urban preference but with competitors getting fair racing.
Petri added it was about what's best for their athletes who will train four years for the event, "dreaming night [after] night of becoming an Olympic champion".

Whether it was crocs or currents that tipped the balance, ultimately it was the sport's governing body World Rowing and the International Olympic Committee (IOC) that had the final say on the river's suitability.

On Thursday they approved it after a technical assessment by an engineering firm and the Games' infrastructure authority – which looked at the riverbed, competition course, river flows, water levels and likely weather conditions during the Games.

"Based on the extensive analysis undertaken, we now know that the Fitzroy River is capable of providing fair competition conditions during the period of the Games," World Rowing president Jean-Christophe Rolland said.
There was also now "confidence" in the river for canoe sprint athletes, said Thomas Konietzko, president of that sport's governing body, Paddle Worldwide.
The state premier was delighted. "The Fitzroy has passed with flying colours," an upbeat Crisafulli told parliament. "It's official. Signed, sealed and delivered."

In backing Rockhampton, the state government ignored a 2025 report it commissioned itself, which found the location unsuitable and concluded the best option would be to use a course built in Sydney for the 2000 Olympics.
The Fitzroy now needs to pass a final assessment of its design, value for money and long-term community legacy. As the decision rests with the state government, it's unlikely to fall at this hurdle.
But a wider debate will continue over whether Rockhampton is the right place to invest heavily in rowing facilities – and whether it can accommodate the 2032 influx of visitors.
The city is surrounded by cattle producers and normally experiences its peak number of guests every three years during Beef Week.
So what about the crocodiles?
They're not mentioned anywhere in the latest update from the IOC and World Rowing and they weren't considered in the technical assessment.
The safety management plan for this weekend's school regatta does however mention the word "crocodile" 28 times.
"The Fitzroy River is within recognised crocodile country," it says.
"Event planning must therefore assume that a crocodile sighting is possible… No natural waterway in crocodile country can be guaranteed to be crocodile-free."
Procedures this weekend include suspending racing and competitors returning to the bank if a croc is spotted. The official signal for a sighting is the call of "crocodile, crocodile, crocodile".

Asked specifically about crocodiles, New Zealand's Wickham told the BBC the primary concern was ensuring the "fairest possible course" for rowers. "We would obviously expect any course chosen to be safe for rowers," he added.

The company owned by Australia's richest person Gina Rinehart, Hancock Prospecting, which supported Rockhampton's bid and has pumped millions into sports including rowing, pointed to "fake media" concerns about risks posed by flooding and crocodiles in the Fitzroy.
"The people of Rocky for many years have sent their own children to train in this river, and for competitions, without a single crocodile incident," a spokesperson said in a statement.
Brisbane 2032's chief executive has said organisers are making contingency plans "as we would for any venue".
The 2000 Olympics venue in Sydney is ready and waiting as a backup – though that would be unconscionable for Queenslanders.

articles.title: ‘Cocaine eyes’ to cash bribes: 5 revelations from Project South wiretaps

image.caption: Const. Timothy Barnhardt is facing a long list of charges in connection with allegedly assisting organized crime. (@10rcop/X)

blocks.text: A police officer doing drugs before his shift, a trunk of police uniforms to sell, details on drug deals and plans to open massage parlours are some of the revelations Project South investigators allegedly captured through wiretaps as part of their sweeping corruption probe, according to newly reportable details from an Information to Obtain (ITO) application in the case.
A publication ban was lifted on those allegations, and many others, from the Project South ITO this week in a ruling from Ontario Superior Court Justice Laura Bird.

“The importance of public scrutiny in this case cannot be overstated. What is, perhaps, most concerning about the allegations of widespread police corruption in this case is the fact that the York Regional Police only stumbled upon it in the course of their investigation,” wrote Bird in her decision.

The investigation began in June 2025, when York Regional Police thwarted an alleged plot to kill a senior corrections official from Toronto South Detention Centre (TSDC). Subsequently, police discovered that Toronto police Const. Timothy Barnhardt allegedly ran an unauthorized search on the official's licence plate less than a month before the attempted hit.
“There is no evidence that anyone was suspicious of Mr. Barnhardt or his associates until that moment," Bird wrote.
"That is something that should be of tremendous concern to the public because it demonstrates that a trusted public official can engage in widespread illegal conduct and go undetected.”
CBC News was part of a group of media organizations fighting to lift a publication ban on the ITO — which lays out months' worth of evidence police had compiled from wiretaps and other warrants.

The allegations in the ITO have not been tested in court, but many of the conversations intercepted by investigators paint a picture of the corruption investigators allege Barnhardt and other Toronto police officers and civilians engaged in over several months in 2025 and early this year before their arrests.
These are five of the most shocking conversations police intercepted.
Going to daycare with ‘cocaine eyes’

In early October 2025, investigators intercepted Barnhardt buying cocaine from Const. Saurabjit Bedi in a Brampton, Ont., plaza, according to the ITO. Barnhardt’s vehicle was bugged with audio and video recording devices and investigators say the pair are “seen and heard weighing out the drugs and can be heard negotiating a price of $230 for Barnhardt to pay.”
Afterward, Bedi called Barnhardt and the following exchange was captured, according to the portions of transcript in the ITO.
Bedi asked Barnhardt if he “looked f--ked up when you saw me? … cuz I’m going to daycare now.”
Barnhard replied: “Just put your sunglasses on that’s all, you got … what do they call them … cocaine eyes.”
From there police say the pair discussed drug dosages.
In December 2025, the ITO said police also observed Bedi “consuming what appeared to be cocaine” in the parking lot of 12 Division before starting his shift.

Both Barnhardt and Bedi are charged with trafficking cocaine. None of the charges against them have been tested in court yet. Barnhardt’s lawyer declined to comment on allegations from the ITO and Bedi’s did not respond to a request for comment.

items: Toronto cop charged in Project South allegedly didn't care if selling information harmed people

blocks.text: ‘All they want is protection’
Police intercepted Barnhardt and Bedi drinking and doing drugs in late November 2025 while discussing plans for a marijuana dispensary and a massage parlour, according to the ITO.
Bedi explained to Barnhardt that he has “girls,” and “all they want is protection and safety and we get their cuts.” He also allegedly told Barnhardt it would be better to use hotels.

items: Inmate and jail guard investigated, but not charged in Project South alleged murder plot

blocks.text: Investigators say Barnhardt then clarified to Bedi he was not talking about escorts, but rather massage parlours.
Both men are charged with conspiracy to obstruct justice and breach of trust.
‘What about all this s--t in the f--cking trunk man?’

In late October 2025, investigators intercepted a meeting between Barnhardt and civilian Brian Da Costa in Barnhardt’s vehicle. Da Costa is the one who allegedly paid Barnhardt to “routinely” run unauthorized database searches, including the one on the senior corrections official.
But on this night, the ITO says Da Costa paid Barnhardt cash for police uniform items that Barnhardt had in his trunk.
This is a transcript of the conversation included in the ITO:
Barnhardt: "What about all this s--t in the f--king trunk man…?"
Da Costa: "Oh s--t yeah my bad f--k; I forgot for a second what you were trying to hand me."

Barnhardt: "I'm like what the f--k 36, 38, 40 are the pants, and the f--king NCO pants are in here too, there is like 1, 2 ,3 jackets.... l got the other jacket I just gotta pick up with the toque and everything."
Da Costa: "I might qet a couple of bucks for this s--t and get more, okay?"
Barnhardt: "I’m gonna get you the hats and ball caps."
Da Costa: "We gotta go get the badges and s--t okay?"
Then, police said Da Costa was observed handing money to Barnhardt, while counting each bill aloud.
Da Costa: "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, 10."
Barnhardt: "You are the f--king best, man."
Both men are charged with trafficking police uniforms. Da Costa remains in custody. His lawyer declined a request for comment on the ITO allegations.
Barnhardt jokes about visiting massage parlour daily
In early September 2025, Da Costa was intercepted asking Barnhardt if he wanted to partner with him opening a massage parlour, according to the ITO.
Barnhardt: "Oh f--k bro I’ve been trying to do that myself ... l just didn’t have the link for the women" [...] “I’ll put all my effort towards that, f--k it, a hundred percent.... I'm excited."
Da Costa allegedly jokes about receiving free services at the proposed massage parlour, to which the ITO says Barnhardt replied he would be there daily.
‘Inflammatory’ conversation still under pub ban
There is one conversation transcript in the ITO that Justice Bird decided to keep under a pub ban. It involves Barnhardt and Da Costa.
“The comments attributed to Mr. Barnhardt are particularly inflammatory and memorable,” wrote Bird in her decision.
“I am satisfied that they are the type of comments that could create an indelible impression of guilt in the minds of potential jurors that could not be dealt with by resort to alternative measures.”

Elsewhere in the ITO, CBC News previously reported that police say Barnhardt “explicitly stated that he did not care if individuals were harmed” as a result of information he sold to Da Costa from database searches.
This ITO was used by police to obtain more than 50 search warrants in the Project South investigation in early February.

The search warrants were executed as investigators arrested and charged seven Toronto police officers, one retired cop and 19 civilians in Project South. The charge against one of those civilians has since been stayed, and one of the officers retired and pleaded guilty to two charges in July.
The charges against the others accused in Project South have not yet been tested in court.

articles.title: All smiles in Strasbourg but uncertainty clouds Canada’s EU membership plan
articles.summary: Although Mark Carney welcomed offer to become bloc’s first associate member, no one seems to know what that means

blocks.text: Mark Carney received a rapturous reception in the European parliament when he gave his speech on Thursday welcoming a proposal for Canada to become the EU’s first-ever associate member.

Politicians queued to shake his hand and take selfies. One MEP leader described the speech as a historic moment. “Europe has extended a hand, and Canada has taken it,” said the German Green MEP Terry Reintke, who borrowed a Canadian ice hockey shirt for the occasion.

One day earlier, in the same debating chamber, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, issued the unprecedented invitation to Canada to become an associate member – an idea quickly derided by Donald Trump, who threatened Europe with “heavy tariffs” if it became a reality.

But the prospect of Canada’s associate membership is uncertain, not least because no one is sure what it means. “I’m not quite sure why she [von der Leyen] used that term because there’s simply no legal definition,” said one senior politician. “This has just raised lots of questions. So people are talking more about what an associate membership means instead of … this unique partnership and alliance for the future that EU-Canada relations should be about.”

The German chancellor Friedrich Merz’s spokesperson welcomed the initiative for a close partnership with Canada and said Germany was “open to discussing new models that reflect the special significance of the relationship” but called for the associate membership label to be “reconsidered”.
Merz himself has floated “associate membership” for Ukraine, as a stepping stone to joining the bloc, but this was quickly dismissed by other member states.

One EU diplomat said von der Leyen “seemed a bit far out in floating this” and that even before Wednesday’s speech member states had worried that she was overpromising on Canada. A second diplomat said it was “an empty phrase” and it would be up to member states to define the substance.
Any new trading and cooperation relationship with a foreign country would need to be approved by the EU’s 27 member states.

There is a lot of common ground: both sides want to deepen cooperation on AI, energy security, critical raw materials, quantum computing and work together in the Arctic – Carney noted that Canada shared an Arctic border with Denmark, referring to the maritime border with Greenland.

But difficulties went unspoken. While Carney described the 2016 EU-Canada comprehensive economic and trade agreement as “one of the world’s most successful trade agreements”, 10 EU member states have yet to ratify it, including France, Italy and Poland. With all three countries heading into an election year, that looks unlikely to change.

While both sides extol the virtues of deeper trade between allies, they are also pursuing policies that appear to contradict that goal. Last year Canada introduced a buy Canadian policy, to ensure Canadian suppliers get priority in public contracts. The EU is debating its own buy European law, known formally as the Industrial Accelerator Act. The IAA, now being debated in the EU, would oblige member states to meet “made in Europe” content requirements when spending public money on green technologies and electric cars.

Associate membership also raises questions about integration into the EU’s tightly guarded single market. Carney proposed “seamless digital trade in non-agricultural goods and a wide range of services”. But the EU has long insisted that the four freedoms of its internal market – free movement of goods, services, labour and capital – are one package that cannot be split and require alignment with EU rules.
Now the applause has died down, there are plenty of tricky issues to work out, even for the closest of allies.

The fate of of the crew is not known.

Downing the F-15 is also a "propaganda coup", said Yemen expert Adam Baron from the Washington-based New America think tank, as Saudi air support is considered to be "key to any significant pushback" against recent Houthi gains.
"An eye-for-an-eye has been a huge element of the group's public messaging. This is partially to show that air support will come at a price," he added.

articles.title: IS member sentenced to 20 years in prison for role in 2021 Kabul airport bombing
articles.summary:
Mohammad Sharifullah, 28, was convicted of aiding the terrorist group that took credit for the suicide bombing

An Islamic State group member was sentenced Wednesday to 20 years in prison…

blocks.text: An Islamic State group member was sentenced Wednesday to 20 years in prison for aiding the terrorist organization that took credit for a suicide bombing that killed 13 US service members and about 160 Afghans at the Kabul airport five years ago during the US military’s chaotic withdrawal from the country.

A federal jury in Virginia had convicted Mohammad Sharifullah in April of providing material support to the IS affiliate known as Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP). But jurors could not agree whether he bore some responsibility for the airport bombing on 26 August 2021.

US troops were conducting an evacuation operation at the airport when a suicide bomber detonated an improvised explosive device near an entry point known as Abbey Gate. Sharifullah’s role in the attack was scouting a route to Hamid Karzai international airport, prosecutors said.
Sharifullah, 28, received the maximum sentence for his one-count conviction in an international terrorism case that Donald Trump heralded last year during a speech to a joint session of Congress.

Sharifullah did not testify at his trial and declined to address the court before US district judge Anthony Trenga imposed the sentence. The judge said the defendant was a “dedicated terrorist” who expressed no remorse for the “unfathomable” grief and suffering that he had caused.

Trenga heard victim impact statements from several parents of the US service members. From a podium only a few feet from where Sharifullah sat, they took turns paying tribute to their children’s sacrifices and describing how the attack has shattered their families.
Mark Schmitz of Missouri asked Sharifullah to turn and look at him as he spoke about the life and death of his 20-year-old son, Marine Corps Lance Cpl Jared Schmitz.
“They may have taken his life, but they’ll never take his legacy,” Mark Schmitz said. “A bomb killed my son. It did not kill what he stood for.”
Paula Knauss-Selph, whose son, Army Staff Sgt Ryan Knauss, was killed in the Abbey Gate bombing, said the family was “forever changed” by the attack.
“No justice will ever be enough to mend my broken heart,” she said.

Sharifullah requested a 17-year prison sentence, while prosecutors sought 20 years. His lawyers said he was never an ISKP leader and had not been convicted of any conduct related to the airport suicide bombing.
“He was brought here because the government believed he participated in the Abbey Gate attack, a theory which it was unable to prove at trial,” defense attorneys wrote.
Prosecutors said in their sentencing memo that “from his teenage years, when he pledged an oath of allegiance to [ISKP], Sharifullah’s carnage was driven by hate. Hate towards Americans.”

Jurors convicted Sharifullah of providing material support to ISKP. They deadlocked on whether any deaths at the airport “resulted from” that conspiracy. Sharifullah could have faced a possible life sentence if the jury had unanimously decided that question.

According to prosecutors, Sharifullah told a journalist that he wanted to “catch and kill the crusaders” from the United States for invading his country after the attacks of September 11. They said Sharifullah was involved in dozens of other attacks, including a March 2024 assault on a Moscow concert hall that killed roughly 140 people.

Defense lawyers argued that prosecutors failed to present any evidence tying Sharifullah to the Kabul bombing besides his own words during hours of FBI questioning. His team said Sharifullah told FBI agents what he thought they wanted to hear, possibly because he was afraid of being tortured in Pakistani custody before he was brought to the US.

A review by US Central Command found that the Abbey Gate bomber was Abdul Rahman al-Logari, an IS member who had been released from an Afghan prison by the Taliban. According to an FBI affidavit, Sharifullah recognized the alleged bomber as an operative he had known while incarcerated.

articles.title: Trump administration denies entry visas to Palestinian officials ahead of UN general assembly
articles.summary:
It is the second year this administration has barred the Palestinian delegation from US travel ahead of the forum

The US state department said on Wednesday that it had again denied entry…

blocks.text: The US state department said on Wednesday that it had again denied entry visas to Palestinian officials ahead next week’s United Nations general assembly gathering in New York.

The state department said in a statement that the Palestinian Authority (PA) and the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) had “failed to live up to their commitments”, accusing the groups of “taking actions to internationalize the Israeli-Palestinian Conflict including through the International Criminal Court (ICC) and International Court of Justice (ICJ)” and of “glorifying terrorism” among other allegations.

“As a consequence of their failure to reform, contrary to their commitments to the United States, and their ongoing activities that undermine the prospects for peace, the United States will extend sanctions that deny visas to PLO members and PA officials,” the department said.
The move marks the second year in a row that the Trump administration has barred the Palestinian delegation from traveling to New York to attend the UN general assembly in person.

The foreign ministry of the Palestinian Authority denied the allegations made against them by the state department in a statement on Thursday, describing the visa sanctions as an “unjustified measure” that “contradicts the efforts being made to restore trust, develop Palestinian-US relations, and prepare the necessary political climate for implementing the two-state solution and achieving peace and stability in the region.”

Among the Palestinian officials barred from entering the US is Mahmoud Abbas, the longtime president of the Palestinian Authority, according to reports. The UN general assembly is set to vote on a draft resolution on Thursday to allow Abbas to address the gathering remotely, according to two officials familiar with the planned vote, per the New York Times. Last year, Abbas addressed the gathering by video conference.
This year’s UN general assembly general debate begins on 22 September.

articles.title: Canada welcomes EU proposal to become 'associate member'
articles.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said a Canada-EU alliance would create a "beacon for other democracies".

blocks.text: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has welcomed the European Union's ambition for Canada to become its first "associate member", calling for closer cooperation on defence, critical minerals and energy security.
Carney told the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Thursday that Canada and Europe were "stronger together" in the face of "geopolitical rupture".
His comments came a day after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed "opening the door" to Canada's associate membership, a status that does not currently exist.
US President Donald Trump earlier called the idea "laughable" and threatened "very serious tariffs" on Europe if he considered it a "hostile act".
Canada and the US are locked in an escalating trade dispute, with each side imposing tit-for-tat tariffs after bilateral talks collapsed last month.
"Today our societies are being battered by new storms," Carney said during his address, naming them as climate change, "the erosion of democratic norms" and the "weaponisation of trade".
"Economic integration is now being weaponised, tariffs being used to exert pressure," he said.
"Financial mechanisms have been used for coercion. Supply chains constitute weak points to be exploited."
He said a Canada-EU alliance would create a "beacon for other democracies", while stressing the two sides were not seeking to form a new power bloc.
"I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival - only with better manners," he told MEPs.
"This is about sovereignty, our ability to live as we wish. We do not seek power to dominate others."
Asked about the proposal on Wednesday, Trump told reporters: "If I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe, on many things.
"If it's a good intention, that's fine. If it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe, which is a possibility."
Responding to Trump's comments at a press conference following his address, Carney said: "This alliance is a positive process, that's my response to the American president."
"Canadians are united that nobody is going to tell us what language we speak, no-one is going to dictate our culture, or with whom we can strike agreements internationally," he added.
Carney said Canada was "not in a position, nor seeking, to become a full member of the European Union", describing the proposal as a "different framework".

Speaking at the European Parliament on Wednesday, von der Leyen said she wanted Canada to become the EU's first associate member, with closer cooperation in areas such as manufacturing, technology, defence, energy critical minerals and economic security.
It is unclear exactly what that relationship would look like because the "associate member" status does not currently exist within the EU and could take years to implement.
Any new arrangement would require the agreement of all 27 EU member states, with some governments having previously expressed reservations about creating a new form of membership.
The EU and Canada already have a free-trade agreement, and cooperate in areas including trade, defence and research.
In his address, Carney said Canada and Europe could strengthen their "strategic autonomy" through "deep co-operation in the full range of strategic capabilities, including critical minerals".
He said Canada could supply liquefied natural gas and hydrogen to support European energy security, while benefiting from Europe's expertise in clean-energy technologies.

He also proposed pooling technological resources and deepening "people to people ties", including allowing young people to "work, study and live where they want on either side of the Atlantic" through Canada joining the EU's Erasmus+ programme.
Carney described the proposed relationship as "a unique, positive approach that we will define together".
He added that there would be a debate and a vote in the Canadian parliament on the proposals, but emphasised the two sides were still at the "start of a road".
A Canada-EU summit is due to take place in Montreal at the end of October, where Carney said they would "drill down the details".

articles.title: Pickleball courts cause uproar in this normally quiet community in Port Stanley, Ont.
articles.summary: Tensions are rising between residents of the Kokomo Park community in Port Stanley, Ont., and it's all because of pickleball. While the public courts are popular with players, some neighbours…

image.caption: Ashley Hennessey garnered 130 signatures on a petition to keep the Kokomo Park pickleball courts in Port Stanley, Ont., open from 8 a.m. to dusk. Other community members want the courts removed, calling them a nuisance. (Jack Sutton/CBC)

blocks.text: London

Tensions are rising between residents of the Kokomo Park community in Port Stanley, Ont., and it's all because of pickleball. While the public courts are popular with players, some neighbours consider them a nuisance. A petition and even threats of legal action are involved.
Players love the public courts in Kokomo Park, but some neighbours want them out due to noise
Tensions are rising between residents of the Kokomo Park community in Port Stanley, Ont. — all because of pickleball.
Kokomo Park is a quiet neighbourhood, with a condo building, a block of single-family homes, a playground and four public pickleball courts that are popular with some residents and their friends.

"We hang out together, we laugh together, we joke together," said Ashley Hennessey, who plays regularly at the courts. "The good thing about pickleball is it brings you out so that you're getting good healthy workout, good community and get to know people you didn't know before."
But for others, the courts are a source of constant noise.
After receiving a number of complaints, the Municipality of Central Elgin decided in July that the courts could only be used from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m., a change from the previous policy of dawn to dusk.

At a municipal council meeting on Monday, the players submitted a petition with 130 signatures, asking to change the hours to 8 a.m. to dusk, and for the municipality to conduct a noise study and include the players in future discussions.

At the same meeting, St. Catharines-based lawyer J. Patrick Maloney submitted a letter on behalf of Richard Robson, one of the condo owners, and Kokomo Affected Neighbours, a group of condo residents.

The letter threatens legal action if the pickleball courts aren't removed, claiming the use of the courts would exceed provincial noise guidelines and "contravene the general legal principles associated with the tort of nuisance."

"We understand that the pickleball users are pushing for expanded hours, which demonstrates they are not concerned with such nuisance impacts or our clients legal right to the quiet enjoyment of their property," Maloney wrote.
Maloney did not respond to a request for a statement. CBC News spoke with two of the Kokomo Affected Neighbours, but neither wished to comment.
The municipality received both communications at Monday's meeting, but no decision has been made regarding either the players' or the residents' requests.

Hennessey, who started the players' petition, said he and the others want the courts to remain open earlier in the morning due to concerns over the heat and humidity, noting the "advanced age" of many of the people who use them.
"Playing in 30- to 35-degree weather is not healthy," he said. "So we come out, we play earlier in the day and to us that is a reasonable alternative."

The disagreement has led to tensions between neighbours, he said, describing multiple occasions on which condo residents have yelled at him and other players if they arrive at the courts too early or leave too late.

Hennessey said he and the other players are willing to work with the community to find a way to reduce the disruption, and he was surprised to read the lawyer's letter asking for the courts to be closed outright.

"That is absolutely not fair because what we want to hear is the joy ... the laughing, the joking, chirping each other back and forth," he said. "This is what life is about, it's supposed to be about getting along, being peaceful and having a good time."
Courts can get busy in evening, neighbour says

In 2025, Lloyd Mulroney moved into the home directly in front of the pickleball courts, fully aware they existed and were a part of the community, he said. Mulroney said he has even taken to sitting and watching from his porch some mornings, and he and his wife occasionally play.
But the courts can get busy, he said, particularly in the evenings, with upwards of 20 people playing and 15 to 20 cars in the small parking lot.
"There's a lot of cheering and activity that's happening. But if it closes down by 8 p.m., people are respectful, then that works for everybody, right?"
He said there are a lot of "camps" in the community, where the courts are concerned. Some want them gone, some don't care and some, like him, "kind of lay in the middle."
"I think it could have been dealt with a little bit better," he said. "A little bit more collaboration and a little bit more folks concerned for their neighbour."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jack joined CBC London after graduating from Fanshawe College in 2025. He previously studied political science and Russian studies at Dalhousie University in Halifax, NS. You can contact him at jack.sutton@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Rosenberg: Russia's elections will have few surprises, but for the Kremlin they matter
articles.summary: There is no doubt over the outcome of this vote, but for the Kremlin they are still an important moment.

blocks.text: Low expectations that Russia's election will bring peace closer, Steve Rosenberg reports
BySteve Rosenberg
Russia editorReporting fromMoscow and Dmitrov
The system of power in Russia is often referred to as "managed democracy" (where the Kremlin does the managing).
That means huge powers for the president and few political surprises.
This weekend's election is set to deliver another parliament dominated by the party of power, United Russia, and a house of MPs fiercely loyal to Vladimir Putin.
Critics dismiss the vote as neither free nor fair.
But the Kremlin doesn't care what the critics say.
"We have our own political system, our own political process," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov explained recently.
That means no curveballs for the Kremlin. No surprises. So no story?
Far from it.
For the Kremlin, the election of 450 deputies to the lower house of parliament, the Duma, is important. This is the first parliamentary election here since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The Kremlin will use it to claim that most Russians back the president and the war, as well as to promote the political careers of soldiers back from Ukraine: officials say nearly two hundred war veterans are taking part in the election.

blocks.caption: Image caption, This election is being used to promote the political careers of some military veterans

blocks.text: This election is being used to promote the political careers of some military veterans
As for the election campaign, that has provided a window on Russian society four-and-a-half years into the war.
I said no surprises. But there have been some.
"Good evening and welcome to tonight's campaign speeches by candidates for Duma Electoral District 158," said the anchor on state TV.
The studio director cut to a wide shot revealing six empty lecterns.
"The candidates haven't turned up," admitted the host. "So, it's goodbye from me."
In another TV debate (where the politicians were present) one crooning candidate sang his pitch:
"The Communist Party, onwards we go!
"We're with the people, don't you know?"
More X Factor than exit poll.

Yet a musical manifesto is strangely appropriate. In the previous Duma, everyone seemed to be singing from the same hymn sheet. At the final session of parliament in July, MPs stood and applauded as the speaker of the house chanted repeatedly:
"Russia, Putin, Victory! Russia, Putin, Victory!"
It was a signal that all MPs in parliament should back President Putin and the war.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov [centre] backs the war in Ukraine

blocks.text: Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov [centre] backs the war in Ukraine

"All parties in the Duma, every single one, voted in favour of 170 laws to support the special military operation," Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov told me with obvious pride about the last parliament.
"In that sense there is 100% agreement in the Duma."

I caught up with Zyuganov on the campaign trail outside Moscow at a bread and biscuit factory. As I watched rows of identical-looking loaves speeding along the conveyer I thought about Russia's parliament. It's not that all parties in the Duma are identical: some are more nationalist, others – like Zyuganov's party - more left-wing.

But when it comes to backing the Kremlin's legislative initiatives and supporting the "special military operation" they vote the same way. Such "systemic" parties are vital cogs in Russia's Kremlin-centric political machine.
And if a party doesn't support the war?

One such party - Yabloko - is calling for a ceasefire in Ukraine. Back in July it was the only anti-war party in Russia to be registered for the election. Twelve days later, though, the Supreme Court removed it from the ballot. That was widely interpreted as a sign of Kremlin concern that anti-war messaging could strike a chord with Russian voters.

Despite Yabloko's exclusion from the party list, some of its candidates are still running in individual constituency races. Though in recent weeks growing numbers of Yabloko candidates have been detained by police, prosecuted for various offences and barred from the election.
"The police are carrying out a political order. That's no secret," Yabloko candidate Grigory Grishin tells me.
"This way, the authorities are setting the boundaries within which they believe the elections should take place.

"It is well known that the demand for an end to the bloodshed in this conflict with Ukraine is very popular. In my opinion, most people in Russia now want peace and Yabloko helped people express this. That's why it's been excluded from the party lists, and why individual candidates are being barred."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Grigory Grishin says he believes demand for an end to the bloodshed in the conflict with Ukraine is very popular

blocks.text: Grigory Grishin says he believes demand for an end to the bloodshed in the conflict with Ukraine is very popular
For now, Grigory remains a candidate. But the police recently came to his flat.

"Three policemen in civilian clothes asked me to accompany them to the station, which I did. The police said I had posted what they claimed was an extremist symbol: the word 'Navalny' and that, by doing so, I had propagandised extremism via my Telegram channel."
Alexei Navalny was Russia's most prominent opposition leader and Kremlin critic who died in prison in 2024. He'd been convicted on several charges, including extremism.

The Russian authorities insist that the Duma elections are transparent and fair. Critics of the vote point to opposition politicians who have been forced into exile or put in prison. Last year one of the leaders of a prominent independent election monitoring group in Russia was jailed for five years. Grigory Melkonyants was convicted on charges of working with an "undesirable organisation". His election monitoring group, Golos, has shut down.
Fifty miles from Moscow, in the town of Dmitrov, I see little sign of an election.
In the town centre there's a memorial to "Heroes of the special military operation": local people killed fighting in Ukraine.
The war is front and centre of people's minds here.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Olga's son-in-law is fighting in Russia's "special military operation"

blocks.text: Olga's son-in-law is fighting in Russia's "special military operation"

"We feel it," says Olga, whose son-in-law is a soldier in the "special operation". "Because of the people who've gone to fight and the families left behind with sons, husbands, children and grandchildren there. But these elections can't influence what will happen."
"I'd like us to live in a peaceful country, with no war," Polina tells me, "So that you don't have to worry that a drone will fall down in front of you."
Russians have other concerns, too. Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries have sparked widespread fuel shortages, while economic pressures are increasing.

"What worries me," says a barber called Ivan, "is that no matter how much you earn it's not enough. Prices are rising faster than wages. I speak to lots of people in my job. I know how hard-up they are."
Expectations are low that this election will change much.

"Western elections and elections in Russia are completely different things," Grishin explains. "Elections in the West are a way of forming a government, which is replaced later if voters aren't satisfied.

"Elections in Russia never bring a change in government. At best, they're a way of influencing it, of sending a signal. But power in Russia never changed because of an election. That's how Russia is."

articles.title: Climate crisis likely behind devastating Nepal-Tibet floods that killed more than 1,300, first study finds
articles.summary:
Scientists say global heating was a destabilising factor in collapse of 200,000 sq metre glacier in August

Climate breakdown probably weakened the glacier that collapsed causing catastrophic…

blocks.text: Climate breakdown probably weakened the glacier that collapsed causing catastrophic floods and killing hundreds of people in Nepal and Tibet last month, the first scientific study of the disaster has found.

Researchers identified unusually warm conditions before the glacier’s collapse, which sent an avalanche of 110m cubic metres (3,885 cu ft) of snow and ice into the valley below. This triggered flash floods on an almost unprecedented scale, hitting communities downstream without warning.

“Communities in Nepal are paying with their lives for a crisis driven by fossil fuel emissions thousands of miles away,” said Dr Friederike Otto, a climate science professor at Imperial College London, which carried out the study.

“When warming destabilises the roof of the world, no amount of local adaptation can fully shield vulnerable people downstream from this scale of destruction. Without much faster action to transition to zero fossil fuel emissions we will inevitably see more disasters of this scale occurring in the years to come.”

blocks.caption: A impromptu memorial in Kathmandu commemorates some of the people killed in the flooding. Photograph: Narendra Shrestha/EPA

blocks.text: More than 1,300 people were killed and more than 5,000 people remain missing after a massive section of overhanging glacier and rock measuring roughly 200,000 sq metres (2,153,000 sq ft) fell from Langtang Lirung mountain on 26 August.

It dropped about 1,400 metres (4,660ft), slamming into the valley floor with such intensity that it registered as an earthquake, liquidising ice and sparking a freezing flood that careened downriver at speeds exceeding 110 mph.
The devastating flood of water, ice, rock and sediment swept away families, homes, settlements, roads, bridges and other infrastructure, leaving survivors stranded and cut off.

“Rock avalanches of this size are rare, with annual frequency estimates of approximately one event this size every 1,000–10,000 years,” the study said. “This event shows that limits to adaptation are already being reached.”

The research was unlike previous studies by Otto and her team at World Weather Attribution (WWA) – a collaborative project between Imperial and other climate specialists worldwide – in that the role of climate breakdown could not be ascribed to one particular weather event.
Instead, the researchers found the disaster was the result of a compound crisis, with a number of factors made worse by decades of atmospheric heating as a result of greenhouse gas pollution.

Dr Ben Clarke, who researches extreme weather and climate change at Imperial, said the “fingerprints of climate change” were clear in the long-term changes that happened around the glacier before its catastrophic collapse.

blocks.caption: ‘Communities in Nepal are paying with their lives for a crisis driven by fossil fuel emissions thousands of miles away,’ said Dr Friederike Otto. Photograph: Suryams Upreti/AAP

blocks.text: Among the study’s key findings were:
after newsletter promotion

items: In the region where the collapse happened, climate breakdown has caused about 2C of warming since pre-industrial times, and about 1.5C of warming in July and August specifically;
July and August 2026 were the warmest on record locally, reaching 5C above the 30-year average in the days before the collapse;
The freezing threshold in the Himalayas has risen by about 100 metres per decade since the 1980s, with higher and longer thaw temperatures weakening mountain slopes shaped by permafrost;
The warming temperature had already driven substantial glacier recession, removing stabilising ice from around the site where the collapse occurred and contributing meltwater;
A 7.8 magnitude earthquake in 2015 further contributed to slope failure, though its specific contribution to the disaster in August could not be confirmed.

blocks.text: Otto, Clarke and the WWA team said their study did not directly ascribe climate breakdown as the fundamental cause of the catastrophe. Instead, it was best understood as a destabilising factor on the existing geology.
Clarke said: “We found that climate change is transforming the high mountain environment, influencing many of the possible drivers of this collapse.”

blocks.caption: A major earthquake in Nepal in 2015 may also have contributed to the glacier’s collapse. Photograph: Ishwar Rauniyar/The Guardian

blocks.text: Nepal has filed a formal request with the UN loss and damage fund for financial support to address the destruction caused by the flood, a process that requires proof of a link to the climate crisis. The country’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, has also demanded that top emitting nations such as China and India “wake up” and accept shared responsibility for the disaster.

Madhab Uprety, senior technical advisor for the Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, which is part of WWA, said only aggressive cuts to global emissions could begin to address the “losses and damages faced by vulnerable frontline communities”.

He added: “In addition to the human tragedy on an unimaginable scale, the cost of recovery for this disaster is substantial. For a nation that’s done virtually nothing to contribute to this problem, it underlines the need to find fairness in helping climate vulnerable nations cope with the problems they have not unleashed.”

articles.title: Handbags, jewels, watches: Inside Singapore's dirty money auction
articles.summary: The BBC goes inside a fortified storage facility to view luxury goods seized by Singapore police in a $2.2 billion money laundering case that are now up for auction.

blocks.text: Singapore has begun auctioning off luxury goods that were seized by police in a sensational $2.2 billion money laundering case that gripped the city state in 2023.
The items are being held inside Le Freeport, a fortified storage facility, where the BBC's Vandhna Bhan was allowed inside for a look.

articles.title: Watch: Leaked photos reveal extensive damage at US bases in Gulf
articles.summary: The photos, provided by active military personnel, show a severed radar jet, flattened trailers and severely damaged buildings as a result of Iranian strikes.

blocks.text: The BBC's US partner CBS obtained photos showing widespread damage to multiple US military sites in the Middle East as a result of Iranian strikes.
