articles.title: Battle of Chile director Patricio Guzmán dies aged 85
articles.summary:
Passionate documentary maker won international acclaim for unsparing but poetic films exploring the impact of the Pinochet regime in Chile

Patricio Guzmán, the film-maker who chronicled…

blocks.text: Patricio Guzmán, the film-maker who chronicled Chile’s bloody 1970s political strife and its subsequent social and political turmoil in films such as The Battle of Chile and Nostalgia for the Light, has died aged 85. According to Chilean news outlet Emol, Guzmán died on Tuesday in Paris after a cardiorespiratory arrest.

Guzmán’s chief preoccupation throughout his career was the carnage unleashed by Augusto Pinochet’s coup in 1973 against Salvador Allende, Chile’s elected president. He later told the Guardian: “I’m a film-maker who was very marked by the ways of the dictator. It has remained with me for ever. I cannot leave it behind.” However, he resisted the idea that he was an activist, political film-maker, adding: “I’m not a sociologist. Neither am I a politician. I make films that are metaphorical and poetic; I interpret reality through my own personal way of looking.”

Born in Chile in 1941, Guzmán initially worked in advertising before studying film, first in Chile and then in Madrid. On his return to Chile, Guzmán responded to the febrile political atmosphere after Allende’s election in 1970, eventually completing the mammoth Battle of Chile documentary that chronicled Pinochet’s ultimately successful attempt to overthrow Allende, resulting in the latter’s suicide. Guzmán did not shrink from the brutality of the period, even including footage shot by camera operator Leonardo Henrichsen as he is shot dead by the soldier he is filming.

blocks.caption: A still from The Battle of Chile. Photograph: Collection Christophel/Alamy

blocks.text: Guzmán was helped in the endeavour by French film-maker Chris Marker, who supplied film stock and connections that proved vital to make the film. Guzmán himself was arrested but eventually released, but the film’s cinematographer Jorge Müller was not so lucky – along with his girlfriend Carmen Bueno, he was arrested, tortured and “disappeared” in 1974.

Guzmán completed The Battle of Chile outside the country, releasing each of its three parts – The Insurrection of the Bourgeoisie (1975), The Coup d’État (1976) and Popular Power (1979) – through the rest of the 70s. Described by the Guardian as “an outstandingly photographed example of a newsreel film that captures the drama and volatility of the period”, it has continued to attract acclaim since then. Guzmán revisited the film in the mid-90s with Chile, Obstinate Memory, in which he returned to the country after a quarter-century of exile. In 2001 he completed The Pinochet Case, after the Chilean former dictator was arrested in London in 1998.

The director moved on to more metaphysical subjects with a trilogy of films starting in 2010: Nostalgia for the Light, The Pearl Button and The Cordillera of Dreams. They sought to explore Chile’s traumatic past by absorbing the country’s magnificent natural landscapes. His final film, My Imaginary Country, was premiered in 2022 and covered Chile’s dramatic 2019 street protests.

articles.title: Carney's new love-in with EU has everything to do with Trump
articles.summary: The Canadian PM is in Strasbourg this week seeking a "unique alliance" - and there is one clear catalyst.

blocks.text: "Wouldn't it be lovely if Canada was the 28th state of the European Union rather than the 51st state of the United States?" asked Finland's President Alexander Stubb this summer.

The question was rather tongue-in-cheek. US President Donald Trump, who is currently locked in an escalating tariff tussle with Ottawa, has, on a number of occasions, declared his ambition to make Canada the 51st American state - causing deep offence amongst many Canadians.

Finland is one of the EU's 27 member states and a close ally of Canada as a fellow Arctic nation. Teasing tones aside, President Stubb put his finger squarely on the pulse of deepening EU-Canadian relations. "Canada is more Europe-minded than most Europeans!" is a smiling retort you often hear in Brussels at the moment.
On Sunday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters Canada was seeking a "unique alliance" with the EU.

And in a speech on Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she wanted to work "on opening the door" for Canada to be the EU's "associate member" - which would involve closer ties on various sectors including manufacturing and energy.

The catalyst for this very public, ardent new love-in is Donald Trump. Just the other day, the US president posted a map of North America on his Truth Social site, including Canada and Greenland - a territory that's part of EU country Denmark - all overlaid with the US flag.

Trade negotiations between the US and Canada broke down late last month. European countries, which have been hit by their own Trump tariffs, have privately watched the spat play out with a mixture of interest and, for many, admiration.

While the EU, led by the European Commission, simply accepted new blanket Trump tariffs without fighting back, Carney has prominently stood up to the US president, swiftly imposing counter-tariffs on the United States.
When it comes to courting the EU, Canada appears to some to be even keener than one of the bloc's closest neighbours.

"Canada right now seems more interested than the UK to get as close to Brussels as possible, as a non member state" says Mark Leonard, director of the European Council of Foreign Relations think tank. "It's remarkable."

Canada, but not the UK, successfully joined the European Union's Security Action for Europe (SAFE) defence fund earlier this year. The UK remained on the sidelines following a row over costs and political tensions. A summit designed to reset and improve EU-UK relations has just been delayed - again - over cross-Channel differences.

By contrast this week, Carney is invited as a special guest to the European Commission President's annual State of the Union address in Strasbourg, France on Wednesday. Carney will hold a speech in the European Parliament there on Thursday, a day after President von der Leyen outlines the EU's political and policy priorities.

Officials on both sides insist this is more than just "blah blah politics", as one EU diplomat put it to me. He was speaking on condition of anonymity so as to be able to discuss the subject freely. Carney and von der Leyen are both expected to mention plans to forge closer ties. "As close as you can get without (Canada) actually becoming an EU member," the diplomat told me.
The US president is by now infamous amongst US allies for what they view as his unpredictability and his penchant to use trade or security ties as leverage.

There's a growing sense in Europe - which has, since World War Two, looked to the US as its closest ally abroad - and in Canada, whose economy has been intertwined with the US for decades, that neither can any longer fully rely on Washington. They believe it's time to diversify.

"The Canadian government is committed to trade diversification, doubling non-US trades in the next 10 years, and doing more with the European Union will be very key to achieving that target," Mark Camilleri, president of the Canada EU Trade and Investment Association (CEUTIA) told the BBC.

An even tighter Canadian-EU alliance, covering far more sectors than trade alone, would continue a recent trend of both parties to form new association agreements around the world. In Canada's case, this includes a sectoral deal with China, which raised international eyebrows earlier this year.
EU insiders put all of this down to the "Trump effect".
But decoupling from the US altogether would seem unrealistic - for both Canada and the EU.
The US is the EU's largest overall trading partner, if you take goods and services together.

Canada and the US have the largest bilateral trading relationship in the world, valued at nearly US$900bn (£668bn) last year. This dwarfs the $130bn of total EU-Canada bilateral trade during the same timeframe.
The vast majority of Canadian exports head to the US.
So, Ottawa could sign new trade agreements, but replacing customers and supply chains built around America's massive market would be a tall order.
This week, I hear, Carney and von der Leyen will vociferously defend a global system of rules-based trade.
"This is not about trying to keep the past alive. We need to forge a new rules-based future in trade and beyond. With or without Washington," diplomats tell me.

There's an EU-Canada summit scheduled for the end of next month. After that, working groups are expected to start the less-than-sexy task of tackling the legal and technical details in the different areas in which the EU and Canada now hope to establish closer ties.
A huge turning point for Europe in its attitude towards Washington came early this year when Trump refused to rule out taking Greenland from fellow Nato power, Denmark, by force.

Around that time, Carney - who's also the former governor of the Bank of England - gave a speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, calling on middle-sized countries to stick together against economic coercion by global super-powers. Europe sat up and took notice.

Why then, you might ask, haven't Europe's leaders been more outspoken in their support for the Canadian prime minister during the current escalation in trade tensions with the US? Carney has been defiant, declaring that Canada was "at war" with the US over trade.
He swiftly imposed counter-tariffs on the US in the name of "sovereignty".
Paolo Gentiloni, a former EU economy commissioner and former Italian premier, commented on social media: "Here is a speech I would like to hear in Europe."
Yet - in public - Europe's leaders have remained cautiously quiet.
Though not, it seems, out of any lack of support for Mark Carney.

A number of Europe's leaders, like Finland's president - but also French President Emmanuel Macron and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, herself once a true Trump fan - are involved in behind-the-scene chats with Carney about deepening relations, I'm told.

But - and it's a big but - no leading European politician wants to stick his or her neck out for Carney in public right now and risk having voters at home blame them for possibly incurring the wrath of - and fresh punitive tariffs from - the US president.

Over the coming months, every large country in the EU holds key elections. Germany's took place just over a week ago. France chooses a new president in April and early May. Italy, Spain and Poland have yet to set a date for their parliamentary elections.
When it comes to applauding Carney right now, Europe's leaders are hiding behind the EU institutions.
Under EU rules, the European Commission deals with trade on behalf of the member states. The EU Commission and EU parliament presidents invited Carney to Strasbourg this week.
But some officials I speak to in Brussels warn that Carney should also wake up and smell the European coffee.

Brussels may feel warmly towards Canada, and believe Ottawa shares many of the same values and priorities, but there are still loud EU voices, like France, that prefer to prevent non-member countries from getting too favourable a deal.
That's despite pressure on the EU to show more flexibility when it comes to accommodating allies, considering the turbulent times we live in.
It's a conundrum the UK faces too.
Carney flies to Liverpool later this week, after leaving the European Parliament, for his first face-to-face meeting with new UK prime minister, Andy Burnham.
As well as discussing UK-Canada ties, who knows - might the two men end up debating ways to best woo the EU, too?

articles.title: Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings
articles.summary: The US president has pushed the issue to the forefront of American politics - even at the risk of losing supporters.

blocks.text: Why is Donald Trump so opposed to regulating AI?
By
North America correspondent
According to Donald Trump, concerns about the dangers of artificial intelligence technology – that "robots will be marching into our cities and getting rid of us all" – are a hoax.

It's the kind of language the US president typically reserves for the objects of his most intense derision – theories about human-driven climate change, investigations into Russian election-meddling, and the drives to impeach and remove him from office during his first presidential term.

Styling himself as the "hoax buster", in a series of social media posts on Monday he issued a full-throated endorsement of what he called "the greatest economic development engine in history" and scorned those who doubted the benefits of the technology.

The ranks of doubters have been growing in recent weeks, however, amidst anxiety over the disruptive nature of AI - if not worries about potentially civilisation-threatening danger - among some industry insiders and politicians, including from within Trump's own Republican Party.
None of that has deterred Trump, however, whose latest social media fusillade was only his latest effort to turn back growing AI scepticism through sheer force of will.

Whether the president views the AI fight as pivotal to his economic legacy, a key battleground in a global struggle for power, or another example of his enemies conspiring against him, he has, by fully joining the fight, elevated the issue to the forefront of American politics. That is even at the risk of crossing longtime allies.

"We think this could be a great technology, but we're not going to give these guys a carte blanche," former Trump adviser Steve Bannon said at a "pro-human" conference on the dangers of AI on Tuesday. "There's been no debate."

Just before Bannon spoke, democratic socialist Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont told the same crowd that Washington policymakers had not addressed the "potentially catastrophic consequence" of unregulated AI.
"Congress under both Democratic and Republican control has been asleep at the wheel," he said. "And now we have a president whose ignorance regarding this issue is truly embarrassing."
Watch: "Great" or "alarming" - Should AI be reined in?
According to Trump, however, what's needed isn't debate or new policies, it's trust in his authority and judgement.

"The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades," he wrote. "We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies."

A desire for centralised presidential authority is a familiar theme for Trump in his second term in office. If he decides something is good, he should have the authority to allow it; if he deems it bad, he ought to be able to end it by unilateral presidential order.

It's similar to his outlook on immigration and trade. He believes that he, as president, should have the sole power to decide who can enter and remain in the country, and when and where to impose tariffs.
Unlike tariffs and immigration, which have been issues of interest for Trump for decades, the rise in artificial intelligence technology is a recent development.
But if this is no long-time, deep-seated interest on the part of the president, what could explain his willingness to press ahead?
The 'hottest' economy and the driving force of AI

Trump regularly likes to tout America as the "hottest" country in the world. Many economists indicate that investment in AI technology – including infrastructure and equipment – has been the driving force in the US economy for several years.
According to a recent report by the forecasting firm ING, tech investment accounted for more than a third of all US economic expansion in the second quarter of 2026.

The stock market is booming, and much of that rise in corporate value (and, by extension, surging retirement portfolios of many Americans) can be attributed to the massive spending on computer chips, data centres and the other infrastructure behind AI.
Anything that threatens this growth, which Trump considers to be a hallmark of his presidency and a key to his political legacy, quickly draws his suspicion.

Trump also sees the AI expansion as a large-scale industrial competition between the world's two largest economies, the US and China. In the zero-sum game of global power, if China is ahead, then America is behind.
"We're leading China in AI," Trump said on Saturday, "and frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI wins."

The president often touts a familiar conservative view that his opponents on the left are against the free market and economic liberties, and rely on alarmism to justify greater government intervention and control.

Of course, Trump – who touts partial US ownership of US Steel and the semiconductor manufacturer Intel, and has no qualms about picking winners and losers in the American economy – is hardly a traditional small-government conservative.
Tech bosses vary in views - and their access to Trump

Trump's close ties to prominent tech moguls and AI entrepreneurs from the start of his second term may also help explain his AI evangelism. Tech entrepreneur David Sacks, a co-chair of the president's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology and his informal AI tsar, has been a longtime supporter. Sacks's publicly aired scepticism of AI regulation mirrors recent comments made by the president.
"I think this is becoming a panic," he said this weekend in an interview with CBS News. "We're in an election season, and there is an incentive for political actors to try and amplify the fear."

Elon Musk, despite a rocky relationship, has shaped the direction of this administration. Mark Zuckerberg of Facebook, Amazon's Jeff Bezos, OpenAI's Sam Altman and former Apple head Tim Cook all had prominent seats at Trump's inauguration.
These men, along with Anthropic head Dario Amodei, hold a range of views on the necessity of greater AI regulation, and have differing levels of access to, and influence on, Trump.
In Amodei's case, his conflicts over the Pentagon's unrestricted use of Anthropic's AI models could have negatively affected Trump's evaluation of Amodei's calls for a slowdown in AI development.

"This is the most prominent debate in the entire industry and has been since the beginning," said Matt Calkins, head of the tech firm Appian. "We knew it would spill into politics at some point because it had to."
Watch: AI needs a 'brake pedal', Anthropic co-founder tells BBC
Where the political debate goes from here is an open question.

With Trump's resistance, it is unlikely that Congress – despite promises of new hearings and proposed regulatory controls – will enact new legislation that Trump would sign into law. On Tuesday, Republican Speaker of the House Mike Johnson appeared to back away from earlier openness to congressional action, instead echoing Trump "AI hoax" rhetoric.

With midterm congressional elections looming, candidates running for office – both Republicans and Democrats – are wary of ending up on the wrong side of public opinion that, according to polls, is sceptical of the promised benefits of AI advances.
But Republicans are also wary of crossing Trump on an issue that has become a political touchstone for the president.

Even though the public is starting to pay attention, Calkins says that the issue has not yet become political dynamite, which means political rhetoric comes with little risk. The moment when AI warnings turn into a high-profile disaster, however, could be looming.
"It is possible that events in the future might electrify the public, and then positions - and talk - might not be so cheap," he said.

Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's weekly US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

articles.title: Runaway horse captured by police on motorbikes
articles.summary: The unharmed horse escaped from its owner before the start of a parade in New Mexico

blocks.text: A runaway horse was chased by police on motorbikes in Santa Fe, New Mexico, when it escaped before a parade on 13 September.
The unharmed horse was eventually cornered by police, before being lassoed.
Police officers followed and cornered the horse on motorbikes, before it was wrangled by a lasso-carrying cowboy.
The horse was given a drink of water before being walked back to the start of the Desfile de la Gente parade, Santa Fe Police Department said in a post on Facebook.

articles.title: People protecting nature and land set up self-defence units amid threat of murder
articles.summary: Defenders of forests and rivers killed at rate of one every three days in 2025, with 85% of deaths in Latin America Nature and land defenders were murdered at the rate of one every three days last…

blocks.text: Nature and land defenders were murdered at the rate of one every three days last year, prompting many communities to set up self-defence units, according to the latest annual death toll by the independent watchdog Global Witness.

Organised crime groups or professional killers were implicated in more than a third of the 124 killings of defenders in 2025 as narco-trafficking activities overlapped with intrusions into indigenous territories and environmental crime, such as illegal logging and wildcat gold mining.
This was particularly true in Latin America, which accounted for 85% of last year’s deaths of people trying to protect forests, rivers and other ecosystems.

Colombia had the highest toll with 39 killings, followed by Brazil with 26 and Honduras with 12. In Asia, the most dangerous country for defenders was the Philippines, with 12 killings – many during crackdowns by state security forces.

blocks.caption: Asháninka territory in Brazil sits along the winding Amônia River. Many defenders are now exposed to more organised crime with less assistance from the international community. Photograph: Jorge Sáenz/AP

blocks.text: Since Global Witness began compiling statistics in 2012, the overall global tally is now 2,375 deaths and disappearances – on a par with a small-scale war.

On a more positive note, the headline figure has declined over the last two years, from 196 in 2023 and 142 in 2024, though the report authors say this is likely to be an underestimate because data collection is difficult in war zones and authoritarian regimes.
Many countries and companies are also carrying out nonlethal attacks on defenders, including criminalisation and online smear campaigns.

Many defenders are now exposed to more organised crime with less assistance from the international community, partly as a result of cuts by the Trump administration. “The dismantling of USAID, which previously supported initiatives for Indigenous peoples to steward their own land, has had particularly serious implications for defenders,” the report says.

Almost three-quarters of the killings documented in 2025 were of Indigenous people and small-scale farmers targeted for defending their land. With less outside help, an increasing number of these communities are establishing their own territorial defence mechanisms.

The report highlights the example of the Kakataibo Indigenous Guard in the Peruvian Amazon. Six of the community’s leaders have been killed since 2020 amid growing incursions into the forest by criminal groups. Starting in 2022 with a few dozen recruits, the guard now has more than 150 volunteers in its 10 bases.

Segundo Ispón, the commander of the organisation, said the self-defence groups provided a global benefit: “Defending our territory is important to us as a community and as a people, and we’re proud to support the climate that we all depend on. In our culture, the work of defending our resources and territory is taught from an early age. But for this next generation coming up, the work is more dangerous than ever.”

At least a dozen other communities in Peru have organised self-defence units. Similar bodies have existed for some years in Colombia and Brazil. But it is risky. Last year, seven Indigenous guards were murdered. In at least five of these cases, the killings were linked to organised crime.

Many forest communities report the narco-threat is growing closer. In July, Asháninka leaders on the Brazilian border with Peru petitioned the government for help after armed and masked men entered their homes, apparently in search of assassination targets.

In the Ucayali basin on the other side of the border, Global Witness said there was a 600% increase in coca production between 2019 and 2023. This is pushing gangs to expand smuggling networks, including through the opening of illegal roads and trails through the forest. Corruption further adds to the risks facing forest protectors who stand in their way because many local politicians and police are in the pay of the traffickers.

blocks.caption: An Indigenous person looks out over Apurímac River valley in Peru. Local leaders, environmental defenders and human rights activists have been threatened after calling for a more effective state presence across affected countries. Photograph: Ernesto Benavides/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Forest communities want help from governments to ease these pressures but there are concerns the opposite may be happening. Under US leadership, many rightwing governments are pursuing military crackdowns on coca growers and drug traffickers, which is pushing narco-gangs further into remote regions and indigenous territories.

Ricardo Soberón, a former head of Peru’s anti-narcotics office, said many communities were also affected on the border of Peru and Colombia. “We are in a situation where transnational criminal groups have appropriated the daily life of the Huitoto, Quichua, Bora, Secoya Indigenous people, who live along the Putumayo basin,” he said.

Of particular concern, he added, were the threats against local leaders, environmental defenders and human rights activists who call for a more effective state presence. He fears the newly elected rightwing governments in affected countries will make matters worse by militarising the conflict in line with the “America shield” priorities of the Trump administration.
Global Witness has urged the authorities to respect and work with nature and land defenders rather than making their role more difficult.

Toby Hill, the lead author of the report, said: “Defenders are the world’s eyes and ears on the ground. It’s thanks to them that we know when ecosystems are being destroyed, where forests are being cleared or rivers polluted. We can’t forget the thousands of defenders around the world who are working every day to protect their territories and cultures under increasing pressure.”

articles.title: What weapon could the US have put into space?
articles.summary: The announcement by the US points to a developing field of modern warfare in the Earth's orbit.

blocks.text: The announcement by the United States that it has deployed a space weapon in Earth's orbit has raised questions about what weaponry is actually in space, and what role it could play in efforts by great powers to dominate that arena.

Washington has given away little in its announcement. Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the "on orbit" weapon was necessary to safeguard US forces against hostile enemy action, but gave no details about the weapon's capabilities or when it was put into orbit.
So what could this weapon be, and what is wider picture like for military developments in space? Who else could have similar weaponry?

Advanced militaries already deploy satellites in space for range of purposes, from supplying secure communications to reconnaissance, and providing precise location information for targeted strikes and detecting missile launches.
As warfare become more technologically advanced, analysts expect the use of military hardware in space to increase.

Dr Bleddyn Bowen, an associate fellow in military sciences at the Royal United Services Institute and associate professor in astropolitics at Durham University, said he was only able to hazard a guess about the weapon announced by the US.
"I would expect there to be some kind of electronic warfare or radio-jamming platform, possibly, this would be a non-destructive kind of anti-satellite weapon," he told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
Such weaponry already exists on Earth and can disrupt satellite communications, he said. "If you take out the radio links then your satellite is very useless."
Bowen also would not rule out some sort of more disruptive and riskier weaponry, which could create a lot of debris and destruction.
"Less likely would be a kinetic kill vehicle of some sort, so a vehicle that would release a projectile of some sort that could ram into a satellite and destroy it," he said.
"Possibly some sort of close inspection and grappling satellite would be another possibility as well."
But while the weapon placed in orbit appears to be a first, the US - and indeed its Russian and Chinese rivals - have had weapons that can be pointed and shot into space for some time.
In fact in the last 10 years, Russia and China have been doing a lot more manoeuvres in space, known as rendezvous and proximity operations (RPOs) - "buzzing" Western satellites.

"Theoretically, these RPO sats can become hunter-killer satellites by physically colliding with them or by nudging them out of orbit," Dr Rod Thornton, reader in Russian Defence and Security Studies at King's College, London, told the BBC.
Bowen adds that the Chinese have demonstrated "space tug capability", saying: "A vehicle can go up to a satellite, can grapple it and move it into a different orbit."
This, he says, can be a positive development - a way of removing space junk as well as knocking out working satellites.
Thornton says that what Russia lacks in space weaponry and satellites, it makes up for in missile capability.

"The Russians... have ground-based missiles which can be launched into space to strike sats in low Earth orbit. They also have ASAT missiles that can be launched from a great height by aircraft," he says.

"From the Russian point of view they see Nato as having much better and more sats than the Russian military can call up, therefore they have invested heavily in ASATs in order to 'level the battlefield' somewhat."
Thornton adds a sobering thought: "As a last resort, the Russians can also launch nuclear weapons into space and the EPM blast would 'fry' any unhardened sats over a wide expanse."

He says that, having so few satellites, Russia would be the "big winner" in any space war, which would involve "missiles fired up into space, manoeuvring sats designed to nudge/destroy them and ground-based lasers".

articles.title: Satellite image reveals major damage that shut crucial oil pipeline
articles.summary: Experts tell BBC Verify the pipeline's closure could cut oil supplies by as much as 3.6 million barrels per day.

blocks.text: Satellite imagery shows a key oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia has been badly damaged after a strike last week, which experts have told BBC Verify could take more than a month to repair and force oil prices even higher.

The image shows the most significant damage is at a pumping station along the East-West Pipeline, which Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on to export crude oil via the Red Sea rather than through the Strait of Hormuz, where ships have been attacked by Iran and the US during their six-month war.

The Saudi government has accused Iranian-backed militias in Iraq of the pipeline strike, which followed days of renewed missile and drone attacks on south-western Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Houthi group - which is also backed by Iran. Saudi Arabia has retaliated by carrying out strikes on Houthi-controlled areas of western Yemen.
New satellite images also show damage to Saudi Arabia's King Khalid Air Base after a Houthi strike last week.
The Saudi government said on Tuesday it would respond "firmly" to attacks by the Houthis.
While the Houthis have been fighting a long-running civil war against Saudi-backed Yemeni pro-government forces, the group has stepped up its campaign in recent weeks.

It seized control of significant new territory across Yemen's south-western coast last week, including areas overlooking the crucial Bab al-Mandab waterway, strengthening its ability to enforce its declared blockade of Saudi shipping.

articles.title: Imran Khan’s sons accuse Pakistani army chief of vendetta against imprisoned father
articles.summary:
Kasim and Sulaiman Khan tell Guardian they believe ex-PM is being ‘slowly killed’ by harsh treatment, driven by Asim Munir

The sons of Imran Khan have accused Pakistan’s powerful army chief…
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi and Shah Meer Baloch in Islamabad

blocks.text: The sons of Imran Khan have accused Pakistan’s powerful army chief of a “personal vendetta” against the incarcerated former prime minister and expressed fears their father is being “slowly killed” in jail, as international pressure mounts over his prison conditions.

Kasim Khan, 27, and Sulaiman Khan, 29, have become strong advocates for the release of their father, who has been held in Adiala prison in Rawalpindi since his arrest in 2023, and is serving a 14-year sentence on corruption charges.
They have not been allowed to speak to Khan for more than six months and have been prevented from travelling from the UK to Pakistan to lobby for his release.

On Wednesday, the supreme court will rule on a case alleging the Pakistan government has been in contempt of court by denying Khan private hospital treatment for a worsening eye condition and preventing family from visiting him or speaking with him in jail for more than six months, in violation of a court order. Khan is being held in solitary confinement, in a cell alleged to be 6ft by 8ft.

blocks.caption: Imran Khan outside court in Lahore after a hearing in February 2023. Photograph: Mohsin Raza/Reuters

blocks.text: Later this month, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) – the political party Khan founded in 1996, four years after retiring from international cricket – is planning a nationwide march demanding his release.

Speaking to the Guardian from London, Khan’s sons – from his first marriage to Jemima Goldsmith – said they were “deeply, deeply concerned” about their father’s health, and that the conditions he was being kept in amounted to “a form of mental and physical torture”.

“The reality is that he is locked in a tiny 6x8ft cell without human contact,” said Sulaiman. “He hasn’t been allowed new books for months and he’s not been allowed to see or speak to his family or a neutral doctor. He has an eye condition which was neglected for months and has meant he’s probably almost lost sight in one eye.”

blocks.caption: Left to right: Sulaiman Khan, Jemima Khan, Imran Khan’s daughter Tyrian White and Kasim Khan at a film premiere in London in February 2023. Photograph: PA Images/Alamy

blocks.text: Late last month, Sky Sports aired an interview with Khasim and Sulaiman during its coverage of a test match between England and Pakistan. The Pakistan Cricket Board, which has close links to the government and whose chair is also the interior minister, made a formal complaint to Sky Sports after the broadcast and the Pakistani team threatened to refuse to return to the field after the lunch break.

“It shows how out of touch they are with the rest of the world, that they thought they could silence media like they do at home,” Sulaiman said of the complaint. “It just exposed them for the authoritarian regime that they are.”

The UN has said Khan’s prolonged detention violates international law and the UN’s special rapporteur on torture said his solitary confinement and detention conditions could amount to psychological torture.
Sulaiman said the family had been told their father, 73, had also been diagnosed with high blood pressure. “More than anything, we just want to speak to him and make sure he’s OK,” he said.
Khan’s sons said they were particularly concerned that the “cruel” treatment was being driven by a “personal grudge” by Asim Munir, Pakistan’s chief of defence forces and army chief.

blocks.caption: Asim Munir praying after laying a wreath on the martyrs’ monument during a ceremony in Rawalpindi last year. Photograph: AP

blocks.text: When Khan was the prime minister, he unceremoniously demoted Munir, and the bad blood between them was well known. When Munir was made army chief in 2023, the persecution of Khan increased notably.

“It’s very clear this is being driven by personal grudge and that’s one of the reasons he’s being treated so harshly, on the orders of Asim Munir,” said Sulaiman. Munir’s powers expanded over the past year as he established himself as a close ally of Donald Trump, who referred to him as “my favourite field marshal”.

Last month, the supreme court ruled that Khan should be taken to a private hospital for treatment for a blood clot in his retinal vein, believed to have destroyed 85% of the sight in his right eye because of a prolonged lack of medical attention.
Khan was instead taken briefly to a government hospital, where he was given several injections and ruled fit to return to prison, prompting outrage from his family and political party.

“There’s still been no light shed on our father’s real condition from an unbiased, neutral physician,” said Kasim. “We believe they’re trying to slowly kill him in there. Just as soon as there’s less pressure, we are sure they will put even harsher restrictions on him and try to finish him off.
“The one with the real vendetta here is the army chief Asim Munir.”

In a statement, the Pakistan government called the allegations around Khan “fake propaganda” and said he was being kept in adequate conditions, with access to home-cooked food, nuts, bottled water, exercise equipment, family visits and regular medical examinations.
“The government of Pakistan categorically rejects allegations that the convicted prisoner is being subjected to punitive solitary confinement, cruelty or deprivation,” the statement said.

It was widely acknowledged that Khan came to power in 2018 with the backing of Pakistan’s military, widely referred to as the “establishment”, which has long held an oversized role in the country’s governance. Khan had promised to build a “naya Pakistan” (new Pakistan), which would end corruption and follow the rule of law. However, his time in power was plagued by allegations of corruption, press censorship and persecution of his opponents.
He was toppled in 2022 after falling out with his military benefactors. He then began a campaign calling for the generals to be kept out of government.

By 2023, as his accusations against the military grew, Khan turned from alleged persecutor to the persecuted. He was arrested and charged with more than 100 crimes, including alleged corruption and sedition, which he claims are trumped up to keep him out of power.
Despite his toppling and imprisonment, Khan still remains popular. “They want to do everything they can to sideline him and disappear him from public life,” Kasim said.

blocks.caption: Supporters of Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf display a poster of Imran Khan at a rally in February on the second anniversary of the 2024 general elections, which the party alleges were rigged. Photograph: Bilawal Arbab/EPA

blocks.text: Sulaiman said that while it was “clear the establishment think they can get away with it without any kind of repercussions”, it was also evident the government had been rattled by international coverage of Khan’s case.
Khan’s sons said that while they were keen to travel to Pakistan, their visas had still not been granted more than nine months after applying.
They emphasised they had no interest in entering politics in Pakistan or leading Khan’s PTI party in his absence.

“We definitely don’t want to get involved in politics in Pakistan in the long term,” said Sulaiman. “Our father always said that one of the biggest problems with Pakistani politics is this dynastic nepotism; that power’s been held by just two families for the last 40 years. It’s a sign of what’s wrong with the political system in Pakistan.”

Speculation has abounded on whether Khan would strike a deal with the military to secure his release. Khan’s closest aide, Zulfi Bukhari, said: “There is only one deal Khan would ever accept: the restoration of democracy, the rule of law and the people’s mandate in Pakistan. If they’re genuinely willing to do that, then fine – let’s talk.”

Kasim and Sulaiman said they did not believe Khan would give up his politics to secure his release. “He’s a very single-minded person,” said Kasim. “I don’t think there’s a chance that he’d ever give it up.”

articles.title: What would it take to make India’s cities better – and safer?
articles.summary:
After a five-storey building collapsed in Delhi, focus is on how urban areas can adapt to growing populations. Plus, Ahmedabad’s ace newspaper delivery driver goes viral

Recently, I may have…

blocks.text: Recently, I may have saved a woman’s life on the road. Somehow, this was something I had expected to happen.

On that day, I saw a truck leave a construction site with a tangled wire trailing behind. I frantically looked to see what the wire was attached to and spotted the scaffolding a few meters ahead. I shrieked and grabbed the hand of the woman walking in front of me just as the metal pipes came crashing down. We hugged for a brief second, and then walked our separate ways.

Mumbai (pictured top) is a city that is being made every day, and so much of the Bandra-Khar area that I inhabit is never not under construction. Since I moved here from Seoul earlier this year, I have learned to be hypervigilant every time I walk the streets.

I was reminded of that moment last week as news broke about the collapse of a five-storey building in Delhi, which killed seven people. Authorities had flagged safety concerns in the neighbourhood months earlier, the Hindustan Times reported, after 23 people died in a fire at another building.

As the world’s most populous country, India can feel like a place where life can be startlingly cheap, and people die every day in tragedies that could have been prevented. According to analysis of government data by the Times of India, between 2020 and 2004 nearly 33,000 deaths occurred due to building collapses, fires or people falling into pits and maintenance holes.

The collapse in Delhi has prompted questions, once again, about the state of urban infrastructure in India’s biggest cities. At a time when the country is undertaking a rapid infrastructure boom – new airports, high-speed expressways, luxury residential towers– daily life in cities like Delhi, Mumbai or Bengaluru appears to be deteriorating.

Indian cities are not walkable, they rank among the worst for air quality, construction is poorly regulated, seasonal flooding is common and waste management remains under pressure. These challenges are only going to increase; the World Bank expects India’s urban population to double, going up to 951 million, by 2050. More than half of the urban infrastructure the country will need by then has yet to be built, it said.

blocks.caption: The problem with India’s roads begins with on-street parking, believe some experts. Photograph: DB Pictures/Alamy

blocks.text: So, what would it take to make our cities better and safer? The experts I spoke to broadly agreed that Indian cities don’t lack rules as much as the political will and institutional machinery to enforce them.

For infrastructure veteran Vinayak Chatterjee, one solution lies in giving urban local bodies more power. He points to a constitutional amendment from 1992 that was meant to strengthen municipalities and give them greater responsibility over urban planning. “But it remains largely unimplemented – in spirit and will. It is a serious matter that affects the very fabric of our urban existence,” said Chatterjee, founder of the Infravision Foundation.

Rahul Goel, an expert on transportation safety and a professor at the Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi, believes the problem with India’s roads begins with on-street parking. “People are using public space for personal use. Everything becomes better when you remove on-street parking,” he said, arguing that freeing up roads would make pedestrians and cyclists safer, reduce traffic jams and make walking easier.

In other cities in the global south, from Bangkok to Manila to Cape Town, one cannot just park their car on the road to run errands, Goel said. He described it as a governance failure, saying there is a need to create more parking spaces and perhaps have civil defense personnel or municipal workers enforce fines.

“Our streets are self-run,” Goel said. “That’s why they are in complete disarray.” He pointed to the Delhi Metro as an example of a space where people follow rules and things are orderly. “When rules are enforced, people follow them.”

blocks.caption: People vacate buildings marked for demolition in Satya Niketan after the collapse of a five-storey building. Photograph: Vishal Kapoor/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The same gap between rules and enforcement is evident at construction sites.

India has detailed guidelines for construction approvals, including how traffic must be managed, what signage must be put up, and creating paths for pedestrians. But compliance remains a significant problem, says Geetam Tiwari, emeritus professor at Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi. In an audit of construction sites on highways, including bridges, Tiwari and her colleagues found widespread violations. Contractors had a financial incentive to complete projects quickly with payments being tied to the pace of construction, she said, adding that penalties for violations were low enough that it was cheaper to simply pay the fine than make fixes.

For unsafe buildings and unauthorised renovations, Tiwari said, the solution also requires bringing stakeholders together: resident associations, landlords, lessees and local authorities to conduct audits, raise awareness and penalise contractors who violate safety requirements. Actions, she said, that should not wait for the next tragedy.

In the aftermath of the Delhi case, the high court has directed authorities to inspect student accommodations for safety. Building owners have been arrested and several municipal officials in charge of the area have been suspended.

A similar governance deficit shows up when it comes to air pollution, another long-time challenge for Indian cities. Ronak Sutaria, founder and CEO of Respirer Living Sciences, has been working on one aspect of this issue: by developing affordable air-quality monitors for construction sites. Respirer’s air-quality monitors are now installed in 5,000 locations across 10 cities in India, helping authorities identify pollution hotspots. (Some cities, including Mumbai, require construction sites to monitor pollution levels.)

“A number of sites are getting alerts [from authorities] and are taking dust-suppression measures, for instance, to bring down [pollution] levels. So, the entire loop is sort of working,” Sutaria said.

Indian cities continue to grow, but the question is whether governance can keep pace. On that afternoon in Bandra, I recall thinking how lucky the woman and I were not to be grievously injured. But we shouldn’t have to rely on luck to survive.
What else we’re reading about

blocks.caption: Xi Jinping, far right, with Russia’s Vladimir Putin and India’s Narendra Modi at this year’s Brics summit. Photograph: Alexander Kazakov/Sputnik/Kremlin Pool/EPA

blocks.text: New Delhi declaration | The Brics summit held in New Delhi over the weekend adopted a declaration with Iran and the United Arab Emirates agreeing to a late-stage compromise on the language about the war in the Middle East. Chinese president, Xi Jinping, who visited India for the first time in almost seven years, announced that China would helm the group’s presidency for the next year.

Political donations | An investigation by the BBC’s Shubhangi Misra claimed that six unrecognised political parties registered in Gujarat received donations of £132m (Rs 1,700 crore) in 2023-24, higher than the income of national parties excluding the BJP. Despite fielding few candidates and evidence of little political activity, the high amounts expose glaring gaps in oversight of political finances.

Women’s health support | Two south Indian states, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, have recently announced policies aimed at supporting women through perimenopause and menopause. Karnataka plans to introduce a women’s health programme that will integrate menopause into the public health system. Tamil Nadu will assess the physical and mental health needs of perimenopausal women.
after newsletter promotion

Calling all emerging writers | Applications are open for South Asia Speaks, a wonderful platform for emerging writers from the region offering free, year-long mentorship and resources to develop a book-length project. The deadline is 30 September – find out more and apply here.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste

blocks.caption: Poet Parag Pawan’s book.

blocks.text: This week, write and professor Amitava Kumar (@amitavawriter), whose latest book, The Social Life of Trains, explores how railways helped shape India’s national identity, suggests the work of a poet he discovered on Instagram:

“Can I begin with a confession? I have been a professor of literature for more than three decades, but I don’t often understand poems. How lovely it is, then, to discover a poet whose lines are as clear and beautiful as the dawn! Recently, I came across the poems of a young Hindi poet named Parag Pawan. They spoke to me and, more importantly, they spoke to our moment. I immediately sat down to translate them into English.

A series of his poems could be translated as Poems for the Unemployed. One of the poems, sharp and precise, begins with the funny, acerbic lines: ‘On the topic of our unemployment / the prime minister gives speeches / but he doesn’t give us jobs. / He works for eighteen hours / while we believe that asking anyone to work / for more than eight hours / is exploitation.’”
Count it
A number worth knowing

blocks.caption: Umar Khalid, who has spent six years in an Indian jail without trial.

blocks.text: That’s the number of days Umar Khalid has spent in jail since his arrest on 13 September 2020 – without trial. Last week, the student activist wrote a searing account describing the daily drudgery of life in prison, published in The Quint. Earlier this year, in his first interview since being jailed, Khalid told the Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Peterson: “Humanity is a privilege that is not granted to people like me.”
Vibe check

blocks.caption: World’s fastest paper delivery service? Ayan Shaikh at work in Ahmedabad. Photograph: Instagram

blocks.text: As more people read news online, watching Ayan Shaikh (@paperboy_ayan) delivering newspapers with serious swag gave me great joy and some hope. The 22-year-old from Ahmedabad posts videos of it on Instagram, and it’s a feat to watch. Watch his papers swerve, reach gravity-defying heights and land with pinpoint accuracy and tell me his deliveries don’t rival Jasprit Bumrah.

Delivering papers was Shaikh’s first job after he dropped out of school. He spent four years mastering the techniques that would allow him to make faster deliveries to earn more money. The first video, filmed by his friend, had 20m views and a recent one has crossed 128m, more views than many Bollywood stars might command. He starts his day at 4:30am, making 300 deliveries in two hours, before he begins a second shift as a gig worker for quick commerce apps.

“I think people love [the videos] because I do it passionately … from my heart,” he said. “If you do things dedicatedly, anything is possible. It won’t work out once, twice, thrice, but it might on the fourth attempt.”
Get in touch

Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us at thisisindia@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

articles.title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire
articles.summary: The state post service delivers pensions, medicine and letters to people just miles from the front.

blocks.text: Watch: Ukraine's post office innovation helps isolated communities
By
Reporting fromZaporizhzhia oblast
Every morning Igor Smelyansky looks at a vast map of Ukraine on his office wall and decides where he should put his people in harm's way.
His aides provide him with live intelligence about Russian attacks and he deploys his teams, balancing their potential operational success against risk to life or limb.
But Smelyansky is no military commander. He is the head of Ukraine's state postal service, Ukrposhta.
And every day he must decide how far to send his postmen and women into the deadly "kill zone" along the front lines where the threat of drone attack is ever present.
"If it's too dangerous to go today, we won't go," Smelyansky told us. "We'll go tomorrow, or we'll go somewhere else. The key is to be as agile as you can."

Ukrposhta does more than just collect letters and parcels. It pays out pensions in hard cash, it takes payment for utility bills. And it delivers vital food and medicine to people on the margins of society.

As such, it offers a lifeline to millions of poor and elderly Ukrainians living in remote villages where shops are rare and trips to the city are expensive and dangerous. In a vast rural nation wracked by war, Ukrposhta is part of the glue that holds the country together.

blocks.caption: Map of Ukraine showing areas under Russian military control. Territories under Russian control are shaded pink, including Crimea, most of the occupied areas of Donetsk, large parts of Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions, and a continuous belt of territory along the Sea of Azov connecting Crimea to e…

blocks.text: That has made the service a target for Russia - which in recent months has stepped up not only its attacks on postmen and women but also sorting offices and logistical hubs. The Kremlin has claimed strikes like this are retaliation for Ukrainian attacks on Russian online retailers like Wildberries.

Speaking in his imposing Soviet-era office building that overlooks Kyiv's famous Maidan square, Smelyansky said: "If we don't go [to a village], we don't have basic supply. We don't have food. We don't have medicine. People will struggle. If we do go, they may delay a decision to evacuate from the areas they probably should have evacuated."
There are many risks. If a post van turns up unannounced, a crowd can form, creating a target for an opportunistic Russian drone operator. But if they call ahead, information could leak.
"Is it a danger?" Smelyansky said. "Absolutely. Because there are Russian sympathisers who can give them the location of the truck that's coming."

blocks.caption: Igor Smelyansky stands in his blue Ukrposhta shirt and smiles at the camera. He has greying dark hair, and wears stubble with a smile

blocks.text: BBC
By attacking Ukrposhta, you put pressure on people… who are depending on the truck coming in

blocks.caption: "By attacking Ukrposhta, you put pressure on people… who are depending on the truck coming in", Source: Igor Smelyansky, Source description: Head of Ukrposhta, Image: Igor Smelyansky stands in his blue Ukrposhta shirt and smiles at the camera. He has greying dark hair, and wears stubble with a smile

blocks.text: If Smelyansky chooses not to send a van in, he faces criticism. "You get messages from people from those villages: 'You betrayed us. You didn't come...' But if I go, I may risk the life of the driver."

Smelyansky says Russia is deliberately targeting his staff because of the vital role they play shoring up Ukraine's resilience, helping people stay alive in their homes through the fighting and bitter winters.
"It's not an accident, it's deliberate," he said. "By attacking Ukrposhta, you put pressure on people… who are depending on the truck coming in." Russia denies targeting civilians.
Since 2022, hundreds of Ukrposhta branches and vehicles have been hit, and more than 50 staff have lost their lives, either on the frontline or on their rounds, according to Ukrposhta.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A file photo of a Ukrposhta post office damaged during strikes in Kyiv in April

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
A file photo of a Ukrposhta post office damaged during strikes in Kyiv in April
We travelled with Kateryna Marynych, a 38-year-old postmistress, near Zaporizhzhia - a city not too far from the southern frontlines.

She lost her home and her husband during the full-scale invasion, and came to the area to rebuild her life. She ran the post office in the village of Lukasheve for two years until it was destroyed in March by a Russian drone, targeting soldiers working nearby.
After her van drew up, a steady queue of elderly folk formed. She sat in the front passenger seat, window open, handing out cash, taking payments.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ukraine's post office provides a vital lifeline for people near the front, delivering pensions and medicine

blocks.text: Ukraine's post office provides a vital lifeline for people near the front, delivering pensions and medicine

One customer, Nadiia, said she was grateful: "It's a long way for us to travel to Zaporizhzhia. Especially now, at a time when there are attacks all around us. The fact that they come here is really nice."

Oleksandrivna, 77, arrived wearing a purple dressing gown, walking with a crutch. When I asked her where she would be without Kateryna, she replied: "We would be stuffed! I am just out of hospital after a stroke. Where could I go for my medicine?"

But Mykola, 64, pointed to another service the post office provides to a largely elderly population. "It is very important," he said. "It's one of the few joys of the month: you come out, have a chat with people, collect your pension, and go home."
For many people in remote communities, Kateryna can be their last link with the Ukrainian state.

She says she hopes her customers are proud of her. "They love me, they need me," she said. "They are waiting for me. Sometimes they call me, especially after attacks on Zaporizhzhia and ask me how I am. We are like a big family. My attitude towards them is like a grandmother or grandfather."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Kateryna Marynych has lost her home and her husband in this war - now, she's also lost her post office

blocks.text: Kateryna Marynych has lost her home and her husband in this war - now, she's also lost her post office

The attacks on Ukrposhta form part of Russia's wider escalation of its war on Ukraine, stepping up fast drone attacks on civilian infrastructure including business infrastructure, energy facilities, transport networks and border posts. Analysts say that as Russia's invasion stagnates on the battlefield in the east, it is looking for other ways of putting pressure on Kyiv.

For safety, Kateryna always travels with her partner, Slava, who drives. While she sorts the cash, he works from the back of the van, taking and receiving parcels, delivering food and water. He also carries a side-arm in a holster, for personal protection; these vans carry a lot of cash.

Both wear body armour when close to the front line. And they have an antenna in the van that shows them the location of the small first-person-view drones that render the frontline so deadly. They have seen drones from the car but luckily have not yet been hit.
She accepted her job was dangerous but would never change it. "It is my work," she said. "If I can't, who will do my job?"
Ukraine's defence comes in many forms - and it's not always delivered at the barrel of a gun.
Additional reporting by Mariana Matveichuk

articles.title: Water levels at San Roque Dam, Pangasinan rivers remain under close watch
articles.summary: PANGASINAN---San Roque dam continued to release water Monday morning as several rivers in Pangasinan remained above normal levels, including one that remained above the critical level. As of 5 a.m.…

blocks.text: (Photo via Liezle Inigo)
PANGASINAN---San Roque dam continued to release water Monday morning as several rivers in Pangasinan remained above normal levels, including one that remained above the critical level.
As of 5 a.m. on Sept. 7, the dam’s water level was at 279.79 meters above sea level (masl), with an inflow of 338 cubic meters per second (cms) and a combined outflow of 746 cms.
Two gates were opened at the dam. Gate No. 2A was opened to 1.0 meter, while Gate No. 2B was opened to 1.5 meters. The Low Level Outlet was also releasing 125 cms.
The elevated discharge comes as authorities continue to monitor river conditions downstream, particularly communities located near waterways and flood-prone areas.

At 6 a.m., the Marusay River in Calasiao was above the critical level, while the Sinucalan River in Sta. Barbara, Pantal River in Dagupan City, and Agno/Bañaga River in Bugallon were above normal levels.
The Camiling River in Camiling, Tarlac was at normal level. No level reading was indicated in the monitoring report for the Bued/Cayanga River in San Fabian and Balingcaguing River in Mabini.
Residents near rivers and low-lying communities are urged to remain alert, monitor advisories, and follow evacuation or other safety directives when issued.

articles.title: 'Takot yan?': VP Duterte doesn't talk, act like someone who is in fear, says Adiong
articles.summary: House Assistant Majority Lanao del Sur 1st district Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong says Vice President Sara Duterte doesn't appear to be fearing for her life, as she has claimed, based on her known demeanor.…

blocks.text: House Assistant Majority Lanao del Sur 1st district Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong says Vice President Sara Duterte doesn't appear to be fearing for her life, as she has claimed, based on her known demeanor.

This, as Adiong chided Duterte for playing the victim card after being issued an arrest warrant for three counts of grave threats, which stemmed from claims of planning to assassinate President Marcos and other members of the First Family.
The Vice President’s ordeal prompted her to declare over the weekend, "I do not feel safe. Pakiramdam ko papatayin nila [pulis] ako (I feel the police is out to kill me).
"I have documented threats and harrassment since 2023. I fear for my children. I do not feel they are safe if I am with them," she also said.
But Adiong doesn't buy Duterte’s fearful facade one bit.
“Kung titignan niyo, hindi po ito yung taong takot (If you look at her, she does not appear to be someone who is afraid). Actually, in fact, it’s the other way around,” he said.

He also pointed to Duterte’s previous public statements that he said appeared to invoke violence against President Marcos, as well as her continued requests for travel clearance, as inconsistent with her claim that she had been under threat since 2023.

“Siya yung nagbibigay ng mga statement na nagpapahiwatig ng violence against the President, pupugutan ng ulo (She was the one making statements suggesting violence against the President, including that he would be beheaded)... So it’s not an indication of someone who’s been receiving threats,” he said.
These notwithstanding, Adiong stressed that any threat against Duterte should be taken seriously and properly investigated by authorities.
He said the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) had given her an opportunity to submit information about the threats she claimed to have received, but no such information had been provided.

“They were given the chance. They were called, invited by the NBI na isubmit po nila kung ano po yung threats na ... natatanggap nila (They were called and invited by the NBI to submit information about the threats they had received.
“Pero hanggang ngayon, wala po silang naibibigay (But until now, they have not provided anything)," Adiong noted.

Seemingly referring to Duterte’s subsequent criticisms on the court and police, the Mindanao congressman stressed that public officials should respect the courts and the law even when proceedings or their outcomes are unfavorable to them.

“In this case, whether or not favorable sa’yo, kailangan mo talaga as an elected official to prove to the people that we have our laws, we have to respect our laws, and only through our laws and through our courts can we defend ourselves."

(In this case, whether or not it is favorable to you, as an elected official you have to prove to the people that we have laws, that we have to respect them, and that only through our laws and courts can we defend ourselves.)
The law applies to everyone

For Adiong, the grave threats case demonstrates that the law applies equally to everyone regardless of status or position, rejecting claims from Duterte’s camp and supporters that the proceedings constitute political persecution.

“Ito pong nangyayari ngayon, ito po ang nagpapatunay na gumugulong po ang hustisya sa ating bansa. Wala pong tinitingnan na status or posisyon ng isang tao pagdating sa pananagutan at sa pag-implement ng mga patakaran o ating batas,” he said.

(What is happening now proves that justice is taking its course in our country. No one’s status or position is considered when it comes to accountability and the implementation of our rules and laws.)
He said the criminal case should also be distinguished from Duterte’s ongoing impeachment proceedings.
“Magkaiba naman po yung mga hukom na tumatayo dito at yung magiging verdict po ay magkaiba (The judges handling these cases are different, and the verdicts will also be different)."

articles.title: DSWD flags bogus UPLIFT aid for students
articles.summary: The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) on Monday, Sept. 7, flagged social media posts offering supposed educational assistance to students under the Unified Package for Livelihood,…

blocks.text: The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) on Monday, Sept. 7, flagged social media posts offering supposed educational assistance to students under the Unified Package for Livelihood, Industry, Food, and Transport (UPLIFT) Assistance.

The posts claim that the government is giving ₱2,000 to elementary students, ₱3,000 to junior high school students, ₱5,000 to senior high school students, and ₱8,000 to college students under the program.
DSWD Assistant Secretary and spokesperson Irene Dumlao said educational assistance is not part of UPLIFT.

“Paalala po natin sa ating mga kababayan na walang educational assistance sa ilalim po ng ating UPLIFT Assistance. Ito pong assistance na ito ay tulong maibsan ang epekto ng pagtaas ng presyo ng mga bilihin (We remind our fellow Filipinos that there is no educational assistance under UPLIFT Assistance. This assistance is intended to help ease the impact of rising prices of goods),” Dumlao said.
The posts also direct users to registration links, which the DSWD said are unauthorized.
Dumlao said there is no need to register for UPLIFT because its beneficiaries have already been identified using the latest Community-Based Monitoring System (CBMS) data.

“Mangyaring huwag po i-click ang inyong mga makikitang link na nagsasabing maaari kayong magparehistro dahil scam po ito (Please do not click on links claiming that you can register because these are scams),” she added.
Qualified beneficiaries under Groups 2 and 3 of the UPLIFT program receive ₱2,000 per month until December.

UPLIFT Assistance is among the Marcos administration’s initiatives to help poor, near-poor, and low-income Filipinos cope with the economic impact of the energy emergency brought about by the geopolitical conflict in the Middle East.
The public may verify information on UPLIFT Assistance and other DSWD programs through the Department’s official social media pages or the DSWD Online Grievance Portal.

articles.title: Alcantara, partner rule doubles tilt in Thailand
articles.summary: Francis Casey Alcantara and Thai Pawit Sornlaksup displayed nerves of steel and hacked out a 7-6 (4), 5-7, 10-8 victory over Indian pair Manish Sureshkumar and Maan Kesharwani to reign supreme in the…

blocks.text: At A Glance

items: Francis Casey Alcantara and Thai Pawit Sornlaksup displayed nerves of steel and hacked out a 7-6 (4), 5-7, 10-8 victory over Indian pair Manish Sureshkumar and Maan Kesharwani to reign supreme in the ITF M15 Nonthaburi in Thailand over the weekend.

blocks.text: (Francis Casey Alcantara / Facebook / Impact )

Francis Casey Alcantara and Thai Pawit Sornlaksup displayed nerves of steel and hacked out a 7-6 (4), 5-7, 10-8 victory over Indian pair Manish Sureshkumar and Maan Kesharwani to reign supreme in the ITF M15 Nonthaburi in Thailand over the weekend.
Alcantara, 34, and Sornlaksup recovered from a second-set stumble and held their ground by protecting their 8-3 advantage to fend of their persistent Indian rivals.
“Thank you Pawit Sornlaksup for an incredible week and for carrying me through some tough matches!” Alcantara wrote on social media.
“It was a pleasure sharing the court with you bro! Special thanks to Coach Coach Carlo Core Tennis Academy BKK for always being there and helping me out again this week,” he added.
Prior to their title victory, Alcantara and Sornlaksup outlasted locals Thantub Suksumrarn and Tanapatt Nirundorn (7-5, 7-5) in the opening round.

They followed it up with a gritty 6-2, 4-6, 11-9 quarters victory over Japanese Shu Muto and Ko Suzuki to book their ticket to the semifinals, where they ultimately pulled off a 1-6, 6-4, 10-4 triumph against Americans Hugo Hashimoto and Michael Blando.
The tournament serves as a training ground for Alcantara, who will be competing in the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 late this month.

articles.title: Ely Buendia, Chito Miranda sell out Dubai concert amid Middle East tensions
articles.summary: Ongoing tensions across the Middle East have cast a shadow over the region’s live entertainment business, with uncertainty surrounding travel, consumer spending and large-scale public events making…

blocks.text: Ongoing tensions across the Middle East have cast a shadow over the region’s live entertainment business, with uncertainty surrounding travel, consumer spending and large-scale public events making concert planning a more complicated proposition.
And yet, some acts continue to defy the odds, demonstrating that music can be more than entertainment in uncertain times.
Ely Buendia and Chito Miranda were among those artists
The two brought OPM nostalgia to Dubai on Aug. 30, performing to a sold-out Coca-Cola Arena.
For the UAE’s Filipino community, the show also offered something beyond nostalgia: a chance to reconnect with home through live music at a time when the region remains unsettled.

Buendia, best known as the former frontman of Eraserheads, and Miranda, lead vocalist of Parokya ni Edgar, represent different eras of Philippine rock but share a deep connection with Filipino audiences.
The concert was presented by Tiana Entertainment Inc., headed by founder and CEO Bojie Yangco, who has worked in live entertainment for more than two decades.

The company has mounted Filipino concerts in markets including the U.S., Canada, Australia, the Middle East and Kazakhstan, with artists such as Rivermaya, SB19, Ben&Ben, Buendia and Miranda among its previous projects.

articles.title: Former UK PM Cameron keynotes 27th World Knowledge Forum
articles.summary: SEOUL - Former Prime Minister of the United Kingdom David Cameron will lead the opening of the 27th World Knowledge Forum (WKF) today, Sept. 8, at the Jangchung Arena here under the theme "The…

blocks.text: SEOUL - Former Prime Minister of the United Kingdom David Cameron will lead the opening of the 27th World Knowledge Forum (WKF) today, Sept. 8, at the Jangchung Arena here under the theme "The Promethean Moment: Architecting the Co-Intelligence Order."

Against the backdrop of profound discussions on the thoughtful coexistence of humanity and Artificial Intelligence (AI), Cameron, the 75th Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, will deliver his keynote address on "A New Order of Co-intelligence in the Age of AI."
Cameron is expected to draw from his experience in reviving the British economy through deregulatory and structural reforms following the 2008 global financial crisis.
He will offer strategic insights on the leadership required to navigate today's compounding crises defined by the AI revolution and heightened geopolitical uncertainty.

Also joining the roster of speakers in this year’s iteration of the WKF are Go Negosyo founder and Association of Southeast Asian Nations-Business Advisory Council (ASEAN-BAC) Chairman Jose Ma. Concepcion III who will also receive the ASEAN Entrepreneurs Award together with Don Lam, CEO of VinaCapital.

Other speakers are Cho Jung-sik, Speaker of the National Assembly, former Prime Minister of Denmark Helle Thorning-Schmidt, former Japanese Prime Minister Ishiba Shigeru, and former New York City Mayor Eric Adams.
This year's forum will bring together close to 70,000 participants and 6,303 world-renowned speakers from 86 countries to share fresh insights for humanity as we enter the era of AI.

Dr. Chang Dae-whan, WKF founder and chairman of the Maekyung Media, said the 27th World Knowledge Forum is being held at a critical juncture, as the established order driving global economic growth collapses and protectionism and geopolitical tensions intensify.
“Confronting low growth and unexpected leadership changes, South Korea urgently requires comprehensive innovation and bold challenges across all sectors.”
“In particular, rapid technological advancements led by AI are reshaping industry and politics, throwing humanity into a sweeping transformation,” Chang said.

He added that while major powers invest astronomical sums in technologies like semiconductors, quantum computing, and robotics, concerns are mounting over winner-takes-all monopolies and job displacement, further intensifying social conflicts.
To break through these simultaneous crises, Chang said Maeil Business Newspaper chose this year's main theme: “The Promethean Moment: Architecting the Co-Intelligence Order.”

“The mythical ‘Promethean Moment’ signifies a historical turning point when humanity received ' fire '—a revolutionary tool that drove civilization forward, yet acted as a double-edged sword if left uncontrolled,” he said.
“Likewise, we hope humanity can overcome this civilizational upheaval brought by AI with wisdom, ultimately architecting a new order where technology and humanity coexist,” Chang added.

Prominent speakers at previous WKFs have included state leaders such as George W. Bush, the 43rd President of the United States; Theresa May, the 76th Prime Minister of the United Kingdom; Nicolas Sarkozy, the 23rd President of the French Republic; and Gerhard Schrfder, the 7th Chancellor of Germany. Presidents of international organizations have also participated, including Jim Yong Kim, the 12th President of the World Bank. Founders and CEOs such as Bill Gates, Co-founder of Microsoft Corporation; Larry Ellison, Chairman and CEO of Oracle Corporation; John L. Hennessy, Chairman of Alphabet; and George Soros, Chairman of Soros Fund Management, have graced the forum. Scholars including Larry Summers, Paul Krugman, Michael Porter, and Gregory Mankiw have also addressed the forum.

articles.title: Government calamity spending surges 35% at end-August as disasters strike
articles.summary: Amid recent calamities, government disaster spending has accelerated rapidly, with total releases from the calamity fund climbing to ₱14 billion at end-August to support response and reconstruction…

blocks.text: Amid recent calamities, government disaster spending has accelerated rapidly, with total releases from the calamity fund climbing to ₱14 billion at end-August to support response and reconstruction requirements nationwide.

Data from the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) showed that cumulative end-August releases jumped by 35.3 percent from the end-July total of ₱10.4 billion. As of Aug. 31, the available balance of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Fund (NDRRMF) stood at ₱26.1 billion.

This total is drawn from a ₱40.2 billion budget for fiscal year 2026—consisting of ₱23.5 billion for the NDRRM Program (NDRRMP), ₱15.3 billion for the Disaster Rehabilitation and Reconstruction Assistance Program (DRRAP) for local government units, and ₱1 billion for the People’s Survival Fund (PSF)—supplemented by ₱322.9 million in continuing appropriations from 2025.

To date, all disbursements have been sourced exclusively from the NDRRMP. The bulk, totaling ₱12.9 billion, was directed toward Quick Response Fund (QRF) augmentations for immediate relief and rehabilitation. Meanwhile, ₱1.1 billion was released for specific rehabilitation and logistics projects approved by the Office of the President (OP).
While the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) was previously the sole recipient of QRF augmentations, several other national agencies have now received standby funds.

The DSWD remains the largest recipient, drawing ₱11.4 billion in total QRF replenishments across six tranches: ₱2 billion in February, ₱1.9 billion in March, ₱2 billion in April, ₱1.7 billion in June, ₱2 billion in July, and ₱1.8 billion in August.
Among other agencies receiving emergency funds, the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) received ₱1.2 billion in August for its first QRF replenishment of the year.

The Department of National Defense (DND) received ₱300 million in July for the Office of Civil Defense (OCD) QRF, while the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) received ₱50 million in July for the Philippine National Police (PNP) QRF.

Apart from emergency relief, the ₱1.1 billion approved by the OP for targeted resilience projects includes ₱650 million for the DPWH to retrofit and strengthen the San Juanico Bridge in Region VIII, ₱385.1 million for the DND-OCD’s NDRRMC Integrated Logistics Hub at Lumbia Airport, and ₱44.8 million for DSWD command center repairs in Clark and rescue vehicle procurement.

Following these releases, the NDRRMP holds an available balance of ₱9.5 billion. When combined with the untouched DRRAP at ₱15.3 billion and the total PSF at ₱1.3 billion, the government retains ₱26.1 billion to address disaster-related and climate-mitigation requirements for the remaining four months of the year.
